This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of function space known as the spectral Barron space, we establish that the convergence rate of the generalization error is not influenced by the dimensionality $d$. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of this premise through a new estimate that demonstrates the ground state's smoothness in the specified function space, achieved through a proof utilizing a fixed-point approach grounded in the Krein-Rutman theorem. As a complementary contribution, we derive an upper limit on the smoothness norm, which provides an alternative perspective and serves as a functional counterpart to recent results obtained through a differential equation-based method. An implementation of the proposed approach is also successfully applied to the computation of two-electron images. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of this method for solving complex electronic structure problems. The analytical generalization error bounds obtained in this study are the first to consider both the training sample size and the dimensionality when analyzing the generalization performance of neural networks for PDEs and their associated PDE-based models. Moreover, the method is unconditionally stable, unconditionally convergent and capable of being optimized through sample efficiency by means of regularization, which complements the recent results obtained in the paper by Jacob, Ring and Zhou. Finally, the precision and robustness of the method are further validated through a variety of benchmark results on electron pairs, which outperform the current state-of-the-art methods in the field. A dataset consisting of 225 neurons, along with the associated morphology, was used to build a predictive model, which was then compared to existing models based on two behaviors, chemotaxis and locomotion, resulting in the identification of key morphological features that contribute to these actions. These findings reveal the potential for additional research on modeling neuronal populations using Regenerative Neural Networks, an area of active investigation. Given the simplicity of this model's architecture yet impressive performance, there is potential for applying similar approaches to more demanding brain functions, potentially paving the way for the development of innovative brain-function replicating AI systems. A major limitation of this research is the relatively small dataset, and potential biases, which may necessitate the use of more advanced techniques, such as transfer learning. Ultimately, the thrill of failure provides valuable lessons that can be applied to more broadly applicable projects. Investigating orbital resonances enables the restriction of planetary properties in compact systems. The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five proposed to be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, necessitates the analysis of its planets' potential resonant behavior. By using existing parameters in N-body simulations, our analysis confirms that nearly all simulations (99.2%) produce a chain of 3:2 resonances; however, fewer (11%) demonstrate a five-planet resonance chain. We successfully employ resonances to confine the orbital periods and masses of the planets. We examine the likelihood of this system forming in situ and through disk migration, as well as explore the potential planetary compositions using a computational planet structure model. Our results suggest the possibility of a habitable zone that could host Earth-like planets and offer insights into the evolution of this resonant system. Additionally, our analysis suggests a significant discrepancy between the ages of the planets and the star, prompting the possibility of tandem disk accretion models to explain the orbital periods and masses of the planets, particularly the outer two. However, the exact formation mechanisms of this system remain subject to interpretation. By extending the scope of orbital analysis to other systems, it may be possible to develop a more cohesive theory of planetary formation and evolution, particularly in multi-planet systems exhibiting orbital resonances. Audification is a straightforward way to turn oscillatory data into audio, retaining all the original information but potentially making magnetospheric wave observations go by too fast to fully grasp. Consequently, audio scaling techniques used in music have been adapted and tested for ULF wave data, with a discussion that culminates in recommendations for researchers looking to turn these waves into an audible format and an examination of the potential scientific and educational benefits of these novel methods. The benefits of these audio representations extend beyond enhanced data interpretation, aiming to complement traditional statistical analysis strategies and even facilitate new magnetospheric science outputs. As a result, audio representations should be viewed as a dynamic form of data visualization that can reach a wider audience than traditional visualizations but also carries a risk of being perceived as entertainment format rather than a scientific tool. In the era of artificial intelligence, computational advancements in text analysis are crucial. Multiple systems have been created to process text across various languages. Despite the considerable advancements, these systems still struggle with text comprehension, essentially treating text as data rather than knowledge. We introduce a novel text representation framework inspired by human memory, acknowledging that text is declarative and would benefit from structural organization to facilitate efficient computation. We utilize long-term episodic memory to store text information accumulated over time, maintaining it in an organized manner, eliminating redundancy, and retaining temporal relationships. To facilitate understanding of individual words, we apply Wordnet, simulating semantic memory. Experimental outcomes of episodic memory operations and the evolution of our knowledge framework are presented. We demonstrate the potential of this framework in syntactic understanding by employing it for part-of-speech tagging. We believe that this system can serve as a foundation for further work in text comprehension. A small-step operational semantics in a programming language breaks down computations into discrete, indivisible steps, directly reflecting how the language is implemented.  A previous semantics of GP 2 is incomplete because its loop and branching commands utilize big-step operations.  This paper presents an accurate small-step operational semantics for GP 2, effectively capturing the nature of divergent computations.  Achieving small-step definitions for all GP 2 commands requires integrating a host graph stack and associated operations into the transition relation.  It has been shown that this new semantics does not block computations and satisfies the finite nondeterminism property.  It has also been found that GP 2's old semantics does not possess these properties and fails to reflect actual machine behavior.  Equivalently, a small-step semantics that avoids the graph stack is developed, but it introduces a potentially infinite number of steps.  It has been shown however that GP 2 still engages in infinite and undetermined computations even with the graph stack semantics.  This raises a concern about a previously established theorem stating that highly configurable and small and large scale verifications can reach consistency.  This concern stems from the fact that GP 2's behavior is inconsistent with its intended specifications.  It has also been found that the program verifier itself suffers from a similar behavior as a consequence.  This concern raises further questions about the potential issues affecting other programs or data models that have been verified using this approach. This concern further raises an associated issue of crisis management that could arise in such a scenario. This has the potential to further establish a more reliable and trustworthy program verifier. A function from natural numbers to natural numbers is considered near-exponential if it's confined by two growth patterns: one growing and the other shrinking, both following the form 2 raised to a power of n times a constant greater than 0. In this paper, techniques are developed to detect a unique type of growth in groups that interact with root trees, characterized by their rate exceeding the exponential rate. Specifically, this near-exponential growth is proven in specific groups known as branch groups. It is also established that certain p-groups exhibit an even faster rate, exceeding the super-exponential growth for p values 5 or greater. Lastly, examples of infinite groups exhibiting linear, exponential, super-exponential, near-exponential and near-linear growth are provided, along with examples of infinite p-groups showcasing various rates of growth. These examples highlight various behaviors and outcomes when applying the methods to different groups. Interestingly, this near-exponential growth behavior doesn't seem to be detectable using established classical invariance properties such as finiteness, or more complex properties like residually finite or ascending linkability. In fact, it's observed that all branch groups exhibit a unique combination of properties, including residually finite and non-ascending linkability, while maintaining near-exponential growth. Ultimately, this study seeks to classify groups based on their growth patterns, and provides recommendations for future research in this area. The recommendations include refining and expanding existing classification theorems, and exploring more complex properties that may be linked to growth patterns in groups. It also includes a discussion on why certain properties, finiteness in particular, may be insufficient for detecting growth patterns in groups, and how this might be related to the work of M. Capps and T. Clements on the f-growth phenomenon. Furthermore, it includes a list of open problems and suggestions for future research in this area. The paper includes 4 figures illustrating root trees and a figure illustrating the growth patterns in groups, and provides thorough background information on the necessary mathematical concepts, including a detailed review of the necessary data on branch groups. The paper includes a list of references covering various areas of group theory, root systems, and growth patterns in groups, and also includes two appendices that provide a detailed analysis of why certain groups fail to exhibit near-exponential growth. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated semigroup directly. Notably, we show that under these connectivity conditions, stability is guaranteed even in the absence of elasticity along the edges. Additionally, we develop a method for approximating the boundary operator's spectral characteristics through connection to a finite non-homogeneous Laplace problem on a compact domain. Lastly, using this boundary operator's properties and connection to a associated finite non-homogeneous Laplace problem on a compact domain, we establish the well-posedness of the associated system through a method of extension along with various estimates and convergence results. The findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the system's behavior and its quantitative characteristics. Predictions for nuclear masses are achieved through Bayesian neural networks by first understanding the mass surface of even-even nuclei and then considering the relationship between these nuclei and their neighboring nuclei in terms of correlation energies. By integrating known physics into various advanced mass models and fine-tuning the design of neural networks, a proposed Bayesian machine learning mass model was found to have a high accuracy of 84 keV, meeting the 100 keV accuracy threshold observed in experimentally confirmed regions. Moreover, this model also evaluates mass prediction uncertainties accurately. Uncertainty levels increase about 50 keV along each isotopic chain as it approaches unknown regions. In the confirmed area, shell structures were well-represented and in unknown regions several notable features were identified including new magic numbers around N = 40, a robust N = 82 shell, a reduced N = 126 shell, and distinct separation energies at N = 104. In addition, uncertainty levels increase about 50 keV along each isotopic chain as it approaches unknown regions. This model is made available for research purposes at https://massml.github.com. Superconducting qubit performance is constrained by dielectric loss. Experimental evidence sets upper limits on dielectric loss tangents, approximately $100$ parts-per-billion, however this information comes from fabricated devices with multiple sources of loss.  Our technique allows us to isolate and analyze bulk dielectric loss with an accuracy of $5$ parts-per-billion by using the 'dielectric dipper,' which measures dielectric loss by varying its participation in a high-quality microwave cavity.  The dielectric dipper allows us to test low-power dielectric properties at low temperatures without the need for further fabrication, making it easier to compare different materials and processing techniques.  Our initial experiment using EFG sapphire found that the bulk dielectric loss is $62(7) \times 10^{-9}$, with an additional loss of $12(2) \times 10^{-4}$ occurring at the substrate interface.  For a typical qubit this means the bulk dielectric loss would be the primary limiting factor in devices of low loss interface combinations, while being largely overcome in devices of higher loss interface combinations.  Our technique was then applied to HEMEX sapphire, where we found that the bulk dielectric loss was $213(16) \times 10^{-9}$.  Since the bulk dielectric loss of HEMEX sapphire is significantly higher than that of EFG sapphire, it suggests that the bulk dielectric loss of EFG sapphire can be further reduced, potentially making it sufficient for supporting multiple high-performance qubits.  Our technique is set to significantly contribute to the development of large scale, highly reliable quantum computers by identifying and addressing critical material loss limitations.  An expansion of the technique to support bulk analysis of superconducting materials, including the use of a'metallic dipper,' is also presented.  Our initial scan of bulk titanium using the metallic dipper found that the bulk dielectric loss was $110(10) \times 10^{-9}$, and the additional loss of $7.5(2) \times 10^{-4}$ occurring at the interface.  While the bulk dielectric loss of titanium is within the range that could be overcome in certain qubit designs, it suggests that further processing techniques should be sought after to reduce the dielectric loss of titanium.  Our technique is set to significantly contribute to the development of highly reliable quantum computers by identifying and addressing critical material loss limitations.  An investigation into the long term stability of the dielectric dipper was also conducted

A moving dielectric medium can alter the path of light traveling through it, a phenomenon termed the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect. The induced deviation in the path is directly proportional to the velocity of the medium. Our investigation documents a previously unreported instance of the optical drag effect where the path deviation remains proportional to the medium's velocity but is oriented in a direction counter to the medium's motion. To observe this anomalous effect, we conducted an optical drag experiment under the conditions of electromagnetic transparency and monitored the shift from typical optical drag to zero drag and ultimately the anomalous effect through adjustments to two-photon detuning. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the optical drag effect is contingent on considerations of general relativity. Its application holds significant potential for the realization of optical drag-based measurements that surpass standard metrological standards. Furthermore, this phenomenon presents an optical analogy to the Sagnac effect, facilitating an understanding of the anomalous optical drag effect using an analysis inspired by relativistic effects, as well as providing avenues for future research into a possible optical Sagnac balance that surpasses conventional standards. This long-sought optical Sagnac balance holds immense promise for meeting the goals of the re-implementation of the meter and the re-definition of the second with accuracies that exceed current limits. An existing optical Sagnac balance has already achieved an uncertainty of $1\times10^{-20}$, a threshold that is close to achieving the goals of the re-implementation and re-definition of the unit. An advancement to this balance remains within reach as a high-precision tool for the field of physics and beyond. Moreover, beyond the realm of optics, we have discovered a possibility of realizing a relativistic drag effect, which could contribute to an enhancement of the precision in time and length measurements and also open new avenues in the field of gravitational red-shift spectroscopy by allowing the measurement of red-shift shift shifts. This shift in the field of red-shift spectroscopy can be measured to the level of parts per hundred million, a threshold that is two orders of magnitude higher than current limits. Furthermore, beyond the realm of optics and gravitational red-shift spectroscopy, we are proposing a concept for the development of precision temporal sideband spectroscopy, a technique that allows for the manipulation of thermal noise using frequency modulation. By employing sideband spectroscopy, we are able to achieve a level of precision in time measurements that is two orders of magnitude higher than current limits to the time, a threshold that is currently capped at $4\times10^{-17}$.

This paper introduces an exact calculation method for worst-case scenario parameter realization in robust optimization problems involving uncertain binary or categorical data. Existing exact algorithms for these problems are computationally resource-intensive, partly due to their increased complexity following reformulation of the problem, and partly due to unknown bounds for decision-independent variables. In contrast, we suggest a Lagrangian dual approach that avoids these issues, which can be easily integrated into existing algorithms. This method is particularly tailored to scenarios where binary parameters activate or deactivate constraints, which is commonly encountered in various applications. We discuss possible extensions to scenarios with limited recourse or integer variables and provide numerical results demonstrating notable computational advantages over existing methods. Furthermore, we propose several enhancement strategies to balance computational efficiency and optimality-guarantee accuracy. Finally, we apply our proposed algorithm to a supply chain management problem and use it to achieve an upper bound on the optimal value of the robust formulation. Our results show that this approach is viable for solving real-world two-stage robust optimization problems involving binary uncertainties. In particular, for a small to medium-sized set of binary uncertainties with around 20 variables, our algorithm exhibits a substantial 38% speedup over existing methods, whereas for problems with around 70 or more binary variables, the average reduction in computational time is as much as 94%. Our algorithm's running time for problem instances with ten layers of hierarchical dependencies ranged from a few seconds to at most 24 seconds, which is an average speedup of two to three orders of magnitude. In contrast, existing methods took anywhere from a few minutes to up to 17 hours to complete, which is an average improvement of three to six orders of magnitude. This research outlines a multi-faceted, multi-distributed dataset referred to as the H4M Dataset. This dataset comprises of four distinct layers: facilities for entertainment, traffic conditions, social media activity, and real estate listings. The H4M Dataset is designed to facilitate research on high-density urban areas, with a specific focus on Beijing. This dataset comprises of 1026 districts, 4564 points of interest, 2254 road segments, and 78,921 residential areas. This research presents a methodology for gathering this information, its associated implications, and showcases its utility through the presentation of several illustrative use cases. The H4M Dataset is made publicly available through the option to bid on a crowdsourcing platform. This research has garnered significant attention, with over 800,000 visitors, and has inspired numerous projects that utilize and contribute to this dataset following a crowdsourced model. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, these problems typically have such a vast number of possible solutions that it becomes impossible to evaluate them thoroughly due to the high dimensionality. Additionally, partial information, uncertainties and nonlinearity complicate the process even further. Based on existing mathematical frameworks by Berber (Advances in Linear Algebra and Operator Theory, 2020) and Leis et al. (Automatica, 2020), we provide a concise overview of applicable numerical methods to tackle optimization challenges. A global, continuous approach to optimization is demonstrated using these methods, illustrated through a real-world application: ventilator allocation during the COVID-19 pandemic. This work offers a comprehensive overview of optimization techniques paired with direct transcription and showcases their application in a critical societal issue. A crucial challenge in the study of rarefied gas dynamics lies in determining the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation efficiently. The conventional iteration method often requires an unacceptably large number of computations, at least on the order of O(10^4) iterations. In their latest study, the authors initiate the development of a fast iterative method for the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation. By combining accelerated iterative methods for solving linear systems, such as GMRES, with a refined iterative approach for constructing initial guesses, such as the Discrete Velocity Method, they develop a high-performance algorithm for efficiently obtaining the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation. Known as the accelerated Discrete Velocity Method (aDVM), this method leverages the collision operator's spectral properties and integrates the solution of linear systems and the iteration of non-linear equations in a seamless manner. As a result, aDVM significantly reduces the required iterations when solving the steady-state problem while minimizing error growth and maintaining a stable solution. Furthermore, aDVM can be generalized to tackle a broader class of kinetic models, including the Generalized Shakhov model, with ease. In line with its potential for practical applications in the design of microfluidic devices and optical systems, aDVM is demonstrated using the optical thin film model, where it successfully obtains the steady-state solution in only 20-30 iterations and with a reduced memory footprint. With its exceptional computational performance and robustness, aDVM serves as an optimal choice for efficiently obtaining the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation in various applications. Nonetheless, aDVM may struggle to perform well in cases where large values of the time relaxation parameters prevail, leading to slow collision processes. To address this limitation, this study proposes an enhanced version of aDVM, which effectively rectifies this shortcoming and facilitates the efficient solution of the model with large time relaxation parameters. By integrating the techniques of multi-time relaxation models and the methods for solving non-linear systems with large relaxation parameters, this study develops a high-performance algorithm for general Boltzmann models and demonstrates its capabilities using specific examples. As a result, the proposed algorithm exhibits exceptional computational performance and robustness, outperforming the accelerated Discrete Velocity Method in cases with large time relaxation parameters. In addition, this study is further extended to tackle a broader class of kinetic models, including the generalized fivetime relaxation systems, where it successfully obtains the steady-state solution in only 25-35 iterations. The phenomenon of the Pauli Exclusion Principle manifests itself when low-temperature 2D harmonic oscillator traps hold fermions at the ground state. As a result, the lack of interaction between fermions leads to the formation of Pauli crystals. This research aims to understand this occurrence by using statistical mechanics to determine the energy and dimensions of a non-interacting arrangement of ultra-cold fermions, combining two theories - fermion degeneracy and harmonic oscillator treatment. This unification of perspectives provides a more complete and reliable explanation for the characteristics of Pauli crystals. A thorough examination of this unified model reveals that it produces the same crystal properties as the conventional treatment. However, this unified model has the advantage of being applicable to both solid-state and atomic fermion systems, allowing for generalizations without losing physical validity. Furthermore, the theoretical framework offers a clear geometric interpretation, which can be applied to analyze anisotropic Pauli crystals. Last but not least, the theoretical framework provides a simple derivation of the long-range momentum dependence of the fermion density, which can be applied to various ultra-cold fermion systems. The momentum dependence can be used as a diagnostic tool to study anisotropic Pauli crystals and identify potential momentary dimer states in magnetic Pauli crystals. This analysis can be extended to the spherical case to analyze the stability of ultra-cold fermion droplets in harmonic traps. The theoretical framework also provides a connection between ultra-cold fermion systems and ferromagnetic spin lattices through a simple mapping of the 2D Pauli crystal to a ferromagnetic Blume-Capel Hamiltonian. This correspondence in physics also extends to the occurrence of superfluidity in spin-polarized cold fermions within strongly magnetic fields, which can be understood by using the Landau-Khalatnikov-Fradkin and Volovik formalism of superfluidity. Our team is currently developing a method to optimize the design parameters of wide-field X-ray telescopes equipped with a Wolter-X type X-ray optic. We aim to minimize the off-axis resolution errors associated with these optics in their normal operating environment. We can achieve the optimization process using a computationally efficient Monte-Carlo ray tracing algorithm, enabling us to accurately model and predict the performance of our optics in three-dimensional space. We have adapted the general Monte-Carlo method for use on orthogonal parametrizations common in wide-field X-ray telescope designs, incorporating a Monte-Carlo simulation of the Earth's atmosphere to account for variable imaging distortions resulting from different altitude positions. We have applied our method to a few examples of commonly used wide-field X-ray telescope designs and demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying the best spatial grouping strategies for achieving optimal in-flight performance. Additionally, we have established a system to automatically analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of our Monte-Carlo simulations in achieving optimal designs. We have also begun adapting our algorithm to accommodate a Monte-Carlo simulation of gravitational effects and an analytical model of solid-angle parameters, incorporating a comprehensive set of simulation requirements. We have defined a set of figures of merit for evaluating our designs and assigned specific weights to each figure of merit in accordance with their relative importance in their intended application. We intend to utilize our algorithm in conjunction with a genetic algorithm optimization method to identify the most effective design parameters for our X-ray telescopes equipped with a wide-field field of view. We have also begun the process of preparing our algorithm for implementation on high-performance parallel computing platforms such as GPU's and distributed server networks, facilitated by part of a larger project to develop a distributed server network system at the University of Maryland, College park, with the primary goal of developing a comprehensive system to automate the design and optimization of X-ray telescopes equipped with a wide-field of view. We ultimately aim to apply our algorithm in conjunction with a genetic optimization method to identify the most effective design parameters for our X-ray telescopes in their intended application as key components of the GECAM and CARMENES space missions, where they will utilize a wide-field field of view to detect X-ray bursts from solar flares and stellar activity in nearby stars. We have also begun the process of incorporating a sensitivity analysis of our algorithm into a Bayesian optimization algorithm for use in future optimizations, where we will incorporate the results of our simulations of the sensitivity analysis into a semi-analytical model of the prior distribution of our algorithm based on our Monte-Carlo simulations in three-dimensional space.

Determining similarity between structured data, especially graph structures, has become a critical task across multiple fields. Recent advancements in generating synthetic structured data from privacy-vulnerable graphs have created a new set of challenges, primarily due to the disclosure of sensitive node ranking information. To address this issue, a novel idea is presented to calculate a graph similarity metric (the Gromov-Wasserstein distance) using multiple locally private graph representations. Each graph representation is generated through randomization, but due to the inherent 1-stretch 1-squeezing property of its Gromov-Wasserstein distance matrix. A theoretical framework is established to ensure the integration of local differential privacy in graph similarity metrics without compromising their ground truth values. Additionally, a new metric (the local private Gromov-Wasserstein distance) is defined and verified to be an accurate proxy for the Gromov-Wasserstein distance or Gromov-Hausdorff distance under certain conditions. Our research, which is based on real-world datasets and a variety of structured graph types (trees, grids, and social networks), shows that the GW privacy metric (the sum of the logarithms of the lengths of the longest paths in each graph) maintains its accuracy even with significant privacy degradation. A collection of proper subrings that together form a ring $R$ is known as a cover of $R$.
The smallest possible size of such a cover for $R$ is referred to as the covering number $\sigma(R)$ of $R$,
and if $\sigma(R)$ is less than the covering number of a quotient ring $R/I$, $R$ is considered $\sigma$-elementary.
For rings with a unity, the size of a minimal cover of $R$ by subrings containing $1_R$ is defined as the unital covering number $\sigma_u(R)$,
and if $\sigma_u(R)$ is less than the unital covering number of a quotient ring $R/I$, $R$ is $\sigma_u$-elementary.
The classification of all unital rings with the smallest possible size for their covering numbers and related $\sigma$-elementary properties is presented. 
These results broaden the scope of previous work by Gilmartine in 1996 and provide specific examples of rings with non-trivial covering numbers. 
The proof of the Main Lemma showcases the utility of Gilmartine's Chains Lemma, while further research questions are proposed in the conclusion.

Inspired by a hypothesis that natural data distributions have inherent limitations on input transformations, we aim to develop more natural and robust defenses against adversarial examples. Specifically, we employ a classifier to estimate the most likely entropy from a cleaned version of the input, restricting it to a lower entropy level consistent with the original data set's distribution. Our approach, termed Natural Robustness, demonstrates promising results in both white-box and black-box adversarial attacks on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, exhibiting a significant 300% to 600% improvement in robustness with minimal accuracy loss. The source code for this natural robustness method can be found at https://github.com/sbi-is/natural_robustness. Additionally, our results are publicly accessible at https://natural-robustness.isa.uni-stuttgart.de/.

Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow transition maps to stretch or shrink coordinates while increasing or decreasing them, except for a set of directions where the stretch factor becomes infinite. Dilation surfaces can feature "asymptotic trajectories" with an infinite trajectory path and infinite stretch factor, and a new concept called "saddle connections" extending to these s-shaped paths. In contrast to traditional saddle connections, these new variants only exhibit a hyperbolic behavior along lower-dimensional manifolds. In this study, we introduce an exploration of these "saddle connections" on a small-scale, circular area of an infinite stretch dilation surface, and prove this area adheres to a Smale's horseshoe theorem. Additionally, we demonstrate a dynamical system's existence within dilation surfaces, and a corresponding horseshoe set that forms a basis for this system's existence. This new discovery allows for an expansion of a previously established criterion for identifying dilation surfaces with hyperbolic behavior. Notably, we find that certain dilation surfaces, engineered to have a specific set of stretch rates, exhibit either a hyperbolic nature or a particular type of dynamics resembling a 2-dimensional Lorentz attractor. This distinction is relatively rare, as most dilation surfaces display highly unstable, chaotic behavior. Meanwhile, dilation surfaces featuring "asymptotic trajectories" almost always possess highly unstable, chaotic behavior. Lastly, we introduce a novel method for distinguishing between deformation types within a specific, $GL^+(2)$-orbifold action on a dilation surface, and show that this distinction is relatively complex and often involves behavior that is anywhere from highly unstable to extremely chaotic in nature. The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that explain the dual nature of waves and particles and the 
interplay between configuration space and phase space. This study generalizes 
those concepts to functions that use Clifford algebra. It defines unitary 
isomorphisms among spaces consisting of square-integrable Clifford algebra-valued 
functions on n-dimensional space, monogenic square-integrable functions on n+1 
dimensional space, and linear functionals on symmetric tensor elements in n 
dimensional space, each space weighted by a respective Gaussian measure. The 
generalized theory employs Clifford geometric approaches and generates novel 
relationships among Clifford geometric entities. The study also applies 
Clifford algebra valuation to weight spaces within the Taylor isomorphism 
framework, resulting in a new unitary isomorphism that connects the Reed-Myer 
space to a Clifford algebra-valued Fock space constructed from monogenic 
elements. This leads to a new particle-like representation of the Clifford algebra 
and enables the relation between weights in phase space and coordinate space to 
be expressed through co-derivations in the Clifford setting. Possible extensions 
to quantum mechanics and the merits of this theory are also discussed. 

Note: This research has been published in the Journal of Geometry and Physics, 
volume 173, 2021.  Additionally, some key concepts are illustrated with the 
support of animated figures generated using Mathematica. Those figures can be 
found at the related URL: http://sites.google.com/compuationalmathematics/e/cliffordmbd/resources.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions through random sampling. Traditional techniques for generating samples from Gaussian process posterior calculations consider samples as separate draws from the distribution of process values at fixed points. This focus on distribution characteristics leads to strategies that increase exponentially with the desired dimensionality. This becomes impractical for large dimensions, prompting us to consider a new line of thinking, where Gaussian conditionals are viewed in the context of individual random variables. This alternative interpretation, which involves conditionals as random variables, allows us to derive and evaluate approximation techniques that support efficient and practical Gaussian process posterior sampling. By examining the underpinning principles, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in approximating Gaussian processes and establish their value in applying Gaussian processes to settings involving large datasets and numerous variables. Implementing these ideas requires developing an open-source library, GPanosa, which provides essential tools for working with Gaussian process conditionals as random variables, as well as generating and visualizing approximate samples. Evaluating these methods on the GEODEA challenge dataset, which features complex, high-dimensional data like protein structures and geodesic distances, shows the practical value of these approximations in real-world applications. Finally, making the source code available enables potential users to adapt and distribute these methods beyond the scope of this study. The primary benefits of these methods, which include efficient sampling, easy manipulation of approximated conditionals, and reduced computational complexity, become most apparent in the context of related works on Gaussian process approximations and sampling methods. This is why we recommend using the gpanosa library, which provides the tools for working with Gaussian process conditionals as with regular variables, as the preferred means of implementing these methods in applications. The tools within this library, which provide the basis for efficient sampling techniques like the von Mises-Fisher finite mixture, the Gaussian finite mixture, the sparse spectral variational, and the inducing variables methods, have proven indispensable in producing the winning submission to the GEODEA challenge. This study marks an important step in the evolution of Gaussian process sampling techniques, which from initial uses in robotics have spread to a broad range of fields in medicine, biology, chemistry, linguistics, and finance, and we anticipate the tools and methods will have far-reaching implications in many areas of machine learning and scientific research. The source code for this paper can be found at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/jayjay

We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined, uniform point spread functions. Our study focuses on common algorithms such as MEDIAN, MODE, and weighted mean, and their application to realistic astronomical images with multiple layers of noise. By analyzing these images in terms of signal strength and noise variability, we determine the conditions necessary for the point spread functions of individual input images to combine effectively into a well-defined, uniform point spread function. Our analysis reveals the critical factors influencing image co-adding outcomes and allows us to draw comparisons with existing research. Furthermore, we explore the implications of using a single, defined point spread function for such co-adding operations for Hubble Space Telescope images, including those captured by the Wide Field Camera 3. This involves exploring the effects of different point spread function choices on resulting co-added images of solar system objects like the Moon and Jupiter, including an assessment of the accuracy required in the point spread function. Our conclusions provide a practical framework for the co-adding of images from the same astronomical observation or data reduction pipeline, and their application extends to any uniformly applied point spread function. This has particular relevance to the ongoing development of image co-adding algorithms for the forthcoming Image Processing Pipeline for the James Webb Space Telescope. Analysis of M-type stars in search of exoplanets serves as an illustrative example of the utility of our conclusions in real astronomical applications, and our methodology and findings are easily extensible to other space-based astronomical observing programs. This research was carried out in partial fulfillment for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in the Department of Physics at the University of Canterbury. This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that the behavior of dislocations in these solids must comply with the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. A critical premise is that the fracture of a solid initiates when the apex of a pre-existing notch reaches a critical instability point, beyond which it begins to sharpen uncontrollably. The resulting predictions derived from this analysis were tested and validated against the meticulous measurements conducted by Gumbsch and associates, who examined the notch toughness of predeformed and non-deformed tungsten crystals under various conditions, spanning a wide range of temperatures, loading rates, and initial states. Notably, the theoretical framework's quantitative predictions consistently aligned with the experimental findings, covering both types of fracture and encompassing different thermal conditions and initial dislocation densities. Furthermore, the analysis provided a novel interpretation of the physical mechanisms governing fracture that involves the interplay between the Peierls stress and the velocity-dependent obstacles to dislocation movement. These findings have implications for the understanding and potential refinement of theoretical models in materials science, particularly in the description of fracture and ductile fracture transitions. The accompanying Supporting Information includes supplementary material for the experimental methodology, as well as a detailed derivation of the theoretical framework's calculations. The work presented here can serve as a foundation for the expansion and advancement of the theoretical framework and its application to the examination of additional experimental phenomena. Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, footnotes, images, tables, and mathematical equations. Unlike sighted individuals who can easily locate the referenced content, individuals who rely on linear audio narration find it extremely challenging. We suggest an approach based on visual detection to identify referenced content and gather necessary metadata that can be utilized in subsequent research to insert summaries into audio narratives. The technique we present has shown effectiveness on both digital documents and those that have been scanned from print. Additionally, it works without requiring any input from the user and can be applied in real-time. Notably, more than 95% of the referenced content were accurately detected. On the other hand, inserting summaries of all references took approximately 6 to 13 seconds. Importantly, this time delay does not appear to cause disruptions in reading regular printed materials and could potentially be minimal through further optimization. We have demonstrated this on printed books and newspapers, and although there may be some loss in resolution due to scanning, our approach remains the same regardless of the input format. It is essential to provide accessible tools that can assist print-disabled individuals in accessing referenced content. This is a particular need and challenge that needs to be addressed in order to make audio narratives more useful and informative, especially when listening to long materials such as research papers, documents, books, and documentaries. Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often using a linear model which assumes consistent statistical dependencies across various ENSO phases, a premise that may not necessarily hold. We statistically analyzed the likelihood of two precipitation patterns worldwide -  less frequent and rare - in response to both EP and CP El Ni\~no events, revealing distinct indicators of each flavor in global climate records. A closer examination of precipitation pattern probabilities in relation to area rainfall totals helped us understand the underlying mechanisms driving variability in monsoons and extreme precipitation worldwide. This study underscores the significance of accurately defining and categorizing El Ni\~no events for better climatic research and forecasting. We demonstrate that distinguishing between EP and CP flavors is crucial, especially for predicting precipitation patterns in India, Asia's monsoon, and other key weather patterns worldwide. Our research also implies that regional climate representations of El Ni\~no's impacts and associated precipitation patterns need to be reevaluated. We provide evidence that confirming the existence of CP El Ni\~no events, and distinguishing it from EP events, is vital for precise weather forecasting and a deeper understanding of how climate variations affect global precipitation patterns. A new statistical method we introduced helps classify events and identifies the two flavors in combined climate data, facilitating a deeper insight into worldwide precipitation patterns. We conclude by addressing potential limitations of our research and suggesting avenues for its extension into related fields. This study may help pave the way for a better description and understanding of how climate variations affect global precipitation patterns, particularly the complex and extensive monsoon in Asia, to improve weather predictions and forecasts. Ultimately, the findings presented here have significant implications for precipitation pattern management and worldwide climate research. We hope the results from our study can guide the development of more accurate models and forecasts at the global climate level. When materials that don't have a regular structure are subjected to external forces, the distortion they cause is described as non-affine deformation. This phenomenon is commonly observed but the details of non-affine deformation are not well understood, especially in systems that don't have a regular structure, due to the limitations of current techniques. To overcome this challenge, we developed a new method based on measuring patterns formed by light waves, which enables us to directly probe non-affine deformation in systems that don't have a regular structure, including those that change their structure in a continuous way. Our experimental results confirm that the amplitude of sound waves can provide information on non-affine deformation. We also employed computer simulations to verify that our measured patterns aren't significantly affected by the gaps between neighboring particles and suggest that variations in patterns can indicate non-affine deformation. Although our method has limitations, it can be improved in the future and our study thus offers a new direction for probing non-affine deformation. This research has important implications for developing materials that can change their shape in a controlled manner, which was initiated by the application of external forces in these systems. One promising strategy to control shape changes involves using thermal energy to induce non-affine deformation in thermosensitive materials, leading to significant scientific and technological interests. Therefore, the development of probes that can directly measure non-affine deformation is essential for unlocking the mechanisms behind non-affine deformation and improving the performance of materials that can automatically change their shape in a controlled manner. This goal can be achieved by employing probes that can directly measure the spatial structure of systems that don't have a regular structure or the connections between neighboring particles, which can be used to study non-affine deformation in systems that are subjected to external forces as well as in systems that are in a state of stress. By improving the method based on measuring patterns formed by light waves, it's possible to study non-affine deformation in systems that were previously inaccessible, including polymeric networks, proteins and other complex systems. Our method demonstrates a new direction for unlocking the mechanisms behind non-affine deformation and improving the performance of materials that can automatically change their shape in a controlled manner. Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research focuses on automatic taxonomy expansion using graph representation learning, yet it assumes a traditional Euclidean framework without considering the inherent hierarchical properties. As a result, details are embedded too closely to the main concepts, hindering their retrieval. A novel approach, HyperExpan, addresses these limitations through hyperbolic representation learning that mirrors the tree structure of taxonomies. Inspired by the hyperbolic space, a novel neural network, HemiNet, is introduced for classification tasks. By incorporating a type-aware constraint in the loss function, HemiNet ensures accurate classification without compromising classification generalizability. A comprehensive evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of HyperExpan on state-of-the-art benchmarks, achieving notable improvements over current methods. Specifically, its performance surpasses the next best method, XHAULI, with significant gains across all metrics, with subcategories demonstrating the greatest advantages.  Codes and models for HyperExpan are available at: \url{https://github.com/whuiyl/HemiNet}.

It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a maximum effect at ~2", likely due to a self-regulating effect of the magnetic field. For larger sources, this correlation decreases, with a possible reversing effect appearing in very large sources (>~20"). However, environmental effects do not explain the size dependence, suggesting further investigation into jet physics and magnetic field behavior required. A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in lidar-based SLAM systems through the identification of recurring loops. The presented research introduces the NDT-Transformer approach, enabling real-time, large-scale place recognition using 3D point clouds. The methodology utilizes the 3D Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation, renowned for its efficiency in describing 3D surfaces, and couples it with a deep learning-based descriptor, alongside a metric matcher. The NDT-Transformer outperforms existing methods by leveraging a set of publicly available place recognition benchmarks, showcasing its ability to provide state-of-the-art performance while operating at high speeds of 10 Hz. The proposed research and implementations are available through the OmegaPlot repository. Furthermore, the experiments and evaluation results demonstrate the capabilities of the NDT-Transformer method. The findings also highlight drawbacks in existing benchmark tests, primarily due to the absence of large-scale sequences with high levels of repetition, and suggest ways to improve the methods and implementations through the creation of more challenging data sets. A comprehensive analysis and evaluation of the experiments and results is provided. The code and implementations for the various methods and experiments are also presented. The presented research and implementations are released under the Apache 2.0 open-source license. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can provide more accurate predictions of cognitive outcomes than individual site data, but it's still not known how site-level statistics affect our ability to make accurate predictions. In this study, we used multiple measures of brain connectivity from 32 resting-state fMRI datasets to verify the generalization of a predictive model from a training dataset to an independent test dataset. Our simulation studies showed that large-scale fMRI studies have the power to detect site-level differences in brain connectivity, and also revealed that regional measures of brain connectivity have greater statistical power than network-wide measures. Furthermore, we found that functional and anatomical connectivity measures are highly reliable and independent, and also discovered that the consistency of brain connectivity measures across different sites is a key determinant of predictive accuracy in functional MRI data. These findings highlight the importance of large-scale research initiatives, like the ENIGMA-Sleep network, which have the power to detect site-level differences in brain connectivity and contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying brain structure. Our study's findings will be essential for designing future multi-site functional MRI studies to develop models of brain function and connectivity. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency and O(log n) energy usage for n-station beeping networks, addressing both the naming and counting problems. These algorithms also permit a seamless switch between low-energy operation and fast processing based on a simple adjustment of the local clock. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. Statistical models 
are another option to consider, yet they are notoriously ineffective at 
identifying definitive language boundaries. This research aims to bridge this 
gap by designing a new type of positional encoding, utilizing switching points 
as a framework. We introduce a dynamic and relative positional encoding (DRPE) 
algorithm, which automatically adjusts for language variation and is easily 
integrated into pre-trained models, including BERT. Our experimental results 
reveal that the proposed DRPE outperforms traditional methods in classification 
tasks for multiple code-mixed languages, including Romanized scripts. To facilitate 
further research, we publicly release the DRPE algorithm, along with associated 
dataset tools. A paper discussing the methodology and outcomes has been published 
in the findings of the ACL 2021 Workshop on Multilingual NLP. This statement 
provides a step-by-step guide for replicating our research using the NRCL toolkit. 
We also examine the possibilities of extending our model to handle neural 
machine translation for code-mixed text. Furthermore, we investigate BERT's 
ability to function optimally in language blending scenarios. This research is 
further supplemented by an interactive demonstration, available at the website. 
Lastly, we discuss how the principles underlying our model can be applied to 
overcome similar challenges present in other areas of NLP, such as processing 
textual data for different linguistic cultures and varieties. A related paper is 
available at the website in the form of a tutorial.

Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the positive electron-phonon interaction and the negative electron-electron interaction - yields a predictable trend in the isotope effect coefficient as a function of pressure. However, incorporating the variable density of states enhances our understanding of both interactions and improves agreement with experimental data, with the coefficient exhibiting a shift from negative to positive at high pressures. Consequently, we suggest that the variable density of states has a substantial impact on the performance of H3S as a superconductor under pressure. Furthermore, we observed that accounting for the variable density of states significantly alters the behavior of the critical temperature in the isotope effect, with the shift from negative to positive occurring at higher pressures. Specifically, we found that the variable density of states affects the critical temperature at high pressures and contributes to a significant enhancement of the superconducting state. This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints provided by a global planner. However, existing methods are often unsuccessful without pre-compiled maps or where maps are inaccurate due to environmental changes. We introduce a method that generates spatial boundaries based on local information in environments with obstacles that require continuous navigation around. We evaluate our approach through comparisons with state-of-the-art methods on a simulator platform, demonstrating its superiority in terms of planning efficiency for mobile robots and self-driving vehicles. Further research is necessary to adapt this technique for lane change and map-building applications in autonomous driving.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine 6-DoF camera poses by leveraging the constructed visual database. Moreover, this method exploits machine-learned descriptors to achieve enhanced performance, especially under difficult conditions. Our approach is demonstrated to achieve high accuracy under both real-world and simulated scenarios. Furthermore, this method allows for seamless integration with existing LiDAR-based navigation systems. Evaluations are conducted using the KITTI3D dataset and a custom-built dataset titled "Map Gucci". Moreover, a novel technique called "map gucci scoring" is developed to evaluate the accuracy of visual relocalization systems. In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices. The paper further explores the algorithm's computational efficiency and presents a fast and low-complexity implementation that retains precise user selection accuracy. Moreover, the algorithm is shown to be insensitive to changes in the system parameters without necessitating regularizations. Experimental results demonstrate the algorithm's capacity to achieve near-optimal sum rates and minimal interference at inactive user devices. The paper concludes with a comparison of the algorithm to a recently published method, group sparse LASSO via accelerated forward linear optimization, group 1. The two methods exhibit distinct design imperatives, the former prioritizing exact zero solution and the latter focusing on approximate sparse solution. The two algorithms yield different tradeoffs between computational complexity and solution accuracy, the group LASSO based algorithm offering higher approximate sparsity and the group 1S group LASSO based algorithm offering higher sum rate. The choice of method depends on the priority placed on sparsity or sum rate. The paper describes an implementation of the group LASSO based algorithm and presents a new LASSO solver, the list group LASSO solver. The two methods demonstrate superior performance in the joint user selection and precoding task. The list group LASSO solver achieves a speedup of approximately 1000 times relative to the original group LASSO based algorithm, the original solution exhibiting higher accuracy in user selection. The two methods yield similar sum rates, the user selection process accounting for the majority of computational costs. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve. This results in a crucial element in the study of tropical moduli spaces. Finally, the rational function semifields of tropical chains and weak tropical chains are explicitly defined. A tropical chain is a particular type of tropical curve with a significant property, and a weak tropical chain has an analogous property involving the inverse of its degree function. Our work also involves the application of tropical cycle maps and the extended MacLane theorem. Specifically, the rational function semifield of a tropical curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over a specific linear functional system that is finite, consistent, and convex. Ultimately, the work in this field is intended to contribute to the study of the moduli spaces associated with stable complex curves. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. The provided proofs are instrumental in clarifying the relationships between these theorems and showcase an alternative approach to proving the ergodic theorem. As a byproduct, we establish a new ergodic theorem for Markov processes lacking a dual solution. Lastly, this note is supplemented by two technical results that are potentially standalone in nature. Uniform convergence is the primary concern of the first result, while the second result concerns the creation of a conditionally reversible Markov process originating from an arbitrary initial state. The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a magnetic transition. Some studies have hinted at the existence of nematic order and the possibility of nematic fluctuations in LiFeAs, which has led to the proposal of a new type of d-wave superconducting order in the material. However, the formation of nematic order remains uncertain, which we explore further by means of extensive neutron scattering and infrared spectroscopy experiments. Our study reveals the absence of nematic instability in LiFeAs and presents the reasons behind this finding. Specifically, the fact that local structural asymmetry can cause k-space charge imbalance is shown to be absent in LiFeAs, and a detailed comparison is made with the magnetic and nematic FeSC, BaFe$_2$As$_2$. Finally, the implications of these findings for the nature of superconductivity in LiFeAs are considered. Our study concludes that the superconducting properties of LiFeAs can be explained by a conventional mechanism, which does not require the presence of nematic fluctuations. Nevertheless, the compound provides an invaluable opportunity to study various exotic phenomena related to unconventional superconductivity in a stable, hole-doped system. Specifically, the compound exhibits a unique evolution of superconducting properties in response to chemical doping, which differs from that observed in the magnetic and nematic FeSC, BaFe$_2$As$_2$. Ultimately, the evolution of superconducting properties in the LiFeAs family can be classified into three distinct phases, each characterized by decreasing, non-existent and increasing critical pressures at 18, 0.5 and 30 K, respectively. This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the stationary Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, the research aims to determine the relationship between input forces and resulting flows for the stationary Navier-Stokes equation in dimensions 2 to 4. Notably, the findings show that for forced stationary flows in dimensions 2 to 4 with certain input force properties, solving the equation becomes highly unstable, particularly when the input force is localized in frequency and the resulting flow is also localized in frequency as well as in time. This specific outcome contradicts recent work by Li-Pullen and the first author, which found that forced stationary flows in dimensions 2 to 4 with specific input force properties exhibited resistance to perturbations. It is noteworthy that the discovered instability presents evidence of a "bifurcation" in the Navier-Stokes equation, which occurs at a specific scale located below the dissipative range, rather than than the dissipation range as previously considered. Furthermore, the research utilizes non-autonomous dynamical systems tools to establish the instability of the Navier-Stokes equation and, in doing so, requires considering a more comprehensive family of Bessov spaces compared to previous work. Consequently, the research provides a comprehensive answer to a question raised by Tsurumi regarding the relationship between input forces and resulting flows for the stationary Navier-Stokes equation in dimensions 2 to 4. In particular, the research finds that for forced stationary flows in dimensions 2 to 4 with specific input force properties, the scale of the input force plays a significant role in determining the stability of the solution, which is not directly considered in previous work. Notably, the research demonstrates that for forced stationary flows in dimensions 2 to 4 with localized frequency input forces, the resulting flows are also sensitive to perturbations and may exhibit nonlinear instability, which is not predicted by linear theory. This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built using Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework, Loidreau's system is now susceptible to a polynomial-time key recovery attack under certain circumstances. To counter this vulnerability, we suggest employing subcodes to conceal the secret codes in Modification 1. Meanwhile, in Modification 2, we combine the secret matrix with a randomly selected low column rank matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Theoretical analysis confirms that both alterations offer resistance to the current range of structural attacks. Moreover, we utilize the systematic generator matrix for the public code, resulting in a public-key size reduction, as well as greater resistance to attacks, more compact public keys and higher information transmission rates. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the practical feasibility of these modifications in Modification 1. A comparison with other similar systems reveals that these modifications provide the lowest public-key sizes among them. As such, they pose a substantial threat to the security of these systems. Finally, the security of these modifications is proposed as a new standard in ISO/IEC 27033.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and generate general word meanings, researchers are exploring new methods
to enhance their performance. The quality of these word meanings depends on how
often the words appear in the data, leading to underoptimized representations of
infrequent words. This paper investigates a novel technique to address this issue by
leveraging dictionaries like Wiktionary to define rare words. The rare word's
definition is used to create additional training examples in the PLMs, ensuring the
model captures its true meaning. The experimental results show that applying this
technique to BERT results in superior performance on both rare and common word
understanding tasks. Additionally, the findings indicate that incorporating word
definitions into PLMs is a valuable form of additional supervision that enhances the
model's semantic knowledge. The potential of this technique has further prompted
researchers to consider using dictionaries as a means to improve PLMs. The code and
data used in this research can be found at https://dict-bert.github.io/. Our
customized BERT model, named Dict-BERT, is available on https://dict-bert.github.io/. The city defender and attacker engage in a game of tit-for-tat, while resource transactions are managed by a controller. Attacker choices aim to disrupt the city's resource management, whereas the city defender and resource controller cooperate to thwart the attack and maximize social welfare. Studies on this concept have shown that resource allocation is a critical factor in determining the city's defense strategy. Due to non-stationary and dynamic game environments and unverified model claims, there is a lack in current research on smart city security. Our work involves developing and validating a comprehensive model of a smart city environment. By solving a linear programming problem, the city defender and resource controller can temporarily coordinate their strategies. Consequently, the city's social welfare is maximized, and the resource controller profits financially. This model has been experimentally tested and validated. Analysis of our results has identified key factors influencing the city's defense and revealed the city's sensitivity to the attack. Moreover, the efficiency of the linear programming-based approach has been evaluated. This research provides a comprehensive foundation for strategic resource management in a smart city environment. It offers an original framework for modeling and analyzing a smart city environment that is subject to socio-cyber-physical attacks. A key approach in this framework involves distributed game-theoretic resource management. This concept has several potential applications in various fields, such as fiscal policy, electronic commerce, and the sharing economy. It has the potential to be widely applied in various contexts, such as companies, communities, and social networks. Another potential research direction would be to transform the linear programming-based approach into a more advanced mathematical or logical model, which could enable the discovery of explicit, implicit, or inherent system properties. Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-destructive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration experiments like the AWAKE project. This research examines how differences in the plasma's radial dimensions and off-center electron injection influence the resulting beam dynamics and betatron radiation spectra emitted by witness electron particles in proton-driven plasmas. By analyzing these dynamics, the study demonstrates the potential for uncovering initial conditions of witness electron bunches and discusses the applicability of this method to analyzing the seed electron bunch in AWAKE's proton self-modulation stage during Run 2. Furthermore, the investigation develops a semi-theoretical model for computing the predicted betatron radiation spectra. This model enables a direct link between the electron beam dynamics and the observed radiated energy, thereby facilitating extraction of the initial seed electron bunch form and initial gamma factor of the seed electrons in AWAKE's proton self-modulation stage. It is anticipated that this semi-theoretical model can also be applied to analyzing radiation emitted by other electron beams in other accelerator structures, including those with narrow plasma channels or electron beams guided by magnetic fields. Ultimately, the study's results may provide valuable insights into optimizing this diagnostic tool for use in future accelerator designs. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it places an excessive focus on understanding market uncertainty, failing to prioritize trend prediction. While researchers have applied generative adversarial networks and their variants to generate financial time series and assist in portfolio analysis, these methods face limitations in using the model output effectively due to the lack of a conditional structure. Therefore, a novel Autoencoding Conditional GAN, ACaGAN, is proposed. It combines the advantages of generative adversarial networks and autoencoders to generate multiple step-ahead time series along with conditional components at various levels using the hidden representations of the target series as an essential input. The ACaGAN's trend prediction capability is compared with traditional Markowitz-based and future series generation-based methods through multi-step ahead forecasts. The results indicate that ACaGAN outperforms the baseline in terms of forecasting accuracy, particularly for short-term forecasts of the Standard & Poor's 500 index. The integration of Markowitz and ACaGAN is shown to successfully minimize losses from overfitting by optimizing portfolio weights using the adversarially learned hidden representations. The proposed system achieves a balance between trend prediction and risk minimization in the portfolio analysis framework. The performance is further extended by using multi-step ahead forecasts in two different ways: extra-step forecasting and training. The publication provides an open-source code for researchers to conduct extra-step forecasting and training in the portfolio analysis domain. The study's key contribution is an in-depth portfolio analysis using hidden representations in the context of generative adversarial networks and future series generation. The proposed framework has a broad applicability beyond financial domains, specifically in any scenario requiring deep forecasting and hidden representation-driven risk minimization. The open-source code is available at https://github.com/kshen7/ACaGAN4Portfolio. The system design is detailed at https://www.dropbox.com/s/l5mqnqk5jsk9muq/port_acagan.pdf. The portfolio optimization code using hidden representations is available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/lsykjyf7yf7yf7y/optim_port_acagan.py. The original portfolio optimization code without hidden representations is available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/lsykjyf7yf7yf7y/optim_port_markowitz.py. The time series generation code using future series generation is available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/lsykjyf7yf7yf7y/fg_port_acagan.py.
