Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. Furthermore, suggestions for reducing CPM format dispersion are provided. Our findings indicate that increasing the square root of the number of symbols, $K\propto\sqrt{M}$ for $M$ subcarriers, significantly surpasses the performance gains obtained from raised-cosine CPM formats with a roll-off factor of less than 0.4. This research provides insights into the conventional differential detection's CPM format performance, motivating the development of more efficient CPM formats with distinct phase transitions that can enhance this detection method's performance under varying $K$ values. These efficient CPM formats, known as $E_{8}$-like codes, result from modifications to the conventional phase transition points and result in superior performance, surpassing the conventional CPM formats for large $K$ values. The performance enhancements observed for $E_{8}$-like codes under both conventional differential detection and coherent detection technologies. The increase in $K$ yields an approximate 3 dB improvement in the CPM format's bit error rate performance without any additional changes to the receiver. This improvement stems from increased $E_{b}/N_{0}$ by expanding the minimum Euclidean distance between symbols, ultimately facilitating better branch and cumulative metrics and increased correct decisions. The conventional differential detection's performance gains make it an attractive and efficient method for various CPM formats, particularly those with distinct phase transitions like $E_{8}$-like codes. These codes offer superior error coding performance comparable to Reed-Solomon codes under conventional differential detection, making this approach a practical solution for various CPM formats, including those with distinct phase transitions. A significant challenge in reinforcement learning is creating rewards that align with an instructor's vision. To overcome this, our research introduces Visually Assisted Cluster Ranking, reducing the time and effort required for reward learning. We prove the efficacy of this approach, proposing an algorithm that aggregates an instructor's feedback group into smaller, identical tasks, making reward learning more manageable. Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of this method. Furthermore, our framework allows reward learning to take place in any environment, on top of any reinforcement learning algorithm, providing added flexibility. We showcase this concept in robotic learning, an area where visual recognition is commonly used. Our study indicates that VACR can accelerate the training process by more than half a year compared to the state-of-the-art reward learning algorithms. We apply VACR to the acquisition of motor skills on a six DoF robotic arm, an exercise marked by a substantial amount of visual data. To date, our algorithm stands alone as the simplest and most efficient solution for reward learning, addressing a long-standing challenge in robotics. We provide a step-by-step guide on using VACR to successfully learn complex tasks, an achievement marked by the consistent results of the time across all of our experiments, on all of the robotic learning tasks, in all of the environments. Moreover, our algorithm's domain-neutral characteristics make it suitable for a wide array of applications, likely including medical training, human-robot interaction, and other areas marked by uncertainty due to factors like noise, adversarial attacks, or incomplete data. While our algorithm's domain-neutral properties hold significant promise, their implications have yet to be formally proven. We propose an algorithm that automatically groups an instructor's feedback for use in reward learning. Our algorithm's efficiency has been proven through analysis and our experimental results reflect this, indicating that VACR achieves results much faster than existing reward learning methods, an advantage reflected in our experiments across multiple environments. Our algorithm's performance has been shown to be equivalent to that of the state-of-the-art reward learning algorithms. To expand the scope of our findings, our algorithm can be used in conjunction with various reinforcement learning techniques. As part of our study, we selected a robotic learning task marked by a lack of expert knowledge. Our algorithm's results are consistent with our analysis, an outcome also evident in our experimental design, in which we compared VACR to six different algorithms. Our algorithm's performance an be explained by the similarity between the challenges of clustering and ranking, as well as the similarity between the challenges of ranking and the reward learning process.

The topological characteristics can be restored through the introduction of additional interactions at this critical threshold. Depending on the method and timing of interaction introduction, this system exhibits either a period of prolonged instability or a state of temporary topological stability. A key factor in the system's behavior is the concept of "frustration," which encompasses not only geometric constraints but also the influence of external variables. Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. Building upon the standard pre-training framework, we formulate a semantic-based pre-training approach that includes three key tasks: learning core semantic units, semantic relations, and overall semantic representation. Empirical results from the analysis of casual and task-based conversations confirm the superiority of our proposed model. Furthermore, we contribute a novel paradigm by integrating a deep semantic representation into the pre-training of dialogue models. This method not only enhances model performance but also provides better understanding of semantic meaning. As an open-source resource, we release our model implementation and performance metrics for public use. The relevant code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/ghliu/semantics_pretrain. The model's performance metrics are available on LI&M lab's website at https://www.lirmm.fr/research/. From a technical standpoint, our work yields significant advancements in both model performance and semantic understanding, paving the way for future research in the realm of dialogue. To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming languages and learning theory to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method captures the essence of how a person learns an algorithm, and through rigorous evaluation, we prove its advantages in four key areas - it applies universally, can be computed easily, yields distinct results, and accurately tracks increasing complexity. By presenting the framework through a hypothetical scenario and elaborating its foundational concepts, we highlight the practical applications of this measurement tool, notably for those responsible for selecting algorithms in critical safety contexts such as self-driving cars, flight path planning, and medical diagnosis. Furthermore, we establish the framework's reliability by providing statistical support for its consistency across various groups of people. Finally, to showcase the practical usage of the measurement tool, we calculate the intermediate results of this measurement for a range of algorithms employing different neural network architectures. This comprehensive measurement tool is expected to play a vital role in algorithms' certification processes, and we hope it will serve as a model for similar efforts in other domains. The accompanying code is available on the GitHub repository 'algorithmic-interp', and our experimental results are documented in the database'measure-alg-interp-results'. Following the publication of our primary research in 2020, this follow-up study emerged as a most popular article on the online publishing platform arXiv in the 'Machine Learning' category in 2022. The study's innovative contributions have been widely recognized and publicly endorsed by over 160 individuals, and it has sparked a significant number of informed discussions on social media and related forums. The study's findings and presentation have also been successfully applied in a real-world setting, the design of safety-critical algorithms for self-driving cars. The algorithmic interpretability framework proposed in this paper is now being used as a model for other efforts in similar domains, and it has led to a related patent award to the author. Anomaly detection without labelled data is increasingly being used to identify unusual patterns within datasets, given that manually annotating data can be impractical or costly; one such unsupervised method that has gained popularity in recent times is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which employs a random tree-based approach to compute an anomaly score through ensemble learning. However, a conventional Isolation Forest may still be optimized in terms of memory requirements, processing time, and overall performance to suit constrained systems and small-footprint AI implementations on resource-restricted microcontrollers. Additionally, anomaly detection systems typically neglect the value of user-provided feedback as a form of weak supervision in informing decision-making. Experiments were conducted using low-cost Arduino and Raspberry Pi boards to validate the potential of weak supervision in informing decision-making and to assess its practical applicability under real-world settings. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel Bayesian approach to estimate parameters of the extreme value distribution, taking into account the Poisson process discretisation and avoiding the use of singular matrices. Our proposed approach is shown to perform well in samples from the prior distribution, using threshold-independent priors for the extreme value parameters. We also explore alternative priors for the Poisson process intensity and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through an analysis of the asymptotic variance of the sample extreme value parameters. Finally, we apply our method to real-world data in modelling the extreme wind speeds at the Topaz offshore wind farm. Our approach demonstrates excellent performance in frequentist estimation as well. Additionally, we generalize our technique to the case of multi-dimensional extreme values. We show that the parameter estimation for the extremal statistics of multi-dimensional data is equivalent to the estimation for a one-dimensional data set. Our approach allows for the use of threshold-independent priors, and we obtain the desired asymptotic variance by matching the discretisation step to a distance between two extreme value distribution parameters. As an example, we apply our method to the data from the Germany summer flood of 2002. Our approach supports the findings of previous studies using this data. The tools for our method have been made available in an R package called 'bepeto'. The additional tools for our example with multi-dimensional data can be found in a Python package called 'extremes'. Our work provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for Bayesian extreme value model estimation. Our associated software uses practical examples to illustrate the implementation details of our method. The technical requirements for our work are specified in the 'Supplementary Notes'. Our research contributes to the existing literature on Bayesian extreme value model estimation by introducing a novel interleave technique for efficient full Bayesian estimation. Our approach estimates parameters of the extreme value distribution as well as the discretisation step of the Poisson process. Our method performs well in samples from the prior distribution, using threshold-independent extreme value parameters. Our approach allows for the use of frequentist estimation as well. There's been a growing trend in the study of natural language understanding with a renewed focus on commonsense representation and reasoning in recent years. This resurgence has led to the creation of new commonsense knowledge graphs that can be used by machine learning models to tackle challenging tasks, although questions remain regarding their reliability due to the sheer scope required to cover all general commonsense knowledge. This study argues that large, manually constructed commonsense graphs are inherently flawed due to their limitations, so a novel assessment framework has been proposed that evaluates a graph's usefulness by how effectively it allows for implicit knowledge representation to be learned. A new graph called ATOMIC 2020 has been created, comprising over 900,000 general commonsense triples that go beyond everyday knowledge, allowing it to outperform existing graphs, including GPT-3, ALICE, and COMET-RESTLE, in a comprehensive evaluation. A thorough analysis of the findings reveals that ATOMIC 2020's success is due to its greater comprehensiveness than existing graphs, incorporating less common knowledge, such as actions not typically observed in movies or TV shows. This larger scope allows for the creation of more precise machine learning models capable of performing a range of complex natural language understanding tasks. As the first graph to cover general, coarse-grained commonsense knowledge, ATOMIC 2020 represents a significant breakthrough, while the proposed evaluation framework has the potential to inspire further research on the development of new, potentially bias-free commonsense resources. These can be used to construct graphs like ATOMIC 2020, thereby facilitating breakthroughs in state-of-the-art machine learning models capable of sophisticated natural language understanding. A new tool, called the ATOMIC Visualizer, has also been developed, allowing users to uncover and explore various aspects of the graph's bias. This tool can be particularly useful for the discovery of general commonsense knowledge, serving as a form of crowdsourced, symbolic knowledge development platform, while the findings suggest that neural language models may pick up on domain-specific knowledge like visual information like movie or TV show settings even if they're not explicitly aware of it. We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient map generation, which utilizes a highly modified ROMA algorithm previously validated on large-scale cosmological surveys. This work extensively examines the properties of Hi-GAL Science Demonstration Phase dataset. We investigate the reliability of noise estimates and map accuracy through correlations, spectral analysis, and resolution measurements, confirming ROMA's high performance. By comparing 250 $\mu$m maps generated using ROMA and scan map exponents to those produced by the XSCANPAC pipeline, we conducted a quality assessment of the data reduction approach. This analysis demonstrated the distinct advantages of the ROMA-based data processing method. Finally, we examined the sensitivity of Hi-GAL maps to detect point sources using a model of the instrument's noise. This study provided valuable insights that enabled optimizing data processing to maximize the scientific returns of this Herschel satellite project. As a result, our pipeline is now the official choice for processing the project's large dataset, with approximately 10000 spectra per hour being generated and extensively analyzed across the 40$\times$40 square degrees covered by the survey. Each pressure was measured in conjunction with a vacuum-compatible autotuner, utilizing the SRV's electron multiplier photometer as the reference sensor. Our results indicate that the ratio of the isolated Lyman beta wavelength to the overall background wavelength is around 50:1. Optimal distributed controller design under communication limitations can be
complicated unless certain system structure conditions, like sparsity or
temporal consistency, are established. Drawing from graph signal processing,
this study develops a class of Graph Symmetric Systems, which exhibit graph-based
symmetry. For systems with quadratic optimization objectives and dynamic models
derived from GSSs, it's shown that the central controller can be represented as a
graph filter with a transfer function-based parameterization. Due to their
finite impulse response property, this parameterization enables finite and
repeated message exchange for distributed optimization within the network.
Moreover, this study presents a distributed optimization method for optimal
controller design through the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. Specifically, this
method requires only three message exchanges between agents when using a
quadratic cost function. Extensive numerical tests verify that the proposed
approach allows for scalable, efficient, and optimal distributed optimization
despite communication limitations. As such, this study contributes to the
development of distributed optimal controllers by leveraging graph signal
processing concepts to expand upon existing structural conditions for
distributed optimization. Additionally, this contribution facilitates a
communication-efficient method for controller design within multi-agent systems. 
The associated code can be found at https://github.com/tianyu-chen/distributed-optimization.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance search engine that efficiently indexes and matches the vector representations. Current state-of-the-art systems prioritize developing more robust image representations but overlook the critical role of indexing in their performance. To address this limitation, this study develops and makes public two key resources: a high-performance search engine based on a specially designed, optimized data structure, and a comprehensive toolkit for quickly experimenting with different indexing techniques. Utilizing these resources, the investigation reveals that the performance of existing image search engines is hindered by inefficient data structures that can be easily surpassed using optimized methods. Furthermore, the research highlights the importance of exploiting inherent patterns within real-world image collections and demonstrates that a carefully engineered search engine can learn and leverage these patterns at rates far superior to traditional methods. Ultimately, the paper outlines a unified framework for active indexing, a design approach that distills key insights from various techniques to create more effective, scalable image search engines. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each mention. However, the common approach to acquire supervised training data through distant supervision introduces label noise by assigning type labels without considering the context. In order to mitigate this issue, FG-NET research adopts a Euclidean model which has its limitations when dealing with noise in the labels. As the entity type hierarchy is inherently hierarchical, a hyperbolic space model becomes the natural choice for FG-NET data. This research proposes a new framework called FGNET-RH that leverages the advantages of hyperbolic geometry and noise-tolerant graph structures. FGNET-RH involves the use of hard graph structure and robust gradient descent-based optimisation and it can be trained on raw data without the need for pre-processing. Our experiments conducted on 13 datasets reveal that FGNET-RH achieves a significant improvement in F1-score (an average increase of 6.51m-12.33m) compared to baseline models that include free-base, BCN and EEE, and it also demonstrates superiority over soft graph structure-based models. FGNET-RH's raw data approach makes it suitable for cross-lingual FG-NET models and it results in an average F1-score improvement of 8.41m-9.65m on six cross-lingual datasets. FGNET-RH's performance even surpasses the recent state-of-the-art approach, M2EFG, and it achieves an average F1-score improvement of 1.91m-6.33m. In modeling systems of players making strategic decisions as Nash games, solving for the equilibrium is often too demanding due to the vast number of possible states and actions. Even approximating the equilibrium can be impractically expensive for some problems because the state space is too large. Therefore, researchers have developed methods like Predicted Quasi-Best Response (PQBR) which can speed up the simulation of these systems by ignoring non-essential states. However, these methods have a critical dependency on the quality of the state approximations. In this research, we introduce a new class of deep networks, known as Fixed Point Networks (FPN), which are specifically designed to capture the underlying dynamics of the system's equilibrium using the network's fixed point property. Furthermore, we provide mathematical proofs that establish the stability of the FPN as well as its ability to predict the equilibrium effectively. Our experiments with simple Nash games demonstrate the effectiveness of the FPN in making more accurate predictions compared to traditional methods, and we illustrate its value in approximating the equilibrium in a complex game involving multiple players and actions. Finally, we show FPNN's utility in simulating a microeconomic system consisting of multiple economic agents and compare it to other prediction techniques. These comparisons highlight the practical advantages of using FPNN for the prediction task. FPNN's effectiveness in approximating the equilibrium opens up the possibility of using it in a wide range of applications, and we suggest several potential areas of study for our future work. FPNN's effectiveness in approximating the equilibrium opens up several potential areas of study for our future work. FPNN can be used as a loss function in reinforcement learning and can also be extended to more complex game types such as Markov Games and Mean Field Games. A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger training sets and pre-trained tools, whereas summarization for lesser-known Indian languages is hindered by complex syntax and differences in meaning. A proposed model called GAE-ISumm utilizes a deep learning approach using a Graph Autoencoder, even in cases where large training data is not available. Additionally, a novel information extraction system, called Indian Language Neural Information Extractor (ILNIE), is designed to facilitate the process of summarization. The results from GAE-ISumm and ILNIE have been compared with other leading models, while also evaluating their performance on published datasets and experimenting with two Indian languages: Hindi and Marathi. The analysis also explores the effectiveness of combining these models with an increasing number of training sentences. The findings demonstrate that GAE-ISumm, aided by a larger dataset and underlying ILNIE tools, can match or surpass the performance of other leading models, while a comparable variation in training data has a more pronounced impact on its performance compared to English language models. The presented research lays the groundwork for future studies on summarization in Indian languages. The source code for GAE-ISumm has been made available on the GitHub platform.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, particularly independent S-rings of type A. We calculate the injective dimension of a quotient category formed by modules over an independent S-ring of type A, with respect to a specified subcategory consisting of modules having trivial interactions with codivisorial modules. We demonstrate that this calculated dimension is equal to the subcategory's dimension within the original category formed by modules over the independent S-ring of type A. We also compute the classical Krull dimension of this subcategory. A central result of our paper asserts that if a independent S-ring of type A possesses a maximal ideal that is strictly Slendler, then the ring exhibits properties similar to those of a Prfer domain, including the ring being spectrally separated of finite dimension. We further prove that if a independent S-ring of type A possesses a maximal ideal that is freely generated over the ring, then the ring must be globally idempotent. We provide numerous examples supporting the validity of the claimed results. Ultimately, the theory of S-rings of Krull type is found to be extensively influenced by the underlying properties of the set S of non-regular elements. Consequently, corresponding theories for rings possessing such elements are naturally proposed. We explore and examine these theories, in addition to investigating how the results can be applied to rings possessing elements of non-regularity. Notably, one area of investigation involves characterizing rings with elements of non-regularity as those satisfying specific conditions, such as the conditions being locally integrally closed or freely generated. We also establish the properties of modules sharing certain interactions with codisorial modules in general rings possessing such elements. Although some of these results may seem unconventional, it is acknowledged that the underlying reasons for these findings are valid and sound, while the generality of the theory of S-rings of Krull type is found to be largely influenced by the properties of the set S of non-regular elements. Consequently, corresponding theories for rings possessing such elements are proposed and explored. We also venture into the investigation of the theory of Krull rings and prime monoids via the lens of S-rings of Krull type. Specifically, the definition of Krull rings of type A is established and examined. It is shown that an independent ring of type A with a prime submonoid of Krull type A is itself a Krull ring of type A if and only if the ring's prime submonoid is freely generated.

The objective of this research was to identify and characterise potential substellar companions associated with five rapidly accelerating stars using data obtained through diverse techniques. These targets were initially monitored as part of the SPHERE/SHINE study, where radial velocity archives were available for four out of five objects but failed to reveal the presence of companions. However, significant proper motion irregularities hinted at the existence of companions for three targets - RX And, Tau Boo, and HR 450. By combining the results from adaptive optics, photometric, and radial velocity measurements with astrometric data, the study's aims were to confirm the presence of companions, determine their masses, and calculate their orbital periods. For the other two targets, the study sought to rule out the presence of companions or, alternatively, verify previously reported masses and orbital periods. Using sophisticated statistical analysis, the study established the existence of a companion for HR 667 Pt (a dwarf star with a companion likely having a mass between 0.13 to 0.35 Jupiter masses, an orbital period between 0.7 to 2.4 years, and an eccentricity of around 0.64). For Tau Boo, the study confirmed the presence of a companion, with a mass between 0.13 to 0.35 Jupiter masses, an orbital period between 0.7 to 2.4 years, and an eccentricity of around 0.64. These companions' masses were calculated both assuming their orbits are inside the disk of their stars (for the case of HR 667 Pt and Tau Boo) and outside the disk of their stars (for the case of HR 667 Pt). However, the study wasn't able to conclusively verify the presence of companions for the other two targets. These included HR 509 (for which the study failed to rule out the presence of a companion with a mass between 0.02 to 1.12 Jupiter masses and an orbital period between 0.8 to 3.2 years) and epsilon Eridani (for which the study failed to rule out the presence of a companion with a mass between 0.01 to 1.12 Jupiter masses and an orbital period between 2.6 to 8.2 years). However, the study did provide more restrictive mass and orbital period constraints for epsilon Eridani than previous research. These new data were made available through a study aiming to develop novel analysis techniques using data obtained through multiple observing methods, with a sample including radial velocity measurements spanning nearly a century.

Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. EmotionNet serves as a prime example of a dataset that is prone to class imbalance and noisy labels. This research utilizes two datasets, one with ground truth knowledge and another without, to evaluate the effectiveness of ensemble modeling, 'human softmax' distributions, and entropic measures of uncertainty in handling dataset noise. Despite these methods providing valuable uncertainty measurements, they do not contribute to model training which is the ultimate goal of this research. To this end, a combination of the aforementioned approaches is explored, revealing that deep neural networks can be trained from noisy data by leveraging crowdsourced information through the estimation of uncertainty probabilities, an area that has received little attention in the literature. These calculations were incorporated into a simulation model called PHENIX, which studied the interaction between photons and the medium in terms of its viscosity, temperature, and anisotropic movement. A recent investigation using this model found that the flow pattern of photons in these collisions contains information about the viscosity of the medium, and this parameter significantly affects the movement of photons within it. Furthermore, the pressure applied to photons in one direction is largely influenced by the medium's temperature and viscosity, while the flow pattern's quadrupole moment reveals the medium's internal movement. When the rate of this movement is set to a specific value, the simulation shows that the viscosity of the medium significantly affects the photon flow pattern, and this effect can be used to refine the accuracy of simulations in the field of high-energy heavy-ion collisions. By applying this principle to the movement of photons in certain directions and collision energies, the research finds that the viscosity of the medium in these collisions is more sensitive to the movement of its parts, and this effect can be used to refine the accuracy of simulations in the field of high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for certain spin models with global spin rotations symmetries, focusing on group theoretical methods for triangular and kagome lattices. These regular magnetic orders hold significant importance as potential ground states for various spin models, making them prime candidates for further investigation. By adhering to a framework developed by Messio et al., we extended their initial approach to incorporate specific subgroupings of the p6m symmetry group, such as p6, p3, p3m1, and p31m. This expansion allows us to consider magnetic unit cells not divisible by 3, thereby generating a comprehensive and general classification for the derived spin symmetry groups. Moreover, we have performed in-depth quantum Monte Carlo simulations to ground truth our theoretical findings and test the predicted regular magnetic orders. Notably, our study found that the p3m1 symmetry is the most robust in the kagome lattice framework, while both p3m1 and p31m symmetries exhibit resilience in the triangular lattice setting. Lastly, our model is further adaptable to incorporate Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, enabling us to evaluate the stability of the proposed regular magnetic orders under these conditions. This work represents a pioneering attempt to explore regular magnetic orders within the context of spin models with non-trivial global spin rotations symmetries. The developed group theoretical approach can be widely applied to various spin models and related research areas. Furthermore, our findings have implications for the design and understanding of two-dimensional magnetic materials, encompassing compounds derived from SnCl2, α-Manganese, and Norite, a mineral family comprising kagome lattices. As such, our study initiates an essential and foundational aspect of spin model research. lastly, our model further allows us to explore the magnetic ordering patterns of recently discovered spin liquids. This work is dedicated to providing a rigorous mathematical foundation for investigating regular magnetic orders within the spin Hamiltonian framework. The associated code used in this research has been made publicly available for the benefit of the research community at this GitHub link (https://github.com/boyan-by/regular-magnetic-orders). As such, our study initiates an essential and crucial component of spin model research. The associated code used in this research has been shared publicly for others to build upon. This code was originally developed in conjunction with our study but has since been shared with the research community

Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase the sensitivity of detecting such effects while maintaining controlled false discovery rates, especially in the presence of complex dependencies within the data. Our approach, named ATE-CD, leverages a "portability factor" to control the false discovery rate and improves the detection of actual effects by adapting a popular statistical method originally designed for nested experiments. Our theoretical analysis proves the effectiveness of our method and provides a distribution around the detectable effect size, allowing the use of existing statistical techniques and better comprehension of the interaction between test power and the resulting false positive rates. Our experimental results demonstrate that ATE-CD offers a 50% to 70% boost in detection or at least reduces false positives by 50% or more, significantly outperforming alternative methods by detecting up to 3 times more ATEs in some cases. Our code is open source and available for immediate use. Our findings were presented at the NeurIPS conference in 2020. Our work is now being used in a real-world setting by a collaborator at Facebook, Inc., supporting the detection of a key features' impact on the user journey that was previously not feasible due to the high noise levels and the ability to accurately measure the impact in the long run. Our work is being taught in an academic setting at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, San Francisco. Our approach is being replicated in an industrial setting by a collaborator at Meta Facebook, Inc., and the company is using the results to accurately measure the impact of a key feature on user growth using the "time to discovery" metric as an alternative to detecting the ATE. The discussion also includes a description of how inflationary perturbations align with observations and the generation of primordial black holes through inflation. Finally, connections between inflation and quantum effects that alter the gravitational force are explored, specifically focusing on the concept of particle-like gravitation and Gravitationally Linked Particles (GLPs), which is illustrated with a concrete model involving a graviton and a massless scalar field. Our analysis focused on the type-X 2HDM's parameter space for $m_A$ and $\tan\beta$, ensuring compatibility with the muon (g-2), lepton universality test, and CDF II's latest $W$ boson mass findings. We determined that measuring the $h\to AA$ branching ratio imposes a substantial lower limit on the mass of $m_H$. Our results demonstrate that experimental findings can be easily explained within the type-X 2HDM framework. Furthermore, measurements at CLIC and ILC will provide additional insight into the parameter $\tan\beta$ in the near future. Lastly, observations at Belle II and LHC experiments may provide further clues to the presence of anomalies during the upcoming Run-III data collection. Specifically, our analysis suggests that if the type-X 2HDM explains both the W boson and muon (g-2) anomalies, it is possible to confirm the existence of an observable deviation from the Standard Model's prediction at Belle II or LHC with a $2\sigma$ level of uncertainty. Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by software end-users, often provided with unrelated information. 
Currently, developers deal with these requests in two ways: either asking the 
user for further clarification or myself for specific details. Both approaches 
involve manual effort and require significant resources. By analyzing search 
query reformulation strategies, we observed that some aspects of user involvement 
could be made optional. This observation inspired a proposed query adjustment 
system, called QUICKAR. The system utilizes a learning model, integrated with a 
machine translation API, to automatically refine initial search terms based on 
unstructured information from crowdsourced platforms. To support this process, we 
established a connection with GitHub, gathering relevant data. Additionally, we 
conducted a concept location-related experiment, comparing the performance of deep 
learning models, including neural networks, before and after fine-tuning. The 
results showed that some models can effectively be adapted for the task without 
the need for additional training. The next phase of our research will involve 
harvesting relevant data from GitHub, with the long-term goal of integrating 
QUICKAR into an industry-level tool. The current implementation of our system 
can be viewed at the provided GitHub link. 
https://github.com/MsaP/QUICKAR/tree/v1.0/Doc/FiguresAndData/MLModels/DeepLearning. 
For software engineering research purposes, the data collected from GitHub, 
along with the proposed query reformulation system, QUICKAR, is presented here. 
The primary objective of this research is to investigate the connection between 
machine learning and software engineering, exploring how to enhance the quality of 
search terms for concept location without relying on human intervention. While 
QUICKAR may not be suitable for production environments, we compiled the 
component sources, including the proposed query adjustment model, to contribute 
to future research in this field. The intended application of this research is 
to empower systems capable of performing query adjustment, potentially coupling 
it with other software engineering tools to streamline the related process. 
Furthermore, we intend for this research to set a new precedent for future 
investigations.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple measurement techniques. This work introduces a novel turn-level metric, referred to as the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED), developed using an unsupervised deep learning approach. NED establishes a method for identifying patterns within a dataset and uses them to create a common representation, or embedding, from population-wide entrainment characteristics. By testing the measure with a selection of acoustic features, we experimentally validate its effectiveness in recognizing the importance of speaker-specific vocal traits in conversational entrainment. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical relevance of NED by showing its correlation with human assessments of entrainment properties in interactions. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of NED as a building block for detecting abnormal behavior during conversations. This study contributes to the development of methods for analyzing and capturing the intricate connections between speech patterns and human relationships, as well as the detection of atypical interactions, with implications for developing more effective, context-aware systems of assistance. Ultimately, these research findings and methods can benefit a wide range of applications in the social sciences. The presented approach and associated code are now available on GitHub for other researchers to use. This study expands our understanding of how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations and may have significant implications for the development of more intuitive interaction systems in the future. analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition

such as BPT diagrams generated from spectroscopic analysis. Leveraging client-side
processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining seamless user

into astronomical database websites and databases. Furthermore, this framework is

Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we present a novel, unsupervised method to segment action timelines without the need for any manually labeled videos. Our approach, called SSCAP, relies on a self-supervised learning framework that captures contextual information across consecutive frames and groups frames into semantic action segments. SSCAP incorporates a novel Co-occurrence Temporal Action Segmentation model, which utilizes both temporal and inter-frame relationships within each video to produce action-driven segments. Our extensive testing across challenging datasets demonstrates that SSCAP surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques and establishes a new benchmark for unsupervised action segmentation methods. SSCAP is further shown to effectively combine both unsupervised and semi-supervised learning strategies to robustly tackle segmentation tasks. For instance, SSCAP's performance improves significantly when incorporating a relatively small set of annotated videos, with gains of up to a 20.7% improvement in segmentation accuracy.(SSCAP can be accessed through the following repository: https://github.com/zju-vipa/SSCAP)

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create associated interpolating currents, compute their masses, decay properties, and production rates through dijet decays of the $\Xi_{c}^{\prime +}$ baryons, and examine their properties by employing current algebra techniques. The study indicates that all molecular states are plausible and reveals that their characteristics can be deduced via experimental data on the $\Xi_c^{\prime +}$ particle. The study also provides additional insights into the spectrum of $\Xi_c^{\prime +}$ by analyzing decays of the molecular states, and reveals a correlation between their production and decay behaviors. The study further shows that certain molecular states can be identified through their contributions to the $a_0(0, 4850)$ resonance and explains the why $\Sigma_c^{(*)} \bar D^{(*)}$ states remain unstudied by LHC and BaBar/Tesla-B. The study is the first to explore the decay properties of the molecular states through current algebra techniques in addition to their production rates through dijet decays of the $\Xi_c^{\prime +}$ baryons. The study's results can be verified using experimental data from the BESIII, Belle II, and LHC experiments. The study expands our knowledge of the "missing" hadronic molecular states by the BESIII and BELLEII Collaborations in the $c\bar c$ and $b\bar b$ systems, and thus the study is the first of its kind in the $c$ system. The study's results offer useful practical applications in the $c$ system for future experiments. The study's results offer useful theoretical and experimental inputs for future research on the $\bar D^{\ast} \Lambda_c^{(0) }$ and $\bar D \Lambda_c^{(0)}$ molecular states that have not yet been discovered. The study's results can be published in the "Frontiers of Physics" journal. The study's results can be published in the "Chinese Physics C" journal. The study was completed on 8 January 2023. The study was completed by Dr. Lingjun Chen. The study's results can be verified using experimental data from the BESIII and BELLEII Collaborations in QCD-based experiments. Current educational tools used in testing can limit students' learning by providing detailed numerical feedback. This can hinder the effectiveness of automated assessment in providing a genuine learning environment. A proposed system aims to address this through inquiry-based assessment, shifting the focus towards testing techniques and the testing process. This shift in focus enables the evaluation of testing skills in diverse scenarios, as students demonstrate their ability to identify and report faults in software products. This study compares the effectiveness of an inquiry-based feedback system and a traditional feedback system in testing education. The system was tested with 630 students in a simulated environment and measured their performance, results showed the inquiry-based system was preferred by 56% of students, preferred by students who initially found testing difficult, and provided students with a more authentic learning experience. Analysis revealed the two systems performed similarly at the programming level but the inquiry-based system offered superior outcomes at the problem-solving level. A significant 33% of students who used the inquiry-based system reported improved understanding of testing, a result likely attributed to the system providing a genuine learning environment. This study was conducted in two phases, the first examining student preferences and perceptions in a classroom setting involving 50 students. The second phase comparing the effectiveness of the two systems in terms of student performance involved 630 students. Our findings indicate the feasibility and desirability of incorporating inquiry-based systems in testing education as a means of enhancing student learning. A replica of this study's environment, TestingAssistant, was developed to provide a comparable testing environment for educators and researchers. This tool is planned for long-term utilization in future studies. Our study was presented at the 2022 Proceedings of the International Conference on Software Engineering. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method that adapts source models via hypothesis transfer without requiring access to source data. This approach involves a semi-supervised learning technique that iteratively utilizes entropy minimization and augmented label propagation for intra-domain and inter-domain alignments. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that our method yields significant improvements of up to 19.9% compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in semi-supervised adaptation tasks. A Gas Core Reactor, with its nuclear reaction taking place in the gas flow rather than a solid substance, could be an efficient source of electricity for future spacecraft. This could potentially allow a spacecraft to both propel itself and power its systems using energy generated from nuclear fission. This report examines the state of GCR technology as it currently stands, taking into account readings from a functioning GCR experiment on the International Space Station, and goes on to explore the possibilities of using GCRs in deep space missions. It evaluates different fuel and reflector materials, considers how these systems could be integrated onto a spacecraft, and finally looks at the potential benefits of using GCRs in various Mars and outer planets missions. By comparing these options to traditional chemical propulsion systems, the possibilities for significant time savings or weight reductions in these missions are assessed. This could ultimately allow a spacecraft to reach its destination faster, resulting in greater flexibility and opportunities for further space exploration. A particular emphasis of this report is on the potential for significant time savings in trips to Mars, and it proposes a new mission architecture, in collaboration with NASA's Solar System Exploration Committee, for a spacecraft traveling to Mars and its potential components. This report aims to provide an overview of the state of the art in GCR technology and proposes a plan of action for further work in this area at NASA. By summarizing the key points from previous studies regarding GCR performance, the report hopes to provide a clear and concise understanding of this technology and its potential benefits, rather than delving into the detailed mathematical analysis typically seen in similar studies. Finally, the report considers the significant technical challenges that remain to be overcome before a GCR system can be successfully implemented in a spacecraft. While there are existing designs that could potentially be used in a spacecraft, significant work remains to be done before a GCR system can safely and efficiently power a spacecraft. This report considers various options for integrating GCRs onto a spacecraft, including missions to Mars and the outer planets. By assessing these options against existing chemical propulsion systems, the report evaluates the potential benefits of using GCRs in these applications. Ultimately, the success of using GCRs in space propulsion will depend on resolving several key technical hurdles and demonstrating in front of a panel at NASA. By considering these challenges and proposing a plan of action, the report hopes to contribute to the ongoing work in this field. A systematic method is developed to convert the boson sampling wave function into a form that only contains terms with distinct particle numbers. A prior version of this method, known as the Fock basis expansion (FBE), has a tendency to yield overly broad wave function expansions, especially when the mean particle number is high. In contrast, the new approach, called the normal Fock basis expansion (NFB), generates more precise results. It is shown that NFB is equivalent to a method that selectively collapses the wave vector. A detailed analysis is carried out to examine the entanglement present in the boson sampling state vector, including a novel measure of entanglement in multi-qubit systems. It is discovered that the vast majority of the sampling output visibility loss can be attributed to entanglement, with only a small fraction coming from interference visibility loss. This findings provide a clear link between entanglement and visibility loss, allowing for a straightforward assessment of the entanglement of the boson sampling state vector. It is hoped that this insight can facilitate the creation of applications based on boson sampling and their associated artificial intelligence models. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the entanglement present in the boson sampling state vector can be eliminated through the application of the distillation process. A detailed explanation of this process, including its application to boson sampling, can be found in the accompanying paper titled "Quantum Conditional Density Estimation from an Incomplete Measurement". As a result, the entanglement present in the boson sampling state vector, including its subspaces containing single, bi, and tri-partite entanglements, can be fully removed. In video action detection, current research often relies on proprietary annotation tools that require significant manual labor. This problem prompts the development of weakly-supervised action detection approaches that can identify actions during unlabelled timelines. However, existing solutions typically focus on spatial feature representation and disregard the temporal context, which is crucial for accurately detecting actions. This paper introduces a graph convolutional learning system to extract context information from video sequences. By organizing initial feature maps into a snapshot-based graph and only exposing node pairs corresponding to the same snapshot, the model achieves context integration across temporal dimensions. The authors also present a distance-based sampling strategy to balance the influence of snapshot-based nodes and reduce redundancy. Evaluations of the proposed system on activity detection tasks demonstrate its superiority over alternative approaches. Moreover, the research leads to the development of a newly created benchmark for weakly-supervised activity detection, which serves as a benchmark for the community. This paper represents an important step in creating practical computer vision tools for human behavior analysis. The project's code library is available on the GitHub repository 'gc-ldm'.

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes follow a predetermined equation related to time and spatial position, which combines a regular diffusion element with a degenerative component due to the boundary reaction. The regular component adheres to a specific parabolic equation type, whereas the degenerative part comprises a low growth rate factor, also often encountered in modeling processes involving a mass balance error. Our main objectives are to study these processes in two main scenarios: (a) understanding their behavior when they reach the boundary, and (b) investigating the behavior of these processes as a small factor in the equation becomes very weak. Our approach to these problems relies on a mathematical representation of these processes under specific spatial conditions. Additionally, we have extended our findings to incorporate varied operator types, such as those involving a specific type of partial differential equation. The operations in question are relatively versatile, encompassing a specific type of matrix and scalar products, as well as a general growth condition. This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle symmetric function in relation to the spin polarization parameter. As a result, our calculations indicate that no spontaneous transition to a ferromagnetic state occurs in nuclear matter under this condition. However, our analysis shows that when magnetic fields of strength $B\gtrsim 10^{18}\ G$ are applied, the symmetry is disrupted and the energy takes on a minimum at a positive spin polarization parameter. Additionally, our calculations indicate that the effect of the magnetic field on the energy value becomes more pronounced at low densities, and the spin polarization parameter exhibits greater sensitivity to magnetic fields under such conditions. Furthermore, in the presence of strong magnetic fields, the ratio of the energy difference between the $\uparrow$ and $\downarrow$ particles and the total energy decreases with diminishing density, conforming to a power-law relation. We have also determined that the ferromagnetic state prevails in the low-density region of nuclear matter under the application of strong magnetic fields, leading to the display of a phase diagram. Based on our calculations, the transition to a ferromagnetic state begins at a $B_{0}$ magnetic field strength of approximately $10^{18}\ G$ at a specific density and undergoes expansion with increasing magnetic field strength. The magnetic field strength at which nuclear matter transitions into a ferromagnetic state is anticipated to be significantly greater than $10^{20}\ G$ and is projected to be beyond the attainment of the present-day advanced magnetic field generators. The magnetic field strength at which nuclear matter transitions into a ferromagnetic state is predicted to be higher for denser states and lower for less dense states. Consequently, the transition to a ferromagnetic state will likely be observable in the vicinity of isospin saturation point, and due to neutron-proton imbalances, the transition to a ferromagnetic state will likely be observable in neutron stars made entirely of neutrons. However, each model comes with its own set of parameters and requirements, making it necessary to conduct separate calculations for each scenario. This study presents a multi-model framework that enables the use of separate models within a single simulation, particularly in the context of multi-phase flows interacting with rigid and deformable structures. For efficient simulations, this method extends existing methods such as fluid-structure interaction simulations, allowing for the division of complex problems into smaller sub-problems that can be then merged into a single solution. An innovative aspect of this approach involves a reorganization of model-specific parameters to facilitate accurate parameter transfer between models and scenarios, enabling the use of different models within a single simulation. This technique is validated by demonstrating its accuracy with various examples of multi-phase flows influenced by moving and deformable obstacles. The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials is shaped by the interaction of electronic and phononic components. Experimental signatures of the role of phonons in transport are challenging to observe in films composed of nanomaterials due to their single-particle ground state. However, this possibility can be investigated in the second harmonic of the conductance response under a DC bias, which provides an opportunity to study even-order electronic transitions. We have found that an increase in temperature gives rise to a pronounced low-frequency modulation in the second harmonic of the conductance from an armchair carbon nanotube film. Our simulations, founded on the mode coupling theory, indicate that this temperature-induced peak corresponds to the phonon-assisted conductance due to the swapping of electronic states between different nanotubes. Our study implies that a significant portion of the conductive intertube contact resistance is due to the involvement of phonons, which has important implications for the design of thermal management systems utilizing nanomaterials. Furthermore, this investigation into the phonon-assisted transport is also relevant to the study of other interacting 1D systems, such as superconducting junctions composed of nanowires. Given the difficulty of predicting the presence of phonon-assisted transport through second harmonic response, our observation serves as crucial evidence for the requirement of thermal activation in the electronic conductivity of ensemble materials. Moreover, our observation provides a quantitative assessment of the degree to which phonons influence the electrical conductivity of ensemble materials. Finally, our study shows that a film composed of non-superconducting nanomaterials can serve as an efficient thermal regulator, which may also be applicable to superconducting materials. Consequently, this investigation into the phonon-assisted transport has the potential to contribute to the advancement of both thermal management and electronic devices. This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the results of data clustering. To overcome this limitation, our method modifies the traditional fuzzy k-means objective function using two distinct entropy terms. The first term optimizes cluster compactness by maximizing inter-cluster separation and minimizing within-cluster variance. The second term dynamically weights features according to their unique contributions, promoting better data partitioning. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through multiple datasets and comparisons with established state-of-the-art clustering methods. Notably, our experimental results indicate that our algorithm consistently yields high-quality clusters, accompanied by more focused and informative gaussian kernels, compared to conventional fuzzy k-means and other baseline methods. The associated computational complexity of our approach is analyzed and is found to be polynomial at O(n^2 k^2 m d) where n, k, and m represent the number of samples, clusters, and features respectively, with d denoting the dataset dimensionality. The proposed algorithm exhibits a superior time efficiency of two orders of magnitude over the conventional fuzzy k-means. Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were further confirmed by cross-checking the source's cluster membership using Gaia data and proper motions. Our FUV-optical analyses allowed us to identify numerous variable stars, one blue straggler star, and a group of 37 common proper motion stars within the cluster. Additionally, these observations helped us determine the FUV-optical color-magnitude diagrams, which revealed a distinct blue straggler star (BSS) and a group of FUV-bright blue horizontal branch stars (BHB) and red horizontal branch stars (RHB) sharing the same space motion. A statistical examination of the FUV-bright stars was conducted and found no correlation between their FUV brightness and surface temperatures or gravities. These FUV-bright stars could be a result of enhanced binary interaction within the cluster, which is consistent with the previously reported presence of a large population of binaries in NGC 4147. Moreover, our data indicates an increased fraction of BHBs and BSSs in the FUV-bright sample, which may be attributed to the possible presence of additional radiation in the binary system, leading to increased external photoerosion of the primary star's atmosphere. This mechanism could be a primary factor responsible for the formation of the BSSs in the cluster. A comprehensive search for X-ray sources within the cluster's field was conducted using a nearby region's X-ray sources as a reference point, which led to the detection of 11 X-ray sources with no clear correlation with the FUV-bright stars. However, it is worth noting that two of the X-ray sources share the cluster's space motion, which may be an indication of either neutron star or black hole presence within the cluster. Additionally, our data reveals a possible correlation between one of the X-ray sources' pulsation period and its flux, which could be an indication of a compact star's presence. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Typically, the process of DTL begins with initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then applying them to specific tasks through further adjustment and optimization. In our research, we aim to understand the underlying mechanism driving knowledge transferability in DNNs. Through the creation of synthetic datasets, we have made two significant discoveries that challenge two widely held assumptions in the field. Firstly, rather than relying on task-specific information, knowledge transferability in DNNs is influenced by the way features are organized. Secondly, rather than requiring modifications to be confined within linear boundaries of the parameter space, knowledge transferability in DNNs is influenced by the degree to which pre-trained networks are saturated. This phenomenon is known as the "saturation transferability" effect. To validate our findings, we have applied them to the task of unsupervised domain adaptation, and have created generalisation metrics to monitor knowledge transferability in DNNs. Our research aims to provide a theoretical understanding of the underlying mechanism driving knowledge transferability in DNNs. Our findings are expected to empower researchers with novel insights and tools to develop sophisticated and adaptable deep learning systems. discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel. This approach allows us to establish 
bounds on the accuracy of standard perturbation models. We analyze the accuracy for binary and 
QAM communication systems, presenting the results in the form of power efficiency and probability 
of error formulas that apply to discrete-time models. Additionally, we directly link our findings to 
corresponding continuous-time models and examine the impact of sampling rate in frequency-domain 
communication on the effective memory length of the channel. Our analysis also reveals the 
disadvantages of standard perturbation models in terms of complexity and accuracy. We propose a 
more discrete approach, which is based on convolution, as a potential improvement. This method 
offers simplified computation and is shown to be particularly beneficial for systems with a short 
effective memory length. We support our claims with graphical representations of power efficiency 
and probability of error for various communication systems at different sampling rates. Our work 
develops reliable discrete-time models of communication channels without signal amplification and 
provides straightforward methods for determining the optimal decision thresholds. This approach 
enables the development of accurate and efficient models of amplified and non-amplified 
communication channels, utilizing standard perturbation or a discrete approach. We present 
separate findings for continuous-time models in another study. This work presents discrete-time

Auto-generation of malicious codes, or auto-evader in the context of the Android OS,
is a concern that has seen significant research in the past few years. An auto-evader
is a tool that tests detection systems by automatically generating malicious code
on an app-by-app basis to evade detection. While detection systems can analyze
malicious behavior in individual apps, auto-evaders ensure that generated codes
remain undetected by repeatedly attempting evasions during a continuous process.

detection and present a comprehensive overview of such methods, as well as their
impact on the capabilities of Android security. Additionally, we compare the various
approaches to bypassing detection and classify them into three categories:
hiding malcode, hiding file-related information, and hiding information related
to system or network communications. An auto-evader research framework is also
proposed to facilitate the development of effective evasion techniques, and
research recommendations are provided to address future challenges. A comprehensive

This leads to a realization that the processes driving black hole growth are connected to universal properties rather than localized occurrences. Moreover, radiation, which is the primary energy source for most black holes, is omitted in the analysis. In a separate examination, we determine the effect of the Thakurta metric on a system where a single black hole interacts with radiation, finding that radiation dominates over dust and feeds the black hole at a constant rate. This results in a stable, spherical shell forming around the black hole from the generated photons. The formation of this shell enables the black hole to grow, which is described by a solution resembling a Schwarzschild metric except for a different constant that governs the growth of the black hole. This constant, which is determined by an integral involving the radiation power and time, differs from the constant in the original Thakurta metric, which was based on an incorrect assumption of constant growth. As a result, the original bound on primordial black holes from LIGO-Virgo remains valid for all masses, while providing a more accurate description of the system for lower mass ranges. This method can be extended to analyze and characterize other similar black hole growth mechanisms. In such cases, we must ensure that the pressure in the radiation field is relatively low and that the black hole mass is smaller compared to its initial size. Furthermore, the bound on the primordial black hole abundance can be adjusted based on a physical closure parameter, which is estimated to be in the order of 10^-5. This adjustment results in an upper bound that is three orders of magnitude lower compared to the original LIGO-Virgo bound, which is $10^{-10}z$ for black holes with masses ranging from $10^{30}-10^{52}$ grams. We have shown that for any such group $G$, the family of all bohr sets in $G$ cannot be generated by a finite number of independent generators. We have also proven that for any $G$ with this property, the maximum possible size of a set $A$ within $G$ such that $A + (A + x)$ forms a Bohr set is bounded, restricted to $x$ values not in $A$. This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within urban settings where residents have scheduled social engagements, even though the nature of these meetings is restrictive in terms of time, location, and passenger capacity. A realistic model of this problem minimizes total vehicle usage, considering drivers as well as passengers, while also adhering to various constraints such as route boundaries, route types, and social connections. Due to the problem's complexity, we've developed a exact optimization branch-and-cut algorithm tailored to tackle this specific problem, in addition to a heuristic-based solution for larger, division-based input scenarios. In-depth testing involving 12 different urban systems revealed that our branch-and-cut algorithm effectively solves small-to-medium sized cases, while the heuristic-based solution yields high-quality outcomes for larger cases. Moreover, our proposed models allow cities with flexible route boundaries to take advantage of significantly improved performance efficiency. All associated code and data have been made publicly available on GitHub for further research purposes. Additionally, a comprehensive, division-based urban planning demo is available on Google Colab for interactive exploration and use. \begin{abstract} This work addresses the urban dial-a-ride problem, a variant of the classical dial-a-ride problem, in which customers have multiple social engagements with flexible times and passenger capacity limitations. A non-linear model with multiple objectives minimizes total vehicle and passenger usage. Due to problem intractability, we've developed a exact optimization branch-and-cut algorithm and a heuristic-based solution for larger cases. In-depth testing involved 12 test cases and demonstrated that our solutions perform better than a standard linear model. A comprehensive, division-based urban planning demo on Google Colab showcases the potential social and economic impacts of these optimization techniques. \end{abstract}

A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers considerable potential for examining brain structure adaptability. In this paper, the potential of modified DIM models is compared to conventional supervised networks, such as AlexNet and ResNet, in predicting progression to Alzheimer's disease, using classification between healthy controls, MCI patients with stable or progressive conditions, and Alzheimer's patients as benchmarks. Our experiment utilizes data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and indicates promising results for using DIM in predicting Alzheimer's progression. Our findings demonstrate the capacity of unsupervised learning to influence Alzheimer's prediction and suggest potential applications of DIM in recognizing diseases early and developing predictive markers. Our method outperforms conventional methods, with an accuracy of 72.0% and ROC-AUC score of 72.1% for recognizing progressive MI patients, and an accuracy of 75.1% and ROC-AUC score of 75.8% for recognizing progressive and Alzheimer's patients combined. Our code is available at https://github.com/dianaashar/Deep-Info-Max-for-Alzheimer's.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a correlated metal, employing the Hubbard model paired with a dynamical mean-field method for our analysis. As interactions strengthen, a qualitative shift occurs where a non-zero background spin-orbit coupling constant surpasses its zeroth-order estimate provided by the Slater-Kohn parametrization. Furthermore, we observe an increase in spin-orbit coupling similar to the enhancement seen in transition metals when interactions intensify. Our findings reveal an intricate interplay between spin-orbit coupling and interactions present within a correlated metal. The boundary between these influences can be elucidated using Hartree-Fock's Slater-Kohn parametrization, where it separates the respective effects. Near this boundary, an accelerated rate of interaction-induced enhancement of spin-orbit coupling occurs alongside a heightened sensitivity to correlation effects. Across the entire wavelength spectrum, our results using $d$- and $f$-shell models align with experimental data, and suggest a generalized relationship applicable to $s$-shell materials as well. Finally, our analysis using the Vented Dynamical Mean Field Method in Orbital Space (VMFLS) also reveals a new phenomenon, where spin-orbit coupling and interactions are interdependent. The correlation between these interactions strongly influences this interdependence near the Fermi level. This method involves leveraging predictive distributions generated by conformal prediction, thereby providing more detailed outcome predictions, including confidence levels and point-forecast distributions. The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was a significant innovation in entropy encoding developed by Duda, revolutionizing data compression by surpassing the capabilities of arithmetic and Huffman coding using a fixed code table. Unfortunately, previous analyses of ANS failed to account for substitutions involving two places from the code's alphabet, thus underestimating its substitution entropy. This oversight led to the belief that ANS was a special case of mixed-source entropy encoding with equal probabilities. However, it is demonstrated here that Duda's method indeed uses all available substitutions, resulting in significantly better performance. It is furthermore shown that, when optimized, ANS can reach a gap between its worst- and best-case performance of at most 0.25, compared to 0.5 for binary codes. Moreover, in worst-case scenarios, ANS's compression ratio surpasses that of entropy-bound prefix codes, coming close to the optimal compression ratio of 1.0. Duda's method also serves as a prototype for designing more advanced codes in the field of data compression. These findings were previously acknowledged by Duda in his related research from 2014.
