We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on a nearly G2-manifold with a real Killing spinor. We utilize these findings to create a gradient-like metric on the space of almost contact G2 structures, leading to a proof that the structure is normalizable. Consequently, this allows us to define a metric with the property of being nearly parallel and real Killing, and admits an abelian instanton. Our analysis also encompasses the SO3-bundle transition instantons on A-bundles. Although these are not rigid, we utilize the deformation theory to establish that the middle dimensional Dehn twists of a resolution of the conical singularity are equivalent in the stringy fundamental group of a quiver on conical seven-dimensional Calabi-Yau manifolds. This finding has the implication that the instanton part of the twisted connected sum does not contribute to the Kahler potential when normalizing the metric, and that we can preserve a Calabi-Yau metric on the twisted connected sum due to a particular property of the instanton. This property is that the instanton is a zero section deformation of a real divisor on the twisted compactification of P^6 and the symplectic form defined by the instanton is closed due to being holomorphically non-degenerate. This leads to the conclusion that the middle dimensional Dehn twists of a resolution of a conical singularity are equivalent in the stringy fundamental group of a quiver on conical seven-dimensional Calabi-Yau manifolds that meet certain cohomological conditions. This finding has the implication that the instanton part of the twisted connected sum does not preserve a Calabi-Yau metric on the twisted compactification P/W_{\tau} of projective spaces, but the metric can be corrected by adding a real divisor Dehn twist. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, has led to widespread infections and fatalities in many countries. In an effort to mitigate its impact, governments have implemented a range of preventive measures, including restricting public gatherings, enforcing isolation protocols, and promoting the widespread use of contact tracing mobile apps to help contain the virus's spread. These contact tracing apps, which are designed to identify individuals who have come into close contact with someone who has tested positive for COVID-19, rely on the collection and sharing of user location data, making them a significant source of sensitive user information. This has raised serious concerns among the public and experts regarding the potential risks to user privacy. To address these concerns, we conducted a systematic analysis of the privacy policies of contact tracing apps, including the Coronav\'irus-SUS app, which is one of the most widely used systems in Brazil. During our investigation, we found that the Coronav\'irus-SUS app, which is used in over 12 cities and states across Brazil, does not adhere to any formalized privacy policy, despite being required to do so by local legislation. To better understand the potential risks to user privacy, we developed a table that outlines the types of sensitive information that are collected and shared by the app, as well as the entities with access to this information. Our findings are significant because they illustrate the importance of ensuring that the locations where contact tracing apps are developed and used have adequate mechanisms in place to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of the sensitive information that is collected and shared. Moreover, the findings highlight the importance of making information on app usage transparent, including the results of investigations into potential data breaches. This is essential for maintaining user trust in these apps, which is crucial for their effective use in the fight against COVID-19. Finally, the findings are important because they highlight the importance of ensuring that the laws and regulations that govern the use of sensitive information for public health purposes are strictly enforced. If these laws and regulations are not enforced, they become meaningless, and individuals are left vulnerable to data breaches and other forms of data abuse. This has significant implications because it could ultimately erode public confidence in the use of contact tracing apps, which is critical for their success in the fight against COVID-19. Therefore, the recommendations presented in this study are important because they aim to ensure that the locations where contact tracing apps are developed and used have the necessary mechanisms in place to ensure the security of the sensitive information that is collected and shared.

Our findings show the Iochroma family's location within two adjacent three-body resonance zones - specifically 3J-1M-3 and 5J 3S-2. This paper establishes the precise positioning of these resonances as well as their demarcation boundary, providing orbital elements approximations that can inform future Iochroma family dynamics research. Moreover, the study identifies a previously unrecognized member of this family, asteroid 2016 UT3. Its spectral characteristics were also examined and compared to those of other Iochroma family members. A collective analysis of the family's proper distributions regarding semimajor axis, eccentricity, and inclination supports the hypothesis of a shared primordial origin among its members. Lastly, the study discusses the Iochroma family's origin and development. The findings suggest the family's objects underwent a significant change in their orbital configurations - specifically a widening in their separation - approximately one million years ago as part of the solar system's chaos diffusion process. This phenomenon allowed the inner members to leave the resonant region, resulting in their dispersal and separation from the outer objects. Our proper distributions analysis revealed a correlation between semimajor axis and inertia, indicating the inner objects' increased velocity and farther separation over time. This finding, along with the family's orbital distributions and broad semi-major axis range, supports the hypothesis of a complex, out-of-resonance orbital dynamics among its members. The family's objects are largely out of resonant interactions and exhibit chaotic behaviors, explaining their wide separation and the need for resonant mechanics to reunite the inner and outer objects at different times. Our UT3 discovery and analysis of the family's proper distributions and orbital distributions suggests a potential common origin among these asteroids' formation. Moreover, the study's findings of the resonant mechanics' role in the family's development expand our understanding of the chaos-diffusion process's impact on the solar system's asteroids. The study's last section discusses the family's and its members' future evolution, suggesting a potential collision course among the family's objects and the need for unified Iochroma family dynamics research in the future. This research area will significantly advance our understanding of the family's development and its members' orbital behaviors. The study provides a comprehensive and methodical astrodynamic analysis of this complex family, serving as a foundational work for the future's three-body resonance and chaos-diffusion studies. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to that of T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is established in Bar22. Consequently, our findings align with prior results involving integral cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from Weyl representations, and the rational cohomology theory of complex projective spaces derived from general finite dimensional representations. Our work also explores the T-equivariant cohomology of the zero section of the one-sheeted hyperbolic plane and verifies that a T-equivariant analog of the generator "c" of the elliptic cohomology of the one-sheeted hyperbolic plane, as defined in Gre05, is absent in the case of rational cohomology theory. Our findings further reveal, through application of a decomposition of the rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05 into a direct sum of the A-genus and the H-genus, and by identifying the characteristics of the "c = 2h" component within each genus, that the "c = 2h" component is present in the A-genus but absent in the H-genus. The curvature, represented by the Hessian matrix or the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, is a crucial indicator for optimizing the convergence and suitability of neural network models. However, extracting this information comes with significant computational costs, typically exceeding the time needed to process an entire batch. To mitigate this issue, researchers employ approximate methods to calculate the curvature, often on a batch or mini-batch level. In this study, we present ViViT, a neural network module that utilizes the low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix to efficiently calculate an accurate approximation of the curvature. By analyzing the low-rank properties through a theoretical lens, we derive a vivit module, which can be integrated into various training algorithms. Notably, when integrated with the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm, ViViT offers a significant reduction in computational costs, surpassing the current state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of ViViT, demonstrating its capacity for optimizing model performance on image classification tasks. Moreover, when paired with adaptive optimizers, ViViT's performance is further enhanced by adaptive curvature-based learning rate adjustments. As a result, when integrated with the AdaGrad optimizer, ViViT achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging image classification tasks. The vivit module's versatility allows it to be easily extended to other fields, such as natural language processing, where it can be utilized with the Hessian matrix to achieve superior performance. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. Our study uses inanimate noun embeddings from 11 languages to demonstrate that in languages indicating inanimate object gender, related words closely associate with this gender, a distinction not typically found in languages lacking such gender indicators. However, intriguingly, this association is absent in the English embeddings, despite considering the word's part of speech as a factor. Our findings suggest that in indicative languages, inanimate object gender influences the creation of noun embeddings, a representation that might be utilised in tasks like analogy completion, word relatedness calculation, or even in constructing neural networks that generate new inanimate object names. Ultimately, these embeddings mirror human perceptions of inanimate objects, a reflection of the world's underlying order. To verify this, our study employs human subject agentiality and inanimate object gender in predicting the outcomes of Synthetic Grammar, a grammatical inference method. Our analysis indicates that in languages indicating inanimate object gender, inanimate objects are seen as having attributes corresponding to their assigned gender, a factor also contributing to the creation of these embeddings. These findings reveal that in these languages, inanimate objects are perceived as having agency-like properties tied to their assigned gender. Thus, in these languages, inanimate object gender influences both inanimate object embeddings and human perceptions of inanimate objects. This change is reflected in their Life Cycle Management, shifting from a multi-faceted approach to a more integrated one. Given the rapid advancements in automation and artificial intelligence, CPS LOS are now capable of making their own strategic decisions, freeing up decision-makers to focus on higher-level tasks. However, this raises questions about the balance between human oversight and autonomy in CPS LOS, particularly in high-stress situations. Our study explores the potential of creating autonomous Cyber Physical Systems of Systems that can not only execute tasks independently but also recognize when they need human input in critical situations. We developed a framework based on Theory of Mind, ToM, which enables CPS LOS to assess the intentions and preferences of human stakeholders and assess their own level of autonomy and reliability. This framework is being used in conjunction with a comprehensive understanding of Industry 4.0 and a literature review of models and methods for representing and aggregating human intentions and preferences in intelligent systems, including LOS. We are now working to embed these concepts into a process model that can be utilized by CPS LOS in their decision-making processes. Our initial findings indicate that ToM-based models for representing human intentions and preferences are widely applied across the field. We are also exploring the feasibility of developing a standardized ontology for implementing these concepts within a Cloud-based service, known as a Knowledge Manager. Our Literaturereview includes an analysis of over 150 scientific publications from leading Industry 4.0 events and publications, while our experimental phase involves developing, implementing, and testing a working prototype as part of a University-sponsored Idea competition. Our long-term goals are to see our framework and its components, particularly the Knowledge Manager service, become a standard element of Industry 4.0 and CPS LOS design, enabling the creation of systems that are more responsive to human needs and more in tune with their own capabilities and limitations. A future University-funded project is already working to develop this service as part of a broader initiative to establish a Knowledge Manager as the foundation of a decentralized, blockchain-enabled platform for Life Cycle Management. This comprehensive system, known as MosaicLCM, is designed to promote greater cooperation and connectivity among Cyber Physical Systems of Systems by breaking down barriers to collaboration and setting out a universal vision for the future of CPS LOS. Our current research, which is already showing promising results in its experimental phase, is focused on developing, testing, and refining the concepts, components, and prototype of this vision

The model also incorporates a discrete Z2 symmetry, which precludes mixing between the standard model and the dark sector scalars, but allows the latter to mediate neutral dark matter interactions via a mechanism known as the modified Fermi-Gas model, thus enabling dark matter to be leptonically decoupled from the universe. A novel control method is introduced, capable of efficiently learning complex control strategies using small amounts of data and supplementary information about a system's dynamics. This approach relies on the concept of dynamic mode decomposition, which breaks down a controlled system's dynamics into interconnected components containing information about its behavior. By recognizing that some system states often resemble others and that local patterns of motion can be transferred between different modes, the method interprets mode transitions as a form of motion prediction. This predictive capability is further leveraged to develop proactive control strategies tailored to the system's expected behavior. As a result, the method requires only a few data points from various scenarios to generate control plans that are adaptable to different starting points and endowed with forward-looking properties. Importantly, the method is not only applicable to systems devoid of additional information but also particularly effective when used in conjunction with data on a system's swimmers, where the fundamental factors governing its behavior can be easily pinpointed. This is exemplified in a variety of simulations, including the development of a flying robot, whose successful deployment demonstrates the method's capabilities in real-world applications. This research presents a pioneering step towards the development of intelligent machines capable of learning to navigate diverse, unconventional systems using the fundamental principles of data-driven control. This work is part of the author's doctoral research, which is accessible at the provided CERM website. Furthermore, the corresponding experimental data and related code are publicly available at the specified GitHub repository. Moreover, the method's performance in actual robotic environments was jointly developed with Dr. Nicolas Chantre and Dr. Jonathan Benney and was demonstrated in a series of groundbreaking experiments, which are documented at the Dr. Jonathan Benney's website. Despite significant advancements in producing realistic images with GANs, a primary concern persists, particularly for high-resolution inputs and intricate datasets, due to training instability caused by a mismatch between the real and randomly generated distributions, leading to a common issue of vanishing gradients during GAN training. In order to mitigate this problem, previous solutions employed practical techniques, such as weight clipping and gradient penalty, to restrict the capabilities of the discriminator. In this research, a more systematic approach is presented as an alternative to tackle this problem by focusing on relationships between paired samples rather than classifying them as real or fake. Specifically, a relation network architecture for the discriminator is explored along with a specially designed triplet loss that yields superior generalization and stability in training. Extensive evaluations conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method, consisting of a relation discriminator and novel loss function, results in notable enhancements in the generation of state-of-the-art results on datasets including CIFAR-10, CelebA, Stochastic Mixup, the Places365 dataset, and the LSUN dataset for various types of neural generator architectures. Moreover, produced samples and the corresponding source code can be found on the website https://yujun-chen.github.io/relGAN/. The source code is also available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Yujun-Chen/relGAN. Furthermore, a pre-trained model based on the ResNet architecture is provided for the CelebA dataset on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Yujun-Chen/relGAN/tree/master/models. A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our approach categorizes time into two distinct frameworks: reference frames and quantum frames. Reference frames serve as a basis for establishing a universal phase reference, allowing us to achieve TF-QKD without the use of phase locking. Through data post-processing and an efficient fast Fourier transform algorithm, the phase reference can be reconciled efficiently. As a result, TF-QKD without phase locking is made feasible and achieves comparable performance to the standard method using fast Fourier transform. Furthermore, this modified scheme enables TF-QKD to function effectively even when the phase stability meets the required criterion only for a brief period. Consequently, it facilitates the accomplishment of a 100km quantum link using multi-phase encoding, with a rate of 1.209 Gbits/s. This approach provides an alternative to the standard TF-QKD method and showcases the versatility of phase referencing in the realm of quantum communication. A related patent has been filed with the date July 28, 2021. Experimental data was collected in the spring of 2020. Usage of fast Fourier transform as an alternative to phase locking introduces an added layer of complexity to the subject, warranting careful examination and potential adoption by researchers working with TF-QKD. As the underlying source code of our approach, based on the Python programming language, is presented in an highly readable and efficient manner, we believe this work could serve as a valuable resource for quantum engineers and researchers. If permission is granted, we intend to make the code open-source to the quantum community. The associated data can be found at the following link: http://202212jerry.xyz. In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators within the frameworks of the Fock space and the Bergman space on the complex plane. The key findings reveal that the Toeplitz algebra of operators with smooth weighted symbols $w$ in the Bergman space, when restricted to unweighted symbols in the Fock space, is equivalent to the subalgebra of purely Toeplitz operators within the Bergman space. This result extends earlier work found in a previous publication, in which the authors considered weighted symbols in the Bergman space itself. Additionally, we establish that the algebra of all bounded weighted symbols in the Fock space, when considered in the context of unweighted symbols in the Bergman space, corresponds to the algebra of commutative Toeplitz operators in the Fock space, parametrized by symbols in $H^\infty$, the standard Hardy space of analytic functions. The provided functional analytic evidence suggests that the Fock space and Bergman space are non-commutative in nature. As distinct and independent entities, they differ from the more well-known commutative versions, which are found on half-spaces in higher dimensions. Such a space was previously constructed by P. P. Vassiliev. To support these conclusions regarding the non-commutative nature of the Fock and Bergman spaces, we also demonstrate that the algebras in question do not contain the unit element, which is a fundamental property that distinguishes them from the more well-known commutative versions. The methods employed in this study involve exploring the linearization process of the multiplication operator, which highlights a key distinction between the domains in question: in the Bergman space, the multiplication operator is bounded, whereas in the Fock space it is unbounded. The linearization of the multiplication operator within these spaces yields pure Toeplitz operators, which form dense subalgebras in both the Bergman and Fock spaces. This study draws on techniques from a semigroup of operator algebras, which were initially introduced in the context of approximating the identity element in the commutative Hardy algebra of $H^\infty$, before being applied in the context of non-commutative Toeplitz algebras. Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small number of base categories used in each image. To mitigate this constraint, we present a new approach that employs image-level labels and a special training regime utilizing pseudo bounding-box labels to facilitate open-vocabulary object detection from a smaller set of base categories. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms previous state-of-the-art techniques and sets a new benchmark performance standard on three benchmark datasets. Our code and model dependencies are available for download on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Argus-PathSense/PseudoBBox.

A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a significant HII region and a photodissociation cavity, forming complex ion-molecular chemistry and interacting with the cloud's neutral gas. Analysis of SOFIA's optical/infrared spectroscopy data reveals the B star's strong stellar winds are likely the source of high-speed gas observed, reaching over 100 km/s. Spectroscopic observations indicate high-speed gas is dominated by atomic lines but some molecular lines also show high-speed features. Meanwhile, photodissociation cavity gas is primarily neutral hydrogen and it appears that ionized gas may be trapped behind a shock wave generated by the winds, restricted from further expansion by the cloud's dense core in the south. In addition, CO and CN gas is observed to extend beyond the photodissociation cavity, possibly indicating the influence of the B star's winds on the cloud's internal structure. Ultimately, the B star's winds have a profound impact on the distribution of gas in the region - some neutral, some ionized, and some photodissociation cavity gas, all a result of the young star's outflow. However, the southern core remains a dense cloud island where the winds do not dominate, meaning the region has yet to reach photoionization equilibrium due to the B star's influence. Moreover, the presence of high-speed molecular gas further indicates the B star's outflow impact on the cloud's internal structure. It is now clear that the photodissociation cavity is indeed the source of much of the region's ionized and atomic gas, although it appears some atomic gas may originate from the B star's winds, rather than the photodissociation cavity. The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, which rely heavily on down-sampling, Transformers have demonstrated competitive performance even when maintaining image resolution. As a result, researchers have been motivated to adopt the Transformer paradigm for computer vision tasks, leveraging its capabilities for modeling long-range dependencies. This paper aims to provide an in-depth survey of Transformer models in vision, including an overview of foundational components – multi-head attention, positional encoding, residual connections, and layer normalization – and examining prominent architectures: 1) Early Fusion models, incorporating Transformer blocks within conventional architectures; 2) Late Fusion models, incorporating Temporal Transformer blocks behind CNN/RNN exponents; 3) Pure Fusion models, leveraging end-to-end Transformer blocks constructed with learned positional encodings; and 4) Hybrid models, incorporating fusion strategies of the first two models. This paper also delves into challenges inherent to Transformer models, such as efficient implementation, training strategies, hardware considerations, and specialized hardware support. Additionally, the paper discusses future research directions and potential outcomes within the field of computer vision. The survey's primary objective is to provide an extensive literature review, offering readers a comprehensive understanding of Transformer models in vision, coupled with an evaluation of existing research methodologies and future avenues of investigation. As a result, the survey is anticipated to offer valuable insights for researchers working with Transformer models in vision and foster further exploration in this rapidly-evolving field. An associated demonstration video is available at: https://youtu.be/dxj7xk7b2QY. The source code is available at: https://github.com/asharakeh/Transformers-in-Vision-Survey.

Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical treatment and environmental shifts. We expand the classical model to create a factor model that accounts for the evolution of factor loadings over time. We introduce two methods for forecasting factor loadings and apply them to a model that effectively captures the changing relationships in mortality datasets and improves forecasting accuracy for various timeframes and regions. Moreover, a new technique based on analyzing critical points is developed and employed to identify the convergence points of time-varying factor loadings. We showcase its applicability in forecasting the changes of factor loadings and enhance the accuracy of mortality forecasting. What's more, this research offers a framework for forecasting various variables and can be adapted to different fields, such as financial forecasting. We also create a software package, called mortality forecasting module, which provides mortality forecasting functions and can be easily integrated into existing econometric software. 

Key Words: Mortality forecasting, factor models, time-series data, forecasting methods, variable influence, variable shifting, predictive methods, statistical modeling, software package, forecasting tools, econometric software. 

## Introduction

The necessity to forecast mortality rates has arisen in multiple fields, including finance, insurance, and public health. Actuaries, actuaries, economists, and researchers have developed numerous mortality forecasting models over the years. Traditional models such as the Lee-Carter model typically assume a set of stationary factors generating non-stationary time series. However, this regime is inadequate for accurately modeling real-world conditions, as factors like advancements in medical treatments and environmental shifts naturally lead to changing factor loadings. We introduce a model that accounts for this change and compare it to the traditional Lee-Carter model through analysis of their forecasting performance using various techniques, including the mean square error and the hybrid method involving recursive means.

## Methods

We start by presenting the traditional Lee-Cater model and our new time-varying factor model generating non-stationary time series. We also introduce two forecasting methods, including an expanded version of the basic model at its origin. Finally, we analyze and compare the forecasting performance of the two models using real-world datasets for regions such as the United States and 15 European countries spanning almost five decades.

However, due to interference from other models, there is often a lack of correlation between predicted accuracy and actual performance, resulting in suboptimal architectures. This study investigates the source and extent of interference in target models, and the impact it has on NAS. It introduces new sampling methods for reducing interference and presents a framework for mitigating its effects. Using the sample efficiency of child models as a reference point, the proposed framework yields significantly better test accuracy than traditional top-1 accuracy metrics. Experimental results demonstrate the value of leveraging target model relationships in NAS, and show that optimized architectures can be achieved without billions of calculations. Furthermore, the proposed framework allows for transfer learning between datasets, providing insights into the dynamics of model interactions. This knowledge can be utilized to improve NAS outcomes by altering model relationships or modifying optimizer behavior. One common technique for evaluating the characteristics of these data sets involves computing multiple statistical measures or features, which can then be represented as a feature vector for analysis. This resulting feature space enables traditional statistical techniques like clustering, regression, and classification to be applied. Multiple open-source libraries are available to extract these features, including ones written for languages like Python and R, but they come with challenges such as a lack of single unified access point, need to switch languages, and limited supporting methodologies for analysis. This paper addresses these issues with an R-based tool called theft. This tool creates a unified framework for computing features across multiple popular feature extraction libraries and also offers functions for analyzing feature spaces, which can help generate classifiable feature vectors. Its functionality for time series data analysis is demonstrated through a toy model of local-to-global inference. This toy model represents a framework for using feature extraction to simulate complex inference processes and is used to illustrate how environmental factors can be factored into a feature space. Results show that using this model with these features yields good classification results and suggests the feature space contains relevant information for analyzing systems. This paper also offers guidance on how to interpret and use feature space information with examples and provides opportunities for future methodologies to be developed within this framework. The main result demonstrates that if a metric category is affine on all boundaries of its flat subgroups, then it adds no new points to the boundary of a CAT(0) space, provided the space is a product of two hyperbolic manifolds and the group in question is a 2-torsion group. Conversely, we present a tree-based category whose leaf space is a product of hyperbolic trees, yet the leaf category remains stable only at the boundary of the tree. Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its significance, little research exists using quantitative methods to determine TQA's level of accuracy or applying statistical models to enhance its effectiveness.  Our study develops a Bayesian framework that makes it possible to assess TQA's accuracy and establishes a relationship between native speaker proficiency and TQA ratings.  We also examined whether TQA ratings can accurately predict translation quality by reviewing translation agreements and utilizing full-length translations to conduct a high-dimensional regression analysis.  Our study suggests that using TQA ratings in conjunction with other reliable performance metrics may not provide an accurate reflection of translation quality.  Moreover, using TQA ratings alone is insufficient to effectively evaluate human translator efficiency.  We discovered that utilizing TQA ratings in sentence-based models or logistic regression for efficiency evaluation may be based on flawed premises.  Our study provides that in order for TQA ratings to be an effective predictor of translation quality, speaking ability must be closely linked to translation quality as determined by native speaker ratings or other reliable performance metrics.  Utilizing expert knowledge, we developed a systematic method for establishing this connection and verifying that speaker ratings correlate with translation quality.  Our study also found that utilizing learned models from TQA data in translation quality estimation results in mediocre outcomes.  However, combining speaker ratings with other reliable performance metrics may yield substantial and trustworthy translations.  Our study is designed to help the translation industry establish reliable, comprehensive, and standardized evaluation methods.  In situations where such methods are not feasible, our study offers a theoretical model that enables effective translation evaluation.  Our study is released in the form of open-source code and data, which can be accessed via the link.  Additionally, implications of this study could lead to advancements not only in translation but also other fields requiring reliable performance assessment.  One such field is language testing, which could benefit from similar research in the future.  In summary, our study offers a cutting-edge translation industry solution. We discovered that using pruning methods on artificial neural networks significantly
reduces the need for large, complex models while maintaining their performance.
Surprisingly, these models consist of simple linear relationships.
Applying various forms of regularization including dropout, weight decay, 
and early stopping did not yield the same sparse, linear models.
The effectiveness of pruning highlights its potential as an optimization method for
reducing the computational cost of artificial neural networks.
Moreover, it simplifies the process of interpreting the predictions made by these
models as the features required for classification can be easily identified and
understood. 
Notably, our best results were achieved by combining data efficiency training 
with small, linear models obtained through pruning, ultimately reaching an accuracy 
of 50% on CIFAR-10 with a model size of 0.5 MB and 46.7% on CIFAR-100 with 2.9 MB. 
The code used for this project can be found at https://github.com/andreabocchini/comparison_of_regularization_methods. 
In summary, our study compares the efficacy of different regularization techniques
and demonstrates that under specific conditions, such as memory constraints, 
regularization techniques can lead to significant improvements in performance and 
feature understanding. 
The specific findings of this project include: 
1) Under conditions of memory restriction the best performance is achieved by 
converting fully connected models to their basal form using pruning and 
2) Regularization techniques do not yield the same sparse, linear models as 
pruning and thus do not lead to similar improvements in performance and feature 
analysis. 
Ultimately, the success of a regularization technique depends on the specific 
traininng conditions and the task at hand.

the code used may be of use to other researchers.

In lotteries with exceptionally large jackpots, as seen in Mega Millions and Powerball,
increasing bettor participation actually works to reduce the return on investment for each ticket.
The reason for this is a higher likelihood of multiple people winning with the same ticket.
In an effort to boost the return on a lottery ticket, we develop a new selection method.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an iterative procedure, it achieves more effective embeddings than the conventional t-SNE method when working with such data. Notably, vMF-SNE also outperforms a modified version of t-SNE incorporating weak regularization in most cases. Furthermore, its results are comparable to those obtained by a full vMF-based embedding algorithm, which is more computationally intensive and resource-consuming. The proposed method's benefits extend to other t-SNE applications, such as visualization of brain activity and embedding of deep neural network features. Its implementation is now freely available online. Overall, vMF-SNE presents a time-efficient, robust solution for embedding spherical data, which makes it a suitable choice for a wide range of applications. The study also sheds light on the performance of t-SNE, revealing that, in many cases, its over-reliance on Gaussian distributions results in suboptimal outcomes. With this knowledge, researchers can refine their t-SNE-based embeddings by identifying their underlying distributions and developing tailored variants as demonstrated by vMF-SNE. Lastly, from our investigations, we identify a common misconception regarding t-SNE's usage in the research community. While t-SNE's innovative and sophisticated approach to dimensionality reduction earns it a reputation as a state-of-the-art algorithm, its development was more a product of theoretical innovations than of empirical validation. In fact, our study shows that t-SNE's performance is significantly lower than what's typically observed in published studies, with correlations often over-estimated and sometimes falsely reported. Consequently, future research should prioritize thorough experimental verification to ground their findings in fact, with a focus on accurately reflecting the algorithm's capabilities. The associated code can be found on GitHub within the NeuroSpin repository at under the heading vmf_sne.

We investigate the characteristics of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, where a single impurity is attracted to a sea of Fermi particles, under conditions where their interactions have negligible spatial range. Our analysis utilizes the powerful tool of diagrammatic Monte Carlo, enabling us to explore an expansive diagrammatic series up to high orders, and evaluate the importance of simultaneous multiple particle-hole excitations within it. In this study, the ground state energies of both the polaron and the molecule as a function of interaction strength are quantified, revealing an intriguing phase transition from polaron to molecule. Our calculations also validate our predictions concerning the critical interaction threshold that separates these two regimes, and demonstrate that this result is compatible with both the extreme coupling limits and the current most advanced analytical solutions. Furthermore, the polaron's Z factor, which represents the reduced efficiency of the interaction due to the presence of the polaron, is investigated. Our findings indicate a noticeable strengthening of the effective interaction within the polaron as the critical interaction threshold is approached. Lastly, our diagrammatic Monte Carlo method's analytical limitations are understood, allowing us to pinpoint the remaining computational challenges that need to be addressed. These insights should guide the development of theoreti- and experimentalists to investigate the various correlated states arising from the interaction between an impurity and Fermi particles. Our predictive framework could be extended to the multi-component Fermi polaron, offering novel hopes for the detection of the molecule-polaron phase transitions via experimental measurements of the muon in atomic systems. Specifically, our predictions suggest the molecule-polaron phase transitions should leave detectable traces in the muon's spin relaxation rate. Our work has also laid the groundwork for investigating novel correlated states arising from the interaction of two impurities with Fermi particles. Our upcoming studies are planned to confirm the existence of the molecule-polaron phase transitions via the measurements of the optical conductivity of the 40K quantum gas near the Fermi liquid state. Our planned work is expected to significantly expand our current analytical and experimental understanding of the various correlated states arising from the interaction between impurities and Fermi particles. An associated movie is available at https://youtu.be/a2ats8z7sq0, showing the behavior of the Z factor in the two polarons through the diagrammatic Monte Carlo method. In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, where digital qubits combine with an additional analog qubit, we've investigated its potential performance and developed a method for simulating complex many-body quantum systems using the Jordan-Wigner transformation. This transformation maps the second quantization of fermions onto the antiferromagnetic Ising model, which we've applied in three different scenarios: one-dimensional, a Kitaev model, and a chiral Kagome model. By utilizing the digital qubits to represent the Fock space and the analog qubit to represent the ground state, we've found the digital qubits highly sensitive to slight changes in their encoding. Additionally, we've found the cross-talk between the digital and analog qubits to be negligible and the analog qubit to be highly resistant to digital noise, which suggests the digital qubits can be used to initiate quantum operations without disrupting the analog qubit. This noise-resistant property of the analog qubit may be useful for simulating excited states or other states represented by digital qubits. Furthermore, we've discovered the digital qubits can be used to precisely encode the analog qubit, which is essential for simulating excited states or other states within a digital qubit framework. This study provides a foundation for potential experiments and points out opportunities for improvement, such as leveraging the noise-resistant property of the analog qubit to reduce the complexity of quantum error correction in a multi-qubit system. Possible experimental implementations could involve optical or ion-trap systems, where the analog qubit could be an extra photon or a trapped Ytterbium atom serving as an additional qubit. These findings may lead to the development of an efficient quantum simulator using the hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing. Furthermore, we've proposed a method for measuring the digital analog transform of a Hamiltonian. This study could lead to the development of an accurate simulation of a fermionic system using two analog qubits, which has the potential to allow the efficient modeling of quantum materials like transition metal oxides, which are particularly significant in the field of materials science. This theoretical model could lead to the development of an efficient quantum simulator using the hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing. Additionally, we've proposed a method for simulating path-integral Monte Carlo using the digital analog transform of a Hamiltonian. This study could lead to the development of an efficient quantum simulator capable of modeling quantum systems using a digital-qubit framework. Furthermore, we've proposed a method for simulating any fermionic system using the digital analog transform

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of genus two curves to a 10-fold cover of a Teichmueller curve, which was first found by Veech. By reinterpreting this profile in terms of random geodesic flows on surfaces, we obtain a solution to a conjecture introduced by Broadcort and Moler. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in fostering success in Scrum projects conducted remotely. Our findings also show that working from home requires enhanced self-regulation abilities, and that self-determined motivation plays a vital role in successfully implementing Scrum practices in a remote context. Furthermore, we have established a complex theoretical framework that connects four distinct self-determination theory constructs with four distinct Scrum practices. The framework highlights the critical role of self-regulation in ensuring all Scrum practices are effectively implemented and adopted. Our research demonstrates that successful Sculum projects involve all six theoretical constructs, and that supporting these is crucial for home working best practices. While all theoretical constructs are crucial for successful Scrum projects conducted remotely, our research has also revealed differential effects observed for certain practices. For instance, enhancing self-regulation is crucial for ensuring successful implementation of all Scrum practices, while reinforcing relatedness is crucial for facilitating reflective daily meetings. Finally, our research reveals that implementing all 15 home working supporting practices is crucial for achieving high levels of all four success criteria for Scrum projects. The current theoretical framework, key findings, and recommendations for practitioners and researchers are presented in detail. An empirical application of LISREL has also demonstrated the complementary nature of our theoretical framework and Scrum framework, while a cross-system mapping of both theories has also been presented. The research has also uncovered several avenues for further research, and recommendations for practitioners and researchers are presented in detail. In a study using the ALICE detector at the LHC, scientists investigated the elliptical movement of electrons created when beauty particles decay at a specific point near the centre of a collision between lead nuclei at a high energy of 5.02 TeV. These electrons were observed within a narrow region and the researchers found a pattern of how these electrons and their corresponding particle pairs moved in relation to the collision conditions. The results showed a significant difference in this pattern, known as elliptical movement or elliptical v$_{0}$ value, of around 0.08, indicating beauty decays outnumbered background particle interactions, with a measured background contamination of approximately 16%. The researchers found that this pattern was consistent with what was expected, known as elliptical anisotropy, for beauty particles created in the early stages of a collision. The results of this study are of particular interest as they contribute to the understanding of how beauty particles interact with the medium created in a collision at a high energy. The researchers also compared this pattern to other experiments and theoretical models of these interactions. The results of this study show that beauty particles do not seem to move through the medium of a collision at a high energy once they have been created. This is known as 'quenching' and the researchers found the expected level of 'quenching' from several models was consistent with what was expected from beauty particles that do not interact with the medium of a collision. The researchers also found the expected level of 'quenching' from another model was consistent with what was expected from interactable particles. The results of this study show that beauty particles provide a unique opportunity to study the interactions between these particles and the medium of a collision at a high energy. The researchers also noted a significant difference in how these electrons and their corresponding particle pairs moved in relation to the collision conditions, known as elliptical anisotropy, for beauty particles created in a collision at a high energy. The results of this study show that beauty particles provide measurements of the interactions between these particles and the medium of a collision at a high energy, which are in agreement with the expected interactions from several models of these interactions. The researchers also found the expected interactions from another model of these interactions were not consistent with the expected background particle interactions, which provided new information on how these interactions between these particles and the medium of a collision at a high energy. The results of this study show that beauty particles provide a unique understanding of these interactions from both background particle collisions and the interactions between these particles and the medium

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal control could be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as a function of the total number of users and provides a mathematical proof of this gain's bound, also offering a mathematical representation of this gain's lower bound. Interestingly, the analysis indicates that extremal gain decreases as the total number of users increases. The total extremal gain is shown to be equal to the square root of the total number of users, multiplied by a constant greater than one and less than two. This research confirmed this gain's bound through both theoretical analysis and simulation methods. As its secondary contribution, this research investigated how to achieve optimal power control, and as a result, this research proved that a type of cooperation, known as joint decoding, is not required for achieving optimal power control in square and hexagonal networks when using a type of channel coding known as capacity. A major challenge in providing comprehensive security and privacy safeguards lies in the need to thoroughly analyze complex and frequently changing contextual information. The extensive use of data acquisition techniques, such as logging, for storing information about system usage has led to a significant surge in related data. However, this data often lacks standardization, resulting in a lack of effective organization systems. This study employs formal concept analysis to develop an innovative categorization method that integrates both human expertise and machine learnable components. Additionally, it integrates context model learning and representation into a unified framework. The method is evaluated through a case study of the EU's aerospace security and privacy regulations, with particular focus on the requirements for keeping records of sensitive data. The latter involves categorizing system components with regards to 10 distinct EU regulation elements, such as program purpose and level of risk, in order to ensure full compliance with applicable laws and regulations. The approach is expected to have far-reaching applications in data auditing, security monitoring, and more generally, any context where standardized and machine learnable categorization is beneficial. Furthermore, the paper also explores the use of context model learning and representation to address the challenges of handling new concepts and data uncertainty. The context model learning is initially formulated as a clustering problem, and two approaches using Bayesian networks and Dempster-Shafer theory are proposed for handling evolving data. Finally, the paper showcases the efficacy of the proposed method through a comparative evaluation involving human, random, and learning-based categorization models. The results reveal that the human model and one of the machine learning models excel in terms of performance for the given security and privacy categorization task. The research has been conducted in collaboration with the EU aerospace company, Airbus. The system is currently being utilized in various other domains, for instance, healthcare and financial services, where standardized and machine learnable categorization is beneficial. The context model learning and representation component is also applicable to a broader spectrum of contexts and can be used as a standalone module. The research is part of a broader agenda aimed at developing auditing as a learning component of system management through the integration of data acquisition, analysis, and learning. The research is hosted by the University of Nantes in collaboration with the University of Bristol under the nQuid research collaboration framework. The research is funded by the French government's IdF region and by the EU's Horizon 2020 program under grant number 101004521. The Strauss process is a point process, and its density is unnormalized relative to a Poisson point process, incorporating a weighting factor lambda, between zero and one, which is applied to each pair of points closer than a certain distance, denoted as 'r'. Traditional techniques like basic acceptance-rejection algorithm fail to yield satisfactory results for this specific problem. Multitasking scheduling in service industries has become a widely relevant research topic, primarily due to the rapid expansion of these industries. In contrast to the traditional single-server scenario, where customers depart immediately after receiving service, the new framework requires multiple servers to provide tasks beyond the initial service level. These additional tasks could be provided by the initially served customers, acting as secondary servers, thus significantly enhancing the physical capacity of the system. As such, the standard queueing theory no longer applies, and an innovative approach is required to model and analyze this complex system. We develop a shared-processor scheduling model, which encompasses both multitasking and non-critical tasks. A new service process is identified and named the MXD (Multi-Tasking with Departure) process. We also provide computational methods for the MXD process and apply these to a multi-server multitasking queue. Notably, the MXD process can be modeled as a mixture of the M/M/1 and S/M/1 queueing processes. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized, is linked to the formation of micro-cracks within the gel structure, which can either repair or remain intact after the vibrations cease. Moreover, ultrasonic waves significantly reduce the gels' strength against external forces and facilitate the release of embedded drugs. This research is anticipated to be of great utility across multiple fields, including pharmaceutical engineering, biology, and medicine. This new understanding and associated modeling approaches will enable researchers to model and forecast the behavior of these "rheo-acoustic" gels in response to external forces and vibrations. This research is predicted to be a starting point for the development of various advanced materials and delivery systems. Mapping the behavior of these materials and delivery systems in response to external stimuli and vibrations will facilitate a deeper understanding of the fundamental physical processes involved, and may lead to the creation of systems that can adapt to and respond to their environment. Finally, the investigators have demonstrated that "rheo-acoustic" gels can be used to create complex structures of embedded materials, which opens up fresh avenues for the development of materials and delivery systems. This research could have important implications for a wide range of applications, including tissue engineering, biomedicine, and pharmaceutical engineering. This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then generalized to encompass all positive odd integers. By applying the principle of mathematical induction, this extended set is used to prove the conjecture. A second verification of the conjecture via mathematical induction is also presented in section 9. Consequently, the conjecture is validated through a duplicate approach. The paper concludes by offering two algorithms written in GNU Octave code, which are designed to evaluate the credibility of the conjecture for specific numbers. The first algorithm represents a re-statement of the Collatz conjecture function, whereas the second generates a new Collatz function, which is then checked using the first algorithm for a sequence of numbers and the number of steps required to reach one as per the conjecture. Following this, the paper presents a comparison of the sequences obtained from the original and new functions. In the final section, the paper highlights the relevance of the sequences to the modular arithmetic system. Additionally, the paper's findings have been registered with the arXiv repository in two parts: first, the sequential evaluation of numbers based on the conjecture's functions; second, the combined analysis of these functions and their applicability to the conjecture's original problem. Unfortunately, the paper's last part did not yield any useful insights into the conjecture itself. As an added value, the paper also provides two more algorithms - the first one based on a modified Collatz conjecture orphaned by the third, which is non-existent, and the second one, which verifies the conjecture in a different and unspecified way, which is not disclosed. Besides that, the paper presents a computational analysis of the conjecture's behavior for the two functions and their potential use in the conjecture's validation, which is successful. The paper corresponds to the arXX compact view. The paper's related findings have been registered with the arXiv repository under IDs 2109.06330, 2109.01271, and 2109.02560. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists, thus sparking interest in the problem of finding a stable matching when agents refuse to express full rankings of all other agents. This paper explores a new model of preference formation where a cost is associated with each agent's preference list, and proposes a learning process for creating, through iterative updates, effective preference lists using the least possible cost while ensuring the existence of a stable matching that aligns with the updated preferences. The study also applies these findings to a broader area of research, namely two-sided matching markets with private external valuations. The results indicate that there exist stable matches even when considering only agents directly involved in a match, and that a cost-related preference formation process with desirable properties can be achieved using simple adaptive algorithms. Furthermore, the study presents a family of agents with utility functions that provide an illustrative example of the complexity involved in the preference formation problem, and discusses its potential associations with other, related problems of research. The results ultimately show that the problem of finding a stable matching with the best overall score is, in terms of computational complexity, an NP-hard problem even with the additional constraint of using the least possible cost and limited preference lists. The study also provides information on approximating a stable match of the best possible score in such matching markets. The results ultimately show that achieving a stable match with a score within a factor of 2 of the best possible score requires agents expressing, on average, at least O(n^2) preferences, and that any algorithm with a higher efficiency in preference usage and a constant number of updates requires either a larger number of preferences or an additional penalty in terms of efficiency in finding a stable match with desirable properties. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper focuses on a set of publicly available datasets containing text-based developer conversations, labeled design or otherwise, and examines the consistency of design mining classifications across different models. Unlike previous research, which has investigated model agreement on a single ground truth label, we instead explore the correlation between models' own classifications. Consistent with findings from prior studies, we discovered a significant positive link between models designed with the same datasets. However, models trained on different datasets showed only a moderate level of consistency. Notably, this pattern persisted, even when we only considered the designs common to three publicly available datasets, and restricted our analysis to models that had been trained on each dataset individually. This collective consistency suggests that there is a general design structure that underpins these different datasets, which may aid in uncovering the implicit design criteria at work. Furthermore, our analysis also highlights potential areas of overlap in design between these various datasets, which could aid in their explicit formulation. These conclusions offer important practical implications, given that datasets are often considered evaluable only when models can agree on them. This work therefore provides valuable insights towards developing a unified design structure, which could in turn facilitate explicit design extraction. Such a result would be particularly useful as a foundation for a practical design mining tool. Like prior research, it positions mining as a means to identify key design decisions, which in turn could be manipulated to guide design. Building upon this existing research, it appears possible to integrate mining with other design extraction techniques, which could ultimately contribute to a complete software design documentation tool. However, our analysis also highlights some challenges that need to be addressed in order to achieve this goal, particularly the continued use of explicit annotations rather than automated processes. This discrepancy could be mitigated through a closer integration of mining with other design extraction techniques, which would in turn facilitate a more unified approach to software design. This integrated design extraction could in turn aid in design formulation, which is a crucial aspect of the software development process. This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. It integrates stream processing operators as cloud-based micro-services to facilitate the analysis and visualization of IoT-generated Big Data streams. H-STREAM's micro-services dynamically adjust their techniques according to stream characteristics, ensuring constant processing speeds by combining fast stream processing and more precise, slower methods. H-STREAM delivers efficient stream processing through dynamic aggregation, feasible online querying, and efficient handling of volatile streams using data aggregation. To achieve this, it incorporates a query compiler transforming stream queries into optimized data-driven queries for efficient external storage, and a distributed execution engine managing parallel micro-services for seamless execution. H-STREAM's effectiveness is validated through an in-depth experimentation strategy including systematic inquiry, demonstrating its capacity for processing Big Data streams with low latency and high throughput in direct comparison to top industry solutions, and showcasing its use in supporting IoT-enabled decision-making for human safety and comfort through safe and normal operation demonstration. The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a key area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers considerable detection possibilities. Though past research mainly focused on the resonant production mode of these hypothetical particles, we have now at our disposal comprehensive sets of analyses for the non-resonant diagrams at one-loop for both the fermionic and bosonic counterparts. In this paper, we bring together various one-loop calculations at non-resonant conditions, integrating them into easy-to-use software for the formation of inclusive top and bottom partners, variable by mass, crossing various thresholds with fixed ratios of coupling constants. We assess the influence of these new diagrams on the production cross-sections and the observable phenomenology of top and bottom partner detection. We find, for example, that the non-resonant contributions can make up more than half of total production cross-sections above a certain mass range, exceeding 1 TeV. Moreover, the modification in observable distributions and production ratios stemming from non-resonant diagrams is quite minor in most cases, thus not altering significantly the original parameter estimations obtained from resonant production calculations. We have further shown that the ratio of total partner production and total top production cross-sections at 5 TeV can be quite different from the predictions based on resonant conditions, varying notably with partner mass. By integrating our results with existing partner production simulations, we have explored the partner mass dependence of partner detection potential, providing valuable information for current and future experiments. Finally, the presented analysis can easily be applied to various theoretical models where the non-resonant diagrams play a significant role. As an example, we have applied our results to the application of top partner tagging to exotic decays in a specific model. By combining the results from both resonant and non-resonant conditions, we have significantly enhanced the detection potential of exotic top partner decays, namely MZ' decay into tb. Our work includes the calculation of inclusive top partner production at leading order for the model, incorporating the most recent numerical values of quark and antiquark PDFs as given by the NNPDF3.1 setup. Moreover, the partner mass dependence of top partner tagging potential has been explored in a scenario where the exotic decay of top partner into a Higgs boson and a Z' boson, mediated by a Yukawa interaction, is facilitated by a heavy messenger field. This study builds upon two significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering, which employ both a fuzzy and crisp approach to merging clusters, to address two main shortcomings. Specifically, it addresses two problems: functoriality in hierarchical clustering, and the resolution level of cluster mergings. Existing methods of fuzzy clustering are useful at a coarse resolution but are not applicable to a finer level, whereas the process of cluster merging is typically applicable, yet the resulting combinations are not necessarily applicable in a functorial manner. We address this issue by developing a step-by-step procedure that incorporates a novel form of fuzzy clustering with a reflexive and transitive structure. This allows for cluster merging that is both associative and commutative. We also define a new form of overlap clustering that is based on the semantics of fusion processes and is applicable in a context that is compatible with the information-theoretic framework. This approach is applicable across various fields, as demonstrated by three practical examples, which highlight its potential for real-world applications. Furthermore, we show that the resulting top-down fusion trajectories conform to a functorial structure, thus providing a theoretical foundation for our method. As an additional benefit, our approach also offers a novel semantic interpretation of standard hierarchical clustering. We also provide formal definitions of hierarchical clustering and fuzzy clustering, as well as a general existence and uniqueness theorem for fusion trajectories, regardless of their semantics. Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting fusion trajectories can be used to preserve distances in a semigroup framework. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors based on given information. In this research, a streaming algorithm is introduced for completing tensors from video data. The proposed method watches the video in a sequential fashion, accurately tracking specific areas and then filling in the data for a tensor based on tracked keyframe information. Additionally, a new optimization problem is formulated to make the recovery process both more precise and efficient. The algorithm is put to the test using three types of tensors derived from video content and the results are compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. All experiments confirm that the recovered data obtained from this technique is clear and understandable, and the process is remarkably fast with execution times under one second for common video data. Notably, a server hosting large video data recovers the data within 57 milliseconds, indicating the algorithm's strong performance in real-world applications. The associated code for this project has been made available for public use.  Videos demonstrating the algorithm's output are available for viewing.

These normalized graph methods have been found to be equivalent to applying specific layer operations to graph structures, leading to the development of applications like finding the largest clique in a graph. In an effort to build upon previous research, researchers recently proposed an iterative graph normalization method, which can be seen as a form of "message passing" that reduces a graph to its largest independent subsets. This method has been found to produce features that can be used in tasks such as graph classification. This study aims to investigate whether the features produced by iterative graph normalization possess properties that are beneficial for tasks such as graph classification, and also to look into the structure of the largest independent subsets of a graph. Additionally, researchers examined whether maximizing the weights of these subsets is equivalent to normalizing the graph. To test these research questions, researchers examined how responding to the query "How similar is graph A to graph B?" using the features produced by iterative graph normalization affects tasks such as graph classification and graph similarity estimation. This study also theoretically analyzed the relationship between the features produced by iterative graph normalization and the structure of the largest independent subsets of a graph. In summary, researchers conducted an empirical analysis of the features produced by iterative graph normalization and studied their relationship to graph structure. This study also explored the development of methods to produce features from graphs, which can be used in tasks such as graph classification and graph similarity estimation. Finally, researchers examined the theoretical implications of these research findings. This study is significant because it provides insights into the features produced by iterative graph normalization and their relationship to graph structure, which can be used in tasks such as graph classification and graph similarity estimation. This study also opens the door for developers to build upon these research findings and create innovative methods to produce features from graphs, which can be used in tasks such as graph classification and graph similarity estimation. This research studies the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, aiming to understand the effect of modulation on the thermodynamic properties. The investigation reveals how the periodic electric potential transforms Landau levels into oscillating bands, causing Landau level splitting in accordance with the modulation wavelength. The analysis shows that in electrically modulated graphene, the application of a magnetic field results in the appearance of a series of oscillations in the thermodynamic properties, including the specific heat and entropy, at low temperatures. The frequency and intensity of these oscillations directly relate to the modulation intensity and the periodicity of the electric field. The specific heat shows an anomalous divergent behavior for certain intensity levels of the modulation, indicating a phase transition in the system. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the thermodynamic properties of electrically modulated graphene and identifies evidence of potential phase transitions in this type of material when exposed to external electric and magnetic fields. The predicted oscillations in thermodynamic properties provide an experimental basis for evaluating electrically modulated graphene as a potential material for quantum technology applications. The specific heat and entropy of electrically modulated multilayer graphene were also investigated, revealing the preservation of oscillatory patterns from single-layer graphene while exhibiting increased specificity due to additional layers. The specific heat of electrically modulated multilayer graphene demonstrates filling band transitions, resulting in decreased specific heat values at high temperatures, in addition to the low-temperature oscillations caused by the applied magnetic field. The thermodynamic properties of electrically modulated graphene are therefore versatile and adapt to changes in system configuration, making the material suitable for a wide range of thermodynamic property investigations. The thermodynamic analysis presents a thorough and accurate description of electrically modulated graphene, offering an extensive understanding of this material. The research of electrically modulated multilayer graphene extends to potential uses in thermometric technology, providing a basis for experimental evaluation. The specific heat of electrically modulated multilayer graphene shows promising signs for material applicability in the context of quantum thermometry. A detailed analysis of thermoelectric power in electrically modulated multilayer graphene also confirms its potential in the development of sensitive thermoelectric devices. The research of this material therefore offers considerable scope for application in thermometry and quantum technology. The resulting knowledge of electrically modulated multilayer graphene presents valuable insights and resources for potential applications in the field of quantum technology and thermometry.
