A frequent emitter of such radio signals, CR Draconis was selected for ongoing monitoring, and the observed radio emissions in 2020, displaying periodic and persistent patterns, were characterized. These signals, characterized by a stable frequency and short-duration bursts, were attributed to a stable whistler-mode cyclotron maser. Comparing the observed radio emissions to simulated data from magnetohydrodynamic models revealed satisfactory correspondence, and the radio emissions were found to be influenced by the rotation of the shorter orbital period component, A. Notably, during the monitoring period, CR Draconis did not exhibit high-frequency flaring, and the origin of the emissions continues to be uncertain. These observations contribute to the understanding of ECMEs as a category of magnetically driven cyclotron maser radio emissions, and the entity class is expanding to include increasingly more flare stars. We introduce Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), a rendering approach that accounts for the complex pose of non-rigid objects, and in particular, virtual avatars. Our method combines a neural renderer with a new, compact method for automatically generating textured meshes from voxelmanipulation results. This improvement enables ANR to produce high-quality images of avatars in dynamic poses. To handle the large number of possible poses anavatar can take, we train ANR using the optimization of a composite loss function consisting of a combination of a 2D loss and a 2D-weakly-supervised loss that reduces the shift in pixel locations when the avatar's pose changes. This loss enables ANR to not only produce realistic images of static and dynamic poses, but also facilitates smooth and accurate pose estimations using only marker-based inputs, without the need to estimate joint positions from RGB images. Our results demonstrate the superiority of ANR over existing real-time virtual avatar methods in terms of image quality, pose accuracy, and overall system speed. Our ANR tool is available for immediate use at: https://www.youtube.com/watch? v=ANRsystem2022 and the related 2022 CVPR paper can be found at https://www.yecaiwei.github.org/files/cvpr2022_anr.pdf. Both of these resources include additional video content.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by unusual or misleading input, whereas humans' learning of abstract patterns allows them to withstand extreme visual distortions. We propose a new set of visual transformation methods rooted in neurophysiological research to evaluate the performance of both humans and networks on an object recognition task. We found that machines excel in certain transformations while faltering behind humans in simpler ones. We identified differences in human and machine accuracy using these transformations, ranked their effectiveness based on human results, and improved the performance of ANNs by training them with a combination of these transformations. This has potential implications for evaluating both artificial and biological vision. Its utilization is freely accessible at visomotorlab.org. We discuss the implications of our results, including their relevance to theoretical models of primates' and humans' neural performance and object recognition tasks. We also acknowledge that our ANNs only mimic primates' and humans' neural performance and do not necessarily reflect their underlying processes. Therefore, we suggest methods for identifying the differences between artificial and biological vision systems through collective human feedback. This is particularly essential as the knowledge gap persists despite advancements in ANNs. We found that humans can consistently recognize the transformations, but their explanations for their performance vary widely and are often grounded in intuitive rather than logical theories. We provide access to human response data, ANNs' source code, and parietal visual cortex neural activity data from the Neuron database for the Mtitek challenge, as well as our VLT challenge dataset. The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{su}_2)$, is examined in this exploration. Certain tangle diagrams associated with three strands that include a spin-$1/2$ closed loop demonstrate a connection to the AW algebra's generators. Both the Chern-Simons theory and the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction show that the link invariants generated by these tangles adhere to the algebra's generator relationships. This reveals that the Chern-Simons theory's expectation values for Wilson loops satisfy AW algebra relations and the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariants fail to differentiate between equivalent linear combinations of links. Additionally, the properties of the 3-strand tangles provide a more straightforward interpretation of the central elements within SU(2) and, by extension, quantum $\mathfrak{su}_2$, as well as an explicit expression for quantum $\mathfrak{su}_2$'s Casimir operator in terms of the tangle's expectation values, which also applies to the algebra's generators. This offers a geometric understanding of the algebra's elements. Moreover, the exploration presents a new, explicit representation of the SU(2) group, which is conjugate to an representation of quantum $\mathfrak{su}_2$. This explicit representation is generated by the tangles' expectation values. Finally, the explorationconcludes with a discussion on the possible generalization of this connection to more complex tangles and its potential use in developing a more in-depth understanding of the interplay between quantum groups and their representations within Chern-Simons theory and Reshetikhin-Turaev invariants. This exploration may pave the way for a more explicit and geometric understanding of the quantum algebra in the framework of Reshetikhin-Turaev construction. A new, explicit and geometric construction of the unitary representation of quantum $\mathfrak{su}_2$ is presented. This exploration offers a connection between the SU(2) representation and the tangles' space which is similar to the interplay established between the SU(2) representation and the Wilson loop's expectation values in the Chern-Simons theory. Such a connection was not explored in the original papers. The exploration is also accompanied by several animations that illustrate the properties of the tangles, available at the web page provided by the author.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets composed of loosely connected three-spin clusters. Specifically, we investigated the thermodynamic behavior of a strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and the previously proposed triangle-square lattice model relevant to La4Cu3MoO12, leveraging a trimer-cluster based computational basis to minimize the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem at low temperatures. Our analysis extends beyond the thermodynamic properties to examine the mean field theory prediction of a phase transition associated with chiral order. We observed a two-peak structure in the specific heat for the breathing distorted kagome lattice model in both the quantum spin liquid and lattice-nematic regimes. Furthermore, we found evidence of a phase transition between these regimes, which is supported by an analytical calculation of the thermodynamic energy using a classical spin model approximation. Our study also sheds light on the triangle-square lattice model, indicating the presence of a phase transition between its proposed ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic regimes, which coincides with the predicted transition temperature as determined by a mean field analysis. Our findings reveal a significant discrepancy between the specific heat capacities at the proposed phase transition temperature as determined by the specific computational approaches we employed. Ultimately, we were unable to confirm the mean field theory prediction of a phase transition associated with chiral order within the triangle-square lattice model in the context of our computational data, which instead indicates that this order disappears as the temperature decreases or the coupling between the clusters increases. Our computational findings align with the experimental measurements of La4Cu3MoO12, which include no evidence of a phase transition or chiral order. Our work has broader implications for the study of quantum cluster models and related materials. As such, we hope our findings inspire future experimental and computational research on these topics. Our computational data for the triangle-square lattice model and the breathing distorted kagome lattice model through a lower temperature of at least 50 millikelvin in addition to our specific model parameters and generated data for the specific heat capacity at that temperature and the thermodynamic energy can be made available upon request. Furthermore, all related code is now publicly accessible via the author's GitHub account. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have been demonstrated to embark on a form of self-supervised learning through text manipulation, thereby acquiring foundational knowledge across diverse domains. Consequently, it is plausible to utilize these models for zero-shot learning tasks, namely for predicting specific classes from given inputs and outputs. To demonstrate this learning modality, researchers have employed datasets such as the Hume dataset, comprising information on dataset names and natural language prompts to extract specific predictions, and the NLP Commons dataset, containing natural language labels and descriptions. To date, learning from these sources has been explored individually, rather than collectively. In our study, we have aggregated a substantial collection of datasets, including over one hundred new data points, and have identified a commonalities in dataset structure, thereby establishing a basis for adapting the GPT-3 model across these collections. By fine-tuning the model on these sources, we have achieved a marked enhancement in zero-shot learning performance, particularly in extracting text predictions and natural language labels, thereby facilitating the development of innovative zero-shot learning algorithms and prompting strategies. As a result, we have successfully conducted zero-shot learning on 121 new datasets, thereby underscoring the feasibility of language-based zero-shot learning. Our study provides essential insights into the development of specific language-based zero-shot learning algorithms and prompting strategies, thereby facilitating the exploration of new research avenues and applications. Furthermore, we have released the collection of datasets, the NLP Commons dataset, and the adapted GPT-3 model for further research and development in zero-shot learning. The related code is publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/jayelizabeth/metaprom. Additionally, we have publicly accessed the adapted GPT-3 model, trained using the NLP-tracking prompt collection, at the following IF link: https://beta.intf.uzh.ch/IF/datasets.html (select model 2022-08-04_23-42-GPT3-177-bf-uncased). Furthermore, we intend to publicly release the collection of natural language labels and descriptions associated with specific prediction tasks (i.e. the Hume dataset) once the associated de-identification process is completed. The related dataset is currently not publicly accessible due to the requirement for a formal dataset release agreement, but it will be released in a forthcoming update to this work. We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter observational methods in measuring strong emission lines and calculating the observed line ratios. This calculation is then compared against simulated line ratios from a large database of spectroscopic redshifts, effectively creating a diagnostic tool, or "Sudoku" - a redshift likelihood indicator. This indicator assesses the validity of lines detected by single-dish and interferometers, as well as those with varying levels of resolution and sensitivity. As part of a companion paper, we present the results of applying this diagnostic tool to millimeter and submillimeter lines measured during SMUG, a survey conducted using the IRAM-30m telescope. This tool not only helps estimate redshift uncertainties but also provides a means of identifying contaminants such as scattering lines and sunspots. With over 30,000 simulated redshifts spanning the 1mm to 350μm wavelength range, our research finds that millimeter and submillimeter lines with multiple emitters tend to have more uncertain redshifts and line ratios compared to lines with a single emitter. This is due in part to the potential for line confusion in the millimeter spectrum. We also find that weak or undetected emission lines, as well as lines with small spectral lines, make difficult redshift determinations. However, millimeter lines with these characteristics that are confirmed to have strong emission in the near-infrared or submillimeter spectrum can have more reliably estimated redshifts. This diagnostic tool is planned to be developed into a interactive web-based calculator to be used by researchers. Irrespective of the method used to measure millimeter lines, our research emphasizes the need for follow-up spectroscopy to confirm redshifts, particularly in the millimeter spectrum. As part of follow-up observations, millimeter lines with redshifts measured during SMUG and previous large millimeter and submillimeter surveys will be re-examined. These lines serve as crucial targets for future mm and submm lines follow-up spectroscopy, including those observed during INTENSE and PLATO, two comprehensive redshift measurement projects. These projects aim to validate or refute the high-z [C I] 370μm line as the primary driver of the observed acceleration in the universe's expansion rate, as part of research for the Community Development Coordination Network (C3D). This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to determine the dynamical spin structure factor of the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice with antiferromagnetic properties. A highly complex phase diagram arises from the lattice due to the conflicting interactions between adjacent spins and their neighbors. By simulating both the ordered 120-degree phase and a potential spin liquid phase at a specific ratio of $J_2/J_1 = 0.125$, we investigate the nature of the spin structure factor and compare it to that of a quantum paramagnetic state at a different ratio of $J_2/J_1 = 0.292$. A low-energy continuum of excitations exists in both the suspected spin liquid and the quantum paramagnetic states, while a more dispersed and broader distribution of the structure factor at low energy levels can be observed in the former. Additionally, the ordered phase exhibits a distinctive pattern of three distinct peaks separated by broad dispersive regions due to spin preservation. A comparative study of the structure factor from inelastic neutron scattering experiments is also presented for reference purposes. A new phase of the $J_1-J_2$ system is expected to be a spin liquid, based on these simulations. A comprehensive investigation of the structure factor across all parts of the phase diagram could potentially lead to a more accurate understanding of the various phases present. Keywords: antiferromagnetic spin liquids, non-magnetic states, triangular lattices, Heisenberg models, matrix product states, and spin structure factor. The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across four dimensions and their implications on $Z_3$ symmetry, where a complex triplet Higgs boson has no initial mass and interaction. By regulating lattice size through variations in $N_\tau$, the investigation reveals that the phase transition depends on this regulation: crossover transitions occur when there are 2 sites and the phase transitions turn first-order for 3 sites and more. Moreover, Polyakov loop and related observable distributions sensitive to the breaking of $Z_3$ symmetry indicate its explicit breaking strength to diminish with increasing $N_\tau$. Additionally, $SU(3)\times U(1)$ center symmetry is found to be intact in larger $N_\tau$ regimes due to a stable non-zero Higgs vacuum state and a resulting mass gap expanding with $N_\tau$. Consequently, $Z_3$ symmetry is now considered a reliable, physical global $U(1)_H$ symmetry. Calculations of related basic physical constants, such as $e$, $\sin^2\theta_W$ and $\Delta$, are also presented. These procedures involve a few $N_\tau$ measurements, such as the electric couplings in the magnetic and rest frames. Moreover, $\sin^2\theta_W$ is determined by the lattice regulated mass of the would-be Goldstone boson ($m_{\phi}$) relation $\frac{8m_\phi}{11}=\frac{2\omega_1}{T}+O(\epsilon_m)$, where $\epsilon_m$ represents lattice cutoff errors. Similarly, $\Delta$ is calculated from a known relation $\Delta=1-\frac{6\omega_1}{T}+O(\epsilon_m^2)$. Also, $\Delta$ is calculated from some selected operator analysis. These constants are then used to find the lattice regulated QCD $\alpha_s$ by relating it to the previously determined $\sin^2\theta_W$ and a known relation $\sin^2\theta_W=\frac{8m_\phi}{11}+O(\epsilon_m)$. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is considered. These findings are based on an innovative model transformation approach that enables separating the effects of low-rank structure and heteroskedasticity. We also provide empirical recovery criteria for partially observed matrix datasets. Moreover, we show that these theoretical bounds can be realized asymptotically as the matrix size increases, as proven by a novel set of asymptotic experiments. These experiments involve fitting a low-rank model to randomly selected matrix components and verifying its correctness. We demonstrate that the theoretical bounds offer precise asymptotic results for multiple estimation methods, including atomic principal component analysis, linear discriminant analysis, and maximum likelihood principal component analysis. Overall, this work provides a framework for the asymptotic analysis of low-rank matrix estimation with heteroskedasticity and rank-one matrix estimation. It enables the direct comparison of various estimation techniques and their respective performance under heteroskedasticity. As a result, this theory can be applied and extended to a broad range of low-rank matrix estimation challenges. Finally, the application of these theoretical tools is demonstrated through a cohort modeling example where MRI technology is used to measure brain tissue densities in individuals with Alzheimer's disease. We use this example to illustrate how the recovery boundary can inform the optimal study design. We derive the optimal number of matrix components required to achieve a specified level of estimation accuracy. This research was presented in a series of papers at the 2020 NeurIPS conference.

In this work, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking into account its complete energy spectrum. The selection of model constraints allows us to analyze the topological properties of the system without relying on symmetry, a common method for categorizing non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. A constrained ring offers an ideal platform to study the properties of non-Hermitian systems, as the constraint itself introduces a controlled amount of non-Hermitian activity into the system. Our findings on the system's eigenvalues, degeneracies, and commutation relations provide a fundamental characterization of the system's algebraic structure. The work is accomplished through a detailed mathematical derivation, and our conclusions are validated by numerical analysis. The resulting model is versatile, applicable to different types of constraints, and can thus model various non-Hermitian systems. The model is particularly effective in systems where Hermitian models fail to provide insights into the system's topological properties. Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with various attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their capability to encapsulate a wide array of real-world phenomena, encompassing chemical reactions, biological pathways, social connections, and other intricate relationships. Mastering network science necessitates the mastery of a comprehensive toolkit spanning numerous fields of study, including graph and probability theory, linear algebra, machine learning, combinatorics, and statistical physics.

This comprehensive resource is designed to provide foundational knowledge of these diverse analytical tools. It aims to equip readers with an all-encompassing understanding of these approaches, allowing them to develop their expertise as specialists in network science. This book serves as an invaluable roadmap for aspiring network scientists, guiding them through the rich tapestry of this rapidly evolving field. Network science is distinguished by its interdisciplinary roots, having emerged from diverse fields such as mathematics, computer science, and sociology. This book seeks to forge a new path forward, one that defines the field as an independent and distinctive area of study with its unique approaches and applications. Network science is characterized by its rapid pace of growth, driven by the emergence of new methodologies and the investigation of crucial social and medical issues. This book aims to provide a lasting foundation for the foundational knowledge and diverse applications in network science. Network science is a young and dynamic field, spanning just three decades, and this book seeks to help it solidify its roots with a forward-thinking vision. This book is designed to help readers not only understand but also tackle complex networks, empowering them to become specialists in the investigation and analysis of intricate systems. This book is intended for advanced undergraduate students, graduate students, and researchers across various fields, including mathematics, physics, biology, sociology, information science, and data science. This book is also suitable for professionals and academics looking to gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental tools and diverse applications in network science. This book is further enriched by the inclusion of numerous figures and hyperlinks to supplementary information such as real-world data sets, software protocols, and suggested reading lists. This book is also accompanied by a comprehensive companion website containing additional resources, including network dataset repositories, software demonstrations, and hyperlinks to network science-centric organizations and conferences. This resource is intended to support the growth of network science researchers and practitioners in their pursuit of this rapidly evolving field. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory and natural populations. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interactions on longer timescales.  We expand the scope of eco-evolutionary dynamics to incorporate slower evolutionary changes which span centuries to millennia.  For instance, feedback loops between changing landscapes and evolving plant life.  We also recognize that rates of ecological and evolutionary changes are influenced by modulators like temperature, thus allowing for synchronization or decoupling between these processes.  Notably, global climate change might amplify instances of eco-evolution and novel system behaviors, making it increasingly difficult to forecast these complex changes.  By adopting an integrated, interdisciplinary approach spanning from genetics to geomorphology and across varying timescales, we strive to improve our understanding of the complex interactions within eco-evolutionary systems.  The potential applications of this broader approach are substantial, including enhanced predictions of complex system behaviors, with potential adaptations in environmental management and conservation policies.  Given the time and resource required for thorough scientific investigation, we recommend a more systematic exploration of the long-term evolutionary history, thereby informing management practices that account for these deeper timescales.  Ultimately, attaining this goal will require significant collaboration across the scientific community, involving experts from diverse fields who are willing to look to the past for insights that can inform a more resilient future.  As such, we advocate for the development of a long-term eco-evolutionary research initiative, one that is focused on the generation-to-generation timescales, bridging the past and the future.  This initiative would serve as a link between deep-time ecological research and contemporary systems, helping to forecast the complex interactions within eco-evolutionary dynamics in a changing world.  By supporting this initiative, we hope to contribute to a better understanding of the intricate, multi-scale networks that link our past, present, and future, thereby informing and inspiring research, practice, and environmental decision-making.  Ultimately, this deeper understanding can help us to systematically and effectively conserve the natural systems and processes that surround us.  As such, we encourage researchers, policymakers, and the public to join forces in supporting and engaging in this critical and long-overdue initiative.  We believe that this community-driven and systematic research effort can help to better predict and prepare for the complex, multifaceted nature of future eco-evolutionary changes. A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing various speech models with minimal adjustments to improve downstream performance. By showing that self-supervised speech models can excel in multiple downstream tasks with little adaptation, SUPERB highlights a significant paradigm in speech and language technology, namely spoken language representation learning. However, models optimized for representation face challenges when confronted with adversarial perturbations. This study investigates the vulnerability of speech self-supervised models to such perturbations, focusing on their ability to withstand manipulations in speech signals. Specifically, we evaluate the perturbation robustness of SUPERB's optimized models and explore the impact of their learnable representations, examining several key factors. Our experiments first demonstrate the significant adverse effect of perturbations on speech self-supervised models. Though they perform well in clean conditions, these models show significant degradation under adverse conditions. Our study then investigates the role of speech structure in handling perturbations and suggests that speech representation models should be designed to accommodate variability in order to enhance their resilience. Additionally, we were unable to confirm the influence of mask prediction loss on model robustness, but did find that using a combination of loss contributes to better cross-domain performance. Our findings and analysis indicate that speech representation models are particularly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, underscoring a pressing need for speech model design that is adversarially robust. As such, we have developed an adversarial robust speech self-supervised learning framework that is grounded in speech representation learning. Our framework incorporates speech augmentation not only to improve model robustness but also to preserve the speech model's primary objectives. We have validated the effectiveness of our framework in improving the perturbation robustness of speech self-supervised models. Furthermore, models developed with our framework show improved adaptability to different speech datasets drawn from multiple sources. Our work highlights the critical importance of developing speech models that are resistant to adversarial perturbations, with the potential to broadly impact speech processing applications. Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers, 
induced by a token usage inefficiency, 
a problem worsened by token usage frequency.
As a consequence, the market equilibrium tokens, 
held by arbitrageurs, 
involve a dual influence, 
a token's market demand enhances its inefficiency, 
while its supply diminishes the inefficiency, 
thus influencing AMM adoption.
Additionally, our analysis highlights a vulnerable spot in the market, 
where token fragmentation can render token owners inactive arbitrageurs, 
ultimately impeding adoption, 
which contrasts pyramid schemes.
We also provide empirical and numerical validation of our theory. 
Lastly, our study is expanded to smaller AMMs, 
yielding similar findings.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how assumptions in clinical trials and observational studies impact results by examining alternative data assumptions. We build upon an existing measure called the E-value which gauges the precision of causal inference under various assumptions but does not account for potential biases. We propose an updated Bayesian approach to estimate this metric, considering both assumptions related to data missingness and model bias. We provide formulas for scenarios involving univariate and multivariate outcomes, and illustrate their use in actual clinical trials. This framework seeks to address a crucial objective: to provide an accurate and unbiased E-value that can be applied to a wide range of clinical trials and data, facilitating the identification of reliable and reliable outcomes. We aim to make available software that performs this analysis, with the ultimate goal of enabling researchers and data analysts to easily conduct a comprehensive sensitivity analysis. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques within Internet of Vehicles is becoming increasingly important as a result of the rapid advancement in vehicle equipment such as cameras, sensors, and GPS systems. However, there are valid concerns regarding the privacy protection of users due to the collaborative nature of Machine Learning. To overcome this limitation, Federated Learning has emerged as a promising approach for shared model training without compromising user privacy. In response to growing concerns about privacy, researchers have proposed the use of Blockchain technology to bolster the security of FL. This research paper conducts a comprehensive review of current literature on Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning for IoT applications, focusing on IoT, IoT sensing technologies, and IoT security modeling. It also presents the conceptual foundations of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning and outlines the relevant framework architectures. Furthermore, the paper highlights the challenges and obstacles associated with Blockchain-Enabled FL and explores potential future avenues for research."

Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform. 
The baseline design will be utilized as a prototype, and our strategy for testing and validating the platform's performance at millikelvin temperatures, including demonstrations of superconducting qubits, will be discussed. 
Ultimately, the successful deployment of this platform at Fermilab's facility will establish a world-class experimental space capable of supporting diverse scientific applications including quantum information science, materials research targeted at novel superconductors, and entangled matter-mass experiments. 
The platform also serves as an essential component in the development of testing systems for quantum processors, enhancing the accessibility and speed of testing in the process. 
This development effort is expected to contribute significantly to the quantum computing community, expanding the availability of available small and existing experimental platforms in the United States and the wider scientific landscape. 
The platform's availability, incorporating both the platform and access to the Fermilab facility, will be open to all qualified researchers with a solid experimental plan, further fostering collaboration and cutting-edge research at the platform.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent, with one notable exception - a study conducted on professional developers in Python revealed a lower incidence of insecure code for crypto-related tasks. This led to the investigation of whether the trend holds true for real-world Python applications. By creating a static analysis tool, researchers examined a large sample of popular Python projects and MicroPython projects, comparing their findings to previous studies. The analysis showed that a substantial proportion of Python projects exhibit at least one crypto API misuse. The good design of some Python crypto libraries appears to significantly reduce the likelihood of misuses compared to studies involving Java and C. The analysis also highlighted the value of hybrid analysis methods in detecting misuses in embedded devices. The results suggest a beneficial impact of sound API design on reducing crypto-related security risks in Python applications. The associated code and report can be accessed at https://seclab.csust.edu/.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to generate accurate results in a timely fashion. Furthermore, the approach is shown to significantly outperform established methods of 3D object labelling. Furthermore, the resulting time-efficient 3D object labelling outcomes can be utilized for a range of applications, such as city planning, navigation, and geographic information systems, reducing the traditional cost-benefit ratio associated with these tasks. Two metropolitan areas have successfully utilized this method for generating affordable panoramic views and immersive street-level video content. Consequently, the strategy is found to be particularly suited to the dynamic and rapidly changing field of urban geography and smart city initiatives. The source code for this method, named VALUE, has been made publicly available for the purpose of promoting further research within this domain.  A corresponding live demonstration is accessible via VALUE.live. The visualization platform showcases the method's output and provides a interactive, three-dimensional street-level view of the monitored area. Furthermore, the portal also enables users to gain insight into the various sub-systems and data processing stages that contribute to the large-scale decision-making process taking place within the system. Lastly, the portal serves as a window into the monitoring system, enabling real-time surveillance of the system in operation.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm that employs proximal averaging, which we translate into a deep learning framework by creating the NuSPAN network. Our framework allows the optimization of model parameters such as regularization weights and the number of iterations, as well as the design of a suitable network architecture through a training process. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithm is more effective than existing alternatives for seismic inversion and conventional deconvolution tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate that the pre-trained NuSPAN network can be utilized as a post-processing denoiser for other sparse models including sparsity-based inversion methods in seismic wave exploration. Our findings are supported by numerical examples in the form of both synthetic data and real-world applications. Our research opens up opportunities for future investigations on generalizing the proposed model for other image reconstruction purposes. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single POS tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should predict sets of possible tags. Our approach involves adapting existing sequential prediction methods to account for errors and rely on additional context for correction. In comparison to current state-of-the-art POS tagging methods, our proposed set-valued prediction model exhibits superior accuracy, particularly for historical corpora, demonstrating an average improvement of 24.2% in categorical accuracy and up to a 50% reduction in error rate in some instances. An implementation of this model can be accessed at https://github.com/sdolido/set-POS-tagging. 

Key Words: historical linguistics, part-of-speech tagging, set-valued prediction, sequence-to-sequence models, set-valued deep learning.

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, along with the corresponding Hamiltonian systems coupled by the Poisson bracket itself. This represents a unique application of the dual momentum map duality to the Lie-Poisson structure of a Lie group. These findings are exemplified through the canonization of the Korteweg-de Vries and the heavy top equations. We claim that the resulting canonical forms contain complete and useful information about the original Lie-Poisson structure. Consequently, these systems are now solvable by Hamilton-Jacobi. Additionally, the resulting canonical forms contain conserved quantities, which were previously hidden within the original Lie-Poisson structure. When restricted to invariants, these systems are equivalent to their canonical forms, indicating that invariant solutions do not appear to introduce additional dynamics. By computing the action-angle variables for the Korteweg-de Vries equation, we found that the resulting Hamiltonian system corresponds to the well-known permanent wave Hamiltonian of gyroscopic NLS. These methods and results are expected to be versatile and applicable to a broad range of Lie-Poisson structures, with the goal of providing a framework for translating Lie-Poisson systems into canonical forms, with potential implications for the theory of integrable systems. Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with widely accepted industry standards, drawing on information like client history and macroeconomic factors.
Advanced machine learning models have been proven effective in predicting non-performing loans, and this paper showcases their application using a South Eastern European dataset. Four distinct models - Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, and Neural Networks - were used, each optimized for its hyperparameters through grid search and the RMSE metric over training samples. An alternative model, LightGBM, was also evaluated and verified as a suitable option. Furthermore, feature selection and feature importance analysis were performed for each model through the SHAP package and the Kullback-Leibler Divergence method. These results not only validate the use of these models but also provide insight into the most significant and relevant feature sets for lending decisions. Consequently, this paper aims to empower banks with effective and efficient decision-supporting tools. The code and dataset used for this paper can be found at https://github.com/mkruzel/Feature-Importance-Analysis. The dataset provided by https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/home-credit-risk can be accessed via the Kaggle platform. The models and calculations were implemented in Python, drawing from popular machine learning and data science libraries including Scikit-Learn, H2O, and Keras. The process was also automated using a Bash script. The validation showed that optimized models have predictability values of up to 87.33%. As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively arranging the space occupied by each satellite in their operational trajectories is essential to prevent collisions and reduce critical encounters. Here, the term "space occupancy" is defined as the area an individual satellite covers during its orbit, taking into account external perturbations and a specified timeframe. Following the discovery of a strong connection between space occupancy in the zonal problem and the principles of frozen orbits and proper eccentricity, frozen-orbit initial conditions in osculating element space were derived and a frozen-orbit polar equation was formulated to define the space occupancy region in an analytically closed form. Further analysis explored minimizing space occupancy at the perigee and descended into the region of co-rotation, revealing a novel polar equation that could be used to determine and optimize (or reduce) space occupancy in various satellite configurations, such as formations and clusters. Numerical simulations demonstrated the effectiveness of the derived initial conditions and space occupancy equations, and these methods could be applied to design and optimize satellite formations and constellations effectively. Ultimately, the space occupancy concept is broad and could be extended to other orbital regimes like the Molniya orbit, and readers are encouraged to suggest relevant applications. Additionally, the work is motivated by a focus on low-Earth orbit satellites, but the concepts and findings are expected to be applicable to other orbital regimes as well. To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created, which allows for intricate quad configurations due to its unstructured layout. Subsequently, we build upon this foundation with a flexible T-mesh structure, which can be manipulated to optimize the mesh topology by assigning varying lengths to its arc segments. Utilizing advanced optimization techniques in the form of integer linear programming, we efficiently resolve the mesh simplification process and refine the resulting topology. Ultimately, we extract high-order quadrilateral meshes from the optimized framework, offering various degrees of precision. Notably, our method prioritizes mesh coherence during the optimization process, which facilitates efficient mesh topology design, efficient high-order quadrilateral mesh generation, and utilizes visually appealing mesh visualizations to provide users with detailed, interactive feedback. We showcase the efficacy of our approach through rigorous comparison with cutting-edge quadrilateral mesh generation methods that employ single-resolution mesh structures, outperforming these benchmarks on a diverse range of challenging CAD-based modeling scenarios. Additionally, we highlight the value of our method by illustrating its applications and extensions in the fields of computational geometry and scientific simulation. A comprehensive implementation of our method, in conjunction with relevant supporting data and code, is publicly available for on-demand access. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by examining how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distribution moments, an inductive approach in this paper offers a precise formula for expressing sample correlation distribution moments in a way that is easy to compute. These formulas can be used to create several types of p-value estimators, including ones based on central moments, the method of variance, the method of score, the wild bootstrap, and the balanced bootstrap. Each of these p-value estimators is simple to compute and provides accurate results. The method of variance is the most efficient, boasting the lowest bias and the highest reliability. The balanced approach has the lowest dispersion and the highest reliance on the data. The strength of these p-value estimators is illustrated by results of simulated tests. We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize such systems through finite dimensional feedback controls in the vicinity of an unstable equilibrium in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces that approximate L^3(Omega) in three dimensions. This research setting has substantial implications as the uncontrolled dynamics' well-posedness issue has been solved in the critical space L^3(R^3) in recent studies. By localizing controls in a small subdomain within Omega, this study provides a solution to the uniform stabilization problem in the critical space and also offers an improved, simplified solution in the more restricted Hilbert space. This work lays the groundwork for a subsequent study which tackles the question of whether finite dimensional localized tangential feedback controls can also achieve uniform stabilization in three-dimensional spaces. This question was successfully addressed in the non-critical space in the work of Abdallah et al. and in the critical space in the work of Saanounou. Building on the latter result in the critical space, this study provides a more challenging and demanding solution in the context of localized controls. Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinearTriangularMatrix and Upper-ColLinearTriangularMatrix, to two sections of the kernel matrix. By breaking down the kernel matrix into these unique matrices and applying vector operations, we can calculate the multiplicative updates of the Sinkhorn weights in linear time. When combined with our previous iterative method, this approach enables the optimal transport solution to be found faster than before. A newly developed algorithm, fast_Sinkhorn_2, utilizing our proposed matrix concepts, achieves a computational time of $\sqrt{N} $ per iteration, slightly surpassing the time complexity of fast_Sinkhorn_1, the previous iterative method. The experiments showcase that, for large $N$, the new algorithm can compute solutions 50% to 66% faster than the previous method. Moreover, under kernel scaling conditions, fast_Sinkhorn_2 can attain a time complexity of $O(N)$ with only a maximum relative error of $10^{-5}$ even when using a first-order approximation of the kernel, thus making the algorithm computationally more efficient than expected. To verify the algorithm's validity, we performed additional error checks, including a $O(N)$ closed-form solution derived from solving a self-adjoint eigenproblem, which helps reduce numerical errors. A new multi-iterative algorithm is proposed by combining fast_Sinkhorn_2 with its closed-form solution for improved algorithm robustness. The algorithm can handle diverse settings found in real-world applications, including different kernels, various boundary conditions, and different cost functions. Finally, the algorithm's performance is enhanced using a precomputed kernel based on optimal transport solutions of a coarse grid to solve the problem. The study's results are then applied to a new algorithm that outperforms fast_Sinkhorn_2. Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an ideal chance to study these impacts in relation to flares and the existing dust. Our goal is to measure the FUV and X-ray radiation emitted by AU Mic, particularly focusing on its planetary system, where massive dust may affect gas dynamics and the delivery of energy. Our space-based observations discovered that AU Mic's far-UV radiation doubles during flares, resulting in up to 120 J cm^-2 s^-1, while its FUV flux remains relatively stable at 50,000 J cm^-2 s^-1. Although our X-ray monitoring could not distinguish the planet positions, we calculated the potential impact of this flux on the atmospheres of AU Mic b and c, where our simulations revealed that mass loss rates could reach up to 10^8-10^9 mg s^-1 for both planets, resulting in atmospheric loss over billions of years. Moreover, UV absorption can restrict the available energy for photochemical reactions in the atmospheres of AU Mic b and c. Our study highlights the rapid changes and unpredictable behavior of young stars' emission, particularly for AU Mic, where our findings support the theory that AU Mic b and c may have breathed their last within the first million years or less. Moreover, it is possible that dust inside the AU Mic system primarily affects the low-altitude atmospheres of the planets rather than the entire gas disk. Our work paves the way for future observations, potentially using James Webb Space Telescope, Hubble, and Roman Space Telescope to visualize exoplanets around active stars. Furthermore, it is essential to conduct mid-infrared observations to determine the effect of the dust grain size on the gas dynamics in the AU Mic system. Lastly, it is crucial to consider the implications of the evolution of young stars and their planets on the formation of planetary systems. The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications. This research provides a comprehensive explanation for the varying drop sizes observed in experiments involving fibers coated with liquids of different properties. The theoretical model can also be applied to other situations where liquid-solid slip is present. However, it is crucial to account for slip boundaries in scenarios involving the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The relationship between slip coefficients and capillary lengths allows for a deeper understanding of the effect of liquid-solid slip on instabilities. This knowledge may also shed light on related processes, such as the formation of tetrahedral drops and concurrent instabilities occurring in flows of viscous liquids. Lastly, a systematic analysis of the effect of liquid-solid slip on instabilities can lead to novel methods for controlling droplet formation in applications like polymer and liquid coatings. The relationship between slip boundaries and instability wavelengths may be leveraged in the design of fibers and nanowires that produce drops or fibers with intricate coatings through the adjustment of material properties and geometric characteristics. The theoretical model presented can be applied to a wide range of situations involving the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, liquid-solid slip, and electronic and optical devices fabricated through the coating of fibers. The resulting knowledge and insights can be used in various areas, such as the design of microfluidic devices, liquid coatings, lubricants, pharmaceuticals, aerosols, and applications involving the simultaneous flows of gases and liquids. The models and theories presented can be extended to other processes, like the example of concurrent flows of gases and liquids, to advance our understanding of related phenomena. The relationship between liquid-solid slip, fiber coatings, droplet formation, electronic and optical devices, microfluidics, liquid coatings, concurrent flows, drugs, and aerosols highlights the potential for a wide range of systems involving the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The theoretical models and equations presented can be used to generate predictions regarding droplet properties, device performance, and liquid coatings.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems. Our work is significantly enhanced by recent existence results in the Lagrangian framework. Our findings demonstrate that Lipschitz stability occurs universally in both Lagrangian and Eulerian systems. We further demonstrate that these results are reinforced when considering spatially dependent $\alpha(r,t)$. An additional outcome of this study is the discovery that Lipschitz stability is an intrinsic property in the Eulerian framework, regardless of the values of the $\alpha$ parameters. Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image deformity angles acquired from both robotic and manual scans. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded highly reliable results both within and between evaluators, with minimal difference compared to the manual approach in terms of coronal deformity angles. Furthermore, robotic scanning exhibited accurate intra-rater consistency, with the manual scanning matching the intra-rater reliability. This study found that robotic scanning yields scoliosis deformity angles comparable to those obtained through manual scanning with ultrasound. This supports the use of robotic scanning as a viable and reliable approach for scoliosis assessment. This research appears in the Journal of Medical Devices. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific probability distributions, this new method accommodates various distribution shapes without modification. Performance metrics and subjective ratings reveal that this approach surpasses a conventional median-based method. However, comparisons with state-of-the-art duration models slightly favor established methods, prompting the need for further research in this area. The proposed method remains appealing due to its ability to model durations using a median value and accommodates multi-speaker durations, in contrast to alternative methods. Moreover, this method allows for the synthesis of natural, varied duration patterns even when a limited amount of data is available. The model can be trained without optimization for duration variation, and naturally, yields more interpretable and complex models. As such, this method holds promise for the development of more sophisticated duration models in the future. Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks. Additionally, a newly developed model that employs a transfer learning-based encoder for feature extraction demonstrated superior performance compared to other models. This approach, which leverages BERT's pre-trained models, offers a more efficient method for modeling tasks involving limited data availability. A accompanying code repository can be accessed at https://github.com/alexandresu/BERT-FE. Our team's results and the presented model offer valuable insights for future tasks involving Indo-European languages, which are typically underrepresented in related datasets. Ultimately, this paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion about the potential benefits and drawbacks of large pre-trained language models, particularly in regards to their potential for replicability enhancement and performance improvement. Furthermore, this work aims to shed light on the significance of model architecture and the application of transfer learning for NLP tasks involving underrepresented languages and limited data availability. Our model's performance has been found to be resistant to perturbations and is capable of generalizing to other related tasks, including task two, which involves the identification of derogatory language. It was also demonstrated that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks. Importantly, our approach allows for the efficient encoding of sequential tasks, which in turn facilitates improved model performance through transfer learning. A method for automatically generating training data through multiple iterations was also developed, which in turn allowed for the simultaneous training of models for related tasks, ultimately resulting in an improved model. This code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexandresu/Multitask-MNLI. Our team's results and the presented analysis offer valuable insights for future research in related areas. It was also discovered that hate speech identification is a more challenging task compared to derogatory language identification, which in turn is more difficult to detect in comparison to task two. Ultimately, our approach allows for enhanced model performance through transfer learning. A subsequent investigation of the presented models' robustness against adversarial perturbations was also conducted

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by combining multiple base models. However, they often waste computational resources on unproductive collaborations between models and struggle to coordinate their actions. This issue is addressed by developing novel methods for MIMO models that facilitate interaction and sharing of features among components. The proposed strategies aim to optimize model efficiency and coordination. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these techniques, with the top-performing methods surpassing traditional ensemble approaches in accuracy while also reducing inference time. Notably, our innovations can be seamlessly integrated into existing top-tier MIMO frameworks, enhancing their performance and efficiency in both image classification and cognitive rehabilitation games tasks. Furthermore, this code can be utilized to support research in the field of multi-agent deep learning without requiring prior knowledge of this topic. As such, our work aims to promote future research into efficient feature sharing in MIMO architectures. The associated image processing demonstration can be found at https://milo-demo-guichalup.github.io. The simplified version of our MIMO model, dubbed Efficient MIMO (EFMIMO), has been developed for the purpose of promoting simplification in deep learning models. For this purpose, a novel dynamic model is introduced that accurately describes a flexible robotic joint as a second-order system with a time delay. In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. This problem is known to be NP-hard, even when parameter k is used. Over the years, researchers have proposed and studied various fixed-parameter tractable algorithms for this problem, often employing specific structural parameters as an alternative for measuring the set's size. Recently, two new structural parameters have been introduced - the feedback vertex number and the color number - both of which can be calculated within linear time. We investigate the feasibility of parameterized algorithms for solving Metric Dimension using these parameters. Our results show that Metric Dimension is solvable in 2^{O(k^w log(k^w))} time, where k is the feedback vertex number, while k or the color number can serve as the parameter. Furthermore, the algorithm runs in 2^{O(t^w)} time, where t is the number of vertices on the longest path in a 2-vertex elimination order for the input graph. This approach demonstrates the efficacy of the parameter k by showing that Metric Dimension is gurobi-affordable for any instance, meaning it can be solved within the limit of two to the power of 69.78, for the specific parameter k. We also extend this result to the case where the input graph allows for an O(t) vertex feedback vertex set. This more general case is solved in 2^{O(f(k) log(k))} time, where f(k) is the size of the set. Using the same technique, we also show that certain problems related to resolving sets, such as the problem of determining whether a resolving set exists, are under the same time complexity as Metric Dimension. However, the problem of generating all resolving sets is found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the set's size. Nevertheless, the problem is solvable in (k + 2)^{O(k)} time, which confirms a conjecture made by Cazals and Vogt. Finally, our results are extended to the case of open dimension sets by using an analogous parameterization scheme. Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates could be distinguished by a unique process where atmospheric water vapor is transferred to cloud droplets via nucleation, leading to potential disruptions in the climate system. To better understand 'hothouse' climates, researchers simulated these environments using a global climate model, focusing on the resulting climate patterns and water cycle responses. In model simulations, a stable 'hothouse' atmosphere was created by adjusting the solar radiation input, achieving a similar low atmospheric temperature structure as in past and future 'hothouse' climates. Results showed that in these stable environments with increased moisture, large-scale cloud formations occurred, but the nucleation process actually increased rather than decreased atmospheric moisture in the low layers. However, when the nucleation process was disabled in the model, significant episodic flooding occurred due to increased precipitation, suggesting a crucial role for this process in shaping 'hothouse' climate environments and water cycle responses. In disabled nucleation scenarios, increased low-layer moisture led to increased depth of cloud-water systems, resulting in increased precipitation and contrasts in spatial distribution. Furthermore, in these nucleation-disabled simulations, episodes of excessive low-layer moisture and increased precipitation occurred more frequently due to increased intensity of tropical clouds, leading to increased spatial precipitation contrasts. In turn, increased precipitation led to increased spatial contrasts in available surface water and increased possibilities for erosion and sediment deposition, implying that the nucleation process has a crucial role in shaping 'hothouse' climate environments and water cycle responses. Ultimately, disabled nucleation scenarios led to increased deposition in the model, suggesting that the nucleation process influences not only surface water distribution but also global geological processes. In summary, the nucleation process has a significant impact on the formation, behavior, and resulting climate patterns and water cycle responses of 'hothouse' climates. By enabling or disabling this process, the contrast in spatial distribution of cloud-water systems, precipitation, and low-layer temperature is significantly influenced. Consequently, the nucleation process has a substantial role in shaping 'hothouse' climate environments and water cycle responses. By understanding this process and these resulting climate patterns and water cycle responses, the formation of 'hothouse' climates and potential future climate states can be better predicted and understood. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin Yang-Mills theory, an expansion of Yang-Mills theory itself. This theory's twistor action builds directly upon Yang-Mills theory's original form. Interestingly, this development echoes how the twistor action for emergent chiral fermions in the BF framework results in a theory describing both photons and neutrinos in their respective massless states. Like the original Yang-Mills theory, the higher-spin theory's flat space action arises from a non-local version of its twistor counterpart. Consequently, this suggests that higher-spin Yang-Mills theory's tree-level S-matrix also takes on a simple, multiparticle-form based on helicity conservation. In the case of chiral fermions, this result provides an alternate explanation for their conformal invariance, as the fermonic action reduces to the conformal wave equation after a specific redefinition. Conversely, for self-dual photons, this result reiterates the established link between the twistor action for photons and the conformal wave equation. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced capability in handling intricate visual data. Despite this progress, current deep learning-based methods for medical image classification remain vulnerable to errors caused by noisy labels. To address this limitation, existing studies typically rely on empirical rules or statistical analyses to correct noisy labels, which can be ineffective or fail altogether. In response to this issue, our research proposes a new method that harnesses Bayesian statistical principles to accurately identify and correct noisy labels within medical image datasets. Specifically, our system integrates intermediate features and predicted class probabilities from pre-trained CNNs to estimate the reliability of class labels. By combining these sources of information, our method develops a decision-making framework for label correction, which significantly enhances the accuracy of medical image classification. Experimental results confirm that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming other noise-correction techniques by a considerable margin. To support our findings, accompanying our work is a publicly available code repository. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new method of defining non-terminating functions with minimal impact on the function's definition and accompanying theoretical proofs. Unlike other clock additions, our approach enables the use of higher-order functions for reasoning about functions that can recurse indefinitely. Unlike a commonly used logics for reasoning about unbounded recursion in domain theory, our method is implemented in a logic with a finite universe and yields a practical implementation with efficient termination. An efficient implementation is obtained by reusing a logic's optimised decision making mechanism for reasoning about types in order to set a suitable depth for reasoning about values in the universe. We demonstrate that our approach is effective for a range of non-terminating functions as well as simpler functions with partial information. We further show that our approach is compatible with a logic's decision making mechanism and set suitable depths for reasoning about functions that can recurse indefinitely. Finally, we show that our approach is not a limitation of the logic in which it's implemented but rather compatible with a logic implemented within a related logic with a different structure. In particular, we show that our approach is compatible with a logic implemented in an logic with a different structure. Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solid-state systems.  Nucleation and growth of crystals via diffusion-controlled processes are key areas where screening affects kinetics, producing supersaturated conditions.  Theoretical models often fail to accurately predict the kinetics of crystal formation, but an alternative "anomalous screening" model has been proposed to explain the observed time and concentration dependencies.  Here, we experimentally investigate the kinetics of potassium chloride crystal formation in a colloidal monolayer covering a granular substrate.  The study provides conclusive evidence that anomalous screening occurs in granular matter, a system where mechanical contact is the primary mode of interaction.  By approximating the kinetic parameter's distribution using a Gaussian and using the proposed time scale for anomalous screening, we have developed a numerical model that effectively predicts kinetics in mechanical screening systems.  The developed model is not limited to granular systems and can be applied to a range of screening mechanisms, including those governed by dissipation and contact.  The numerical model is expected to be generally applicable to a wide range of solid-state systems featuring mechanical screening. Maps of the Milky Way's star field also show that a supernova from a runaway star from the Arches cluster could have had a large relative velocity, around 200 kilometers per second, resulting in a type Ica supernova that would have had little impact on the surrounding cloud. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 230,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Finally, our results show consistent connections between COVID coverage and regional case and death rates throughout the pandemic's duration. The study's findings support prior research highlighting the disparities in news coverage between different regions and populations, and our data provides quantitative evidence of the correlations between COVID coverage, case and death rates, and characteristics of local news outlets and their audiences. The study also demonstrates the effectiveness of the local news infrastructure in informing local communities, and highlights that under-resourced populations relied solely on underinvestigated local news sources during the pandemic, exacerbating existing information disparities and potentially hindering pandemic control. The study's findings were shared with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to inform public health strategies targeting low-income and minority populations who were disproportionately affected by the pandemic. The study's conclusions emphasize the critical role of local news outlets and and their audiences in the U.S. pandemic response and recovery process. The study's results were shared with the local news industry to aid them in better serving their audiences in the future. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when integrated with a point-wise interaction. However, when a far-field approximation, exemplified by the fast multipole method, is employed, conservation issues often arise, primarily with mass and kinetic energy. The angular momentum conservation problem has received little attention and has been predominantly overlooked in the literature. This study investigates the angular momentum conservation failure and introduces an advanced far-field rotation matrix in the fast multipole method to address this issue. By modifying the rotation matrix, which combines the classical Zaretskii-Kong algorithm and a high-order far-field rotation matrix from literature - both common FM algorithms - leads to a perfect conservation of angular momentum. Our proposed method has a time complexity of O(N), maintaining consistency with the basic Zaretskii-Kong algorithm while ensuring far-field accuracy, as demonstrated in our numerical tests with a mesh size of 100x100 particles. Additionally, when conservation is achieved for kinetic energy it automatically ensures the conservation of angular momentum as well. This research contributes a reliable FM algorithm to the community which conserves angular momentum. As a result, our method has a wide range of applications including publications, which typically fail to address this problem without even noticing it. Furthermore, our code is also publicly available for other researchers and engineers to use. The combination of this algorithm with a mass conserving algorithm, which we also have, allows for highly accurate simulations in multiple domains of fluid dynamics. The accuracy of mass and energy conservation demonstrated in our numerical tests shows that these conservation issues are not insurmountable.
