In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various forms of observation limitations and external restrictions. This study focuses on two key issues related to limited information: one involves learning an action policy based on a teacher's demonstrated optimal behavior when observations are incomplete, and the other entails determining a strategy that fulfills a teacher's specifications when observations are imperfect. We use information-theoretic constraints to model these scenarios of limited information. By introducing two new constraints for observation uncertainty, we transform the associated RL problems into two new optimization tasks with these constraints. We then use two novel algorithms to tackle these optimization tasks efficiently, assessing their effectiveness in two distinct scenarios. This study presents the first attempts to address RL problems through information-theoretic constraints, providing new avenues for exploration. We evaluate the performance of these algorithms in two settings where observation uncertainty is high, and compare their results with existing state-of-the-art methods. The study further examines the practical applications of these algorithms in a real-world robot. This work is available on GitHub as an open-source contribution. We conduct a thorough analysis of the computational requirements for these algorithms, evaluating their time complexity and optimization efficiency. We demonstrate that these algorithms have polynomial time complexity and can achieve optimization efficiency with constant values. We confirm the effectiveness of these algorithms through a comprehensive set of numerical experiments. We observe that these algorithms achieve high reward values in two settings, and the optimization process reaches stability in both scenarios. We analyze the effects of varying the Discard fraction in setting one and verify that the algorithm generalizes to different policy spaces. Similarly, we assess the effects of varying the action blurring parameter in setting two and confirm that the algorithm generalizes to different reward functions. We perform a sensitivity analysis of the algorithms' hyperparameters through a systematic method, utilizing a limited number of trials. We conduct a fair comparison of the algorithms' performance by evaluating the differences in the optimization process and final results. One key insight from this study concerns the trade-offs between policy space, observation quality, and reward values, and we illustrate this relationship with a conceptual diagram. We further investigate the computational requirements for each algorithm, assessing their time complexity and optimization efficiency. We validate the effectiveness of these algorithms through a series of numerical experiments and real-world robot trials. In addition to these contributions, we conduct a thorough review of existing open-source implementations for each algorithm, evaluating their performance in two settings and providing valuable feedback for future improvements. This study culminates with a set of questions and challenges that remain unresolved, and we encourage future researchers to tackle these challenges.

The advent of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) has seen an increase in research focus on solving complex partial differential equations (PDEs) and ordinary differential equations (ODEs) more efficiently. These networks combine the capabilities of neural networks with the solution to differential equations, and have shown promising results particularly for data-driven applications lacking explicit physical analysis. Despite the simplified mathematical concept, these networks have proven challenging to analyze both from a computational and mathematical standpoint, with little thorough theoretical study to date. This dissertation aims to fill this gap by proposing an approximate error estimation method for the learning process involved in PINNs, using a combination of tight upper and lower bounds on the learning loss (defined as the mean squared $L_2$-error between predicted and actual outputs). This method, which relies on an unmodified PINN implementation, allows for error estimation without altering the underlining algorithm. To test the efficacy of this method, a range of basic mathematical problems were employed, as well as a few more realistic, physics-based scenarios (such as a Navier-Stokes problem involving 2 flow bodies around a sphere and a wave equation model with various boundary conditions). These tests showed that the proposed method can accurately estimate PINN learning performance, even under stressful data conditions. Furthermore, our research revealed that the proposed method can facilitate seamless learning from interdependent PINNs (where one network is trained using data from another network as training labels), as long as the interdependent training is accounted for within the error bounds. Ultimately, these results illustrate the potential for an initial formal validation of the PINN learning process and highlight the possibility of combining PINNs with rigorous error estimation, thereby enabling more confident applications of neural networks in physical systems. As a final note, this method can likely be extended to other neural networks not involving physics-based components. An implementation of the proposed method can be found at https://github.com/genie-ai/a-posteriori-pinns. This bound holds for a wide class of action sets defined by their consistent estimation properties and applies to various submodels, including linear regression and log-linear models. Additionally, we have shown that the bound is invariant to the dimensionality of the parameter space, thus addressing a significant open question posed by (Chen et al., 2021). Furthermore, we have derived rate optimal, persistent regret bounds for first-order algorithms in the linear regression setting. Alongside this, we have explored the implications of our findings for the estimation of linear models, particularly in the context of misspecified linear regression and log-linear models. Our analysis provides new insights into the trade-off between exploration and exploitation under non-asymptotic conditions and reinforces the importance of meaningful action set definitions. Finally, we have highlighted an instance where the action set definition can be exploited further, specifically in the setting of misspecified log-linear models. Our results from the latter example reveal that the previously established lower bound is effectively tightened. A novel, first-order algorithm, titled the category elimination algorithm, has been introduced to achieve these optimal results and is shown to accomplish two key tasks: the efficient estimation of high-dimensional parameters of log-linear models with limited observations and the discovery of the underlying discrete distribution of a target variable, given prior knowledge of a key function. Building on our earlier analysis, we have extended the applicability of the lower bound in a comparative analysis of the algorithm's performance in the setting of misspecified linear regression. Our results reveal that the algorithm's rate-optimal status extends to this context as well. Finally, we have made a contribution to the theory of misspecified linear regression by establishing a new, non-asymptotic lower bound on the rate-optimal regret bound. This result not only offers a novel perspective on the trade-off between exploration and exploitation but also provides an enduring benchmark for future research, especially in the setting of misspecified linear regression. The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within the data science field led to the development of general techniques for graph attacks a few years ago. However, the area remains largely unexplored, with the community only recently presenting graph-specific attacks unique to Deep Learning. Historically, research focused on improving Robust Training Methods and exploring the bounds of model robustness. This trend continues with the increasing popularity of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Research on graph-based adversarial attacks has also increased, with the 2018 publication of the first GNN attack paper. This work extends reinforcement learning-based attacks on neural networks to GNNs by examining data poisoning attacks on binary classification tasks within multi-class graph datasets. Our research with reinforcement learning shows that it's possible to achieve an attack success rate of 73% under strict constraints, with the constraint being that the attacker only modifies 10% of the graph. This constraint is due to the requirement that the attacker knows the target label only for the selected nodes. When the constraint is removed, the success rate of the attack reaches 100%. This success rate is higher than previous graph data poisoning attacks which had a success rate of about 40%. Also, the constraint has no effect on the required attack time because in both the constrained and the unconstrained versions of the algorithm we use trial and error to choose the attacked node. However, the required quality of the generated attack that drives the trial and error process is different for the two versions of the algorithm. Under the constrained version of the algorithm we require the attacked node to change the label of its neighbors from 50% to 100%. While, under the unconstrained version of the algorithm we require the attacked node to change the label of its neighbors from 50% to 100% and also the label of the attacked node itself. This difference in the required quality of the generated attack is the reason for the big difference in the success rate of the two versions of the algorithm. Finally, the research with reinforcement learning on GNNs opens the road for exploring other types of graph attacks such as the attack that is based on the change of the graph structure. This kind of attack is not included in the research because it was not requested by the community. However, the research community is expected to be interested in this type of attack in the future. With the research on other types of graph attacks, the community opened the road for the development of graph adversarial machine learning and the growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within the data science field.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve accuracy. A method developed for this purpose uses a novel hybrid distance transformation that leverages both angular separation and photometric consistency between matched objects. This approach demonstrates high accuracy, with the ability to correctly match objects of a full catalog with those of a reference catalog in under a few seconds on standard hardware. Additionally, the method can easily be adapted for use on large scales by distributing the calculations across a cluster of nodes. The method's performance is demonstrated through both simulations and real-world data, where it successfully matches components of the Multi-Object Spectrographic Intergalactic Redshift Expedition (MOXE) catalog with those of the Gaia Data Release 2 catalog. This matching allows for an in-depth analysis of the photometric redshifts of MOXE sources and their relationship with their extragalactic neighbor populations. In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the family of its edges, and a hypergraph is said to possess property C(k, ρ) if the intersection of any two sets of at most k hyperedges covers at most ρ vertices. A vertex cover of a hypergraph is a subset of vertices that intersects with every hyperedge, and the smallest such cover is referred to as a minimal vertex cover. It is proven that for k greater than or equal to 2 and ρ greater than or equal to k - 1, there exists an infinite hypergraph whose vertices and edges are subsets of a finite set, and which has the property C(k, ρ) but does not have a minimal vertex cover that has size less than or equal to ρ. Additionally, for k equal to 2, the infinity of such hypergraphs exists as long as ρ is greater than or equal to 2, and an example of such hypergraphs exists for the cases when ρ is greater than or equal to 3 and k greater than or equal to 3. However, an infinite hypergraph with the property C(k, ρ) but without a minimal vertex cover that has size less than or equal to ρ can be constructed using a Ramsey graph if the following conditions are met: k is greater than or equal to 3, ρ is greater than or equal to 2, and k is equal to ρ. Furthermore, an infinite hypergraph with the property C(k, ρ) but without a minimal vertex cover that has size less than or equal to ρ can be constructed using Hilbert's irreducible polynomials if the following conditions are met: k is greater than or equal to 3, ρ is greater than or equal to 3, and k is equal to ρ. However, an infinite hypergraph with the property C(k, ρ) but without a minimal vertex cover that has size less than or equal to ρ and whose edges and vertices are subsets of a finite set cannot be constructed using Hilbert's irreducible polynomials. Finally, an infinite hypergraph with the property C(k, ρ) but without a minimal vertex cover that has size less than or equal to ρ and whose vertices and edges are subsets of a finite set can be constructed if the following conditions are met: k is equal to 4, ρ is equal to 3, and it does not contain a bipartite graph with the property V(2, 2).

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when analyzing large, complex ontologies, enabling researchers to identify patterns and hierarchies. However, existing visual tools primarily focus on hierarchical structures and overlook non-hierarchical associations, leading to inadequate understanding and visualisation of ontology content. To address this limitation, we have developed OntoPlot, a novel visualisation interface that seamlessly integrates all ontology relationships, facilitating the identification and committal to memory of both hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections. OntoPlot's design features a dual-level representation, showcasing hierarchical structures within circular sections and non-hierarchical associations within radial sections. We have evaluated OntoPlot's effectiveness through a user study involving domain experts, demonstrating its enhanced performance over traditional visual tools, especially in visualising and understanding non-hierarchical associations within large ontologies. Furthermore, we have highlighted OntoPlot's potential applications and extensions in research and knowledge discovery projects. The tool, along with associated user guidelines and comprehensive example use cases, is freely available online for further exploration. The research has been conducted with experts in the Brucellosis field, a disease primarily prevalent in rural communities with limited access to healthcare, offering a relevant practical example of discovering and visualising non-hierarchical associations within large ontologies. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN for an end-to-end automatic speech recognition system trained with a mixture of labeled and unlabeled data. Inter-domain loss aids the model in mitigating domain disparities through matched input and output representations, whereas CycleGAN employs different cycles of vision and audio representations to eliminate domain-specific distortions. Our approach is particularly effective because it leverages a model that is already optimized for speech recognition without necessitating any modifications to the model's architecture. We evaluated our method through several experiments using the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech corpora and observed notable improvements across various setups, with gains of up to 6.8% and 5.2% observed in 50x and 20x labeled training data setups on the LibriSpeech corpus. Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to demonstrate the independent contributions of inter-domain loss and CycleGAN in enhancing model performance. Notably, this method is the first to utilize an end-to-end model with the Voxforge and LibriSpeech datasets, and our code is available for download on the PyTorch Waveform Repository.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views behavior as an energetic process aimed at minimizing uncertainty, which can be optimized through Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This study uses the active inference framework to develop a model for autonomous navigation in robot systems, allowing them to be effectively guided directly from the surrounding visual information. Building upon this framework, a novel algorithm has been created that translates image uncertainties into controlled motor actions, thereby guiding the robot's navigation. To evaluate the approach, a novel dataset has been created featuring unknown visually-assisted navigation tasks. From this data, a new robot navigation model has been trained through the optimization of variational free energy, outperforming established state-of-the-art methods on the same tasks. Further analysis has revealed that the model exhibits human-like strategies in navigating between goals, including using contextual information and adapting to the dynamic characteristics of the navigation tasks. This research marks a significant development in the application of active inference to autonomous robot navigation, offering a biologically-rooted groundings for future research. The model's performance in navigating between goals is shown in the video supplied. A related software library for implementing active inference has been developed, available at https://github.com/danielltew.py/active_inference. This repository also serves as the primary source for the code and data used in this study, including the novel active inference navigation model presented here. A pre-trained version of the model can be found via https://www.youtube.com/watch. For additional context and information regarding the study, including access to the model's source code and the dataset of unknown visually-assisted navigation tasks, please visit https://www.dropbox.com/RC2Q7A0n0AA0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA0n0AA. Furthermore, a detailed, step-by-step guide for implementing the active inference framework has been developed, available at https://active-inference.gitub.com/formal-framework/active-inference.gitub. Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions. These mechanisms may also help explain observations of Soret effect research, such as how adding flexible molecules to a mixture can reverse its thermal diffusion behavior. Furthermore, we discovered that rigid versions of flexible molecules exhibit behavior similar to that of their softer counterparts, which suggests that the internal freedom of flexible molecules is a crucial factor contributing to the Soret effect. However, when the mixture contains low-stressfulness, this internal freedom has less of an impact, and the mixture's overall density differences dominate the thermal diffusion behavior, causing the Soret effect to be less apparent, which could also account for certain experimental observations that rigid molecules of similar shape to their flexible counterparts exhibit behavior more similar to pure components. These findings align with theoretical predictions from mode decomposition of thermal diffusion phenomena. In addition to the above research, we also found that the effective Stokes-Einstein when the mixture consists of any two different substances, which helps relax stress due to thermal diffusion and is a crucial factor contributing to the Soret effect, also shows similar behavior. This further supports the understanding that the internal freedom of flexible molecules is a key factor contributing to the Soret effect, and the relevant research has significant implications for the understanding of relaxation processes in mixture fluids. Future work will investigate the influence of various molecular structures on thermal diffusion and be beneficial for the advancement of understanding thermal diffusion and molecular interactions. Additionally, the relevant research has also revealed the possibility of creating thermally driven Marangoni effect in system with liquid and solid components that are not mixed evenly. Furthermore, the finding that the Soret effect in mixture fluids is closely related to the characteristics of individual molecules has also aligned perfectly with the predictions made in theoretical studies, which helps to further the understanding of thermal diffusion and molecular interactions. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model relies on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in the presence of errors and irregular writing styles. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, their compatibility with Automated Essay Scoring has been largely untested. This study demonstrates the potential of utilizing large transformer models for AES purposes. Our findings showcase the performance of three different models - BERT, ALBERT, and Longformer - in achieving an overall evaluation accuracy of 0.71 using an enhanced BERT model, and 0.70 and 0.69 for the ALBERT and Longformer variants respectively. These results suggest a high potential for using large transformer models as a reliable solution for Automated Essay Scoring. Moreover, a dual-purpose model design allows the developed model to effectively process both short and lengthy essays, making it an invaluable tool for educational institutions and researchers in the field. Our code has been made available for peer review on GitHub at https://github.com/muhammadoucchra-alihareed/AES-Transformer. Additionally, this source contains the code used for data processing, model training, and evaluation - all built using the Open-source Transformers library developed by Facebook. Lastly, a comprehensive analysis of our model's performance in comparison to existing state-of-the-art AES models, and an examination of its ability to process essays of varying lengths despite the presence of capacity limitations, are also explored in this research paper. The research further highlights the importance of (1) a more comprehensive assessment framework for evaluating the performance of NLP models, and (2) an enhanced understanding of the implications of using large-sized NLP models on the limitations of device memory available. The research is now part of an ongoing effort aimed at developing a unified open-source model capable of accurately scoring essays across the spectrum of possible lengths, and at reducing the energy consumption associated with the model's memory requirements on device. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain adaptation in pedestrian detection is the presence of false positives dominating detection boxes. This problem stems from newly encountered domains having a higher ratio of non-target to target boxes. This requires suppressing false positives without affecting true positives, an accurate matching between target boxes and proposal boxes being essential to achieve this. Normally, proposal box targeting modules operate within an static framework. However, a new self-supervised approach has been developed to dynamically remove false positives from this framework. This approach, known as Box Re-Ranking, utilizes enriched multi-scale feature interactions to perform self-supervised learning. As a result, Box Re-Ranking is capable of reaching state-of-the-art performance across various adaptive pedestrian detection methods, including Cascade-RPN and CRAFT. Furthermore, Box Re-Ranking is capable of performing self-supervised false positive elimination across multiple domains, resulting in performance comparable to fine-tuning on a targeted domain with a significant reduction in false positives. Analysis of the approach has revealed that false positives are predominantly eliminated at the box proposal stage. While the target box matching module is also affected, its performance is less sensitive to changes in the matching task. Consequently, Box Re-Ranking is suitable for a wide range of domain adaptation pedestrian detection scenarios. Like other domain adaptation approaches, Box Re-R-Ranking is capable of performing unsupervised domain adaptation. Moreover, Box Re-Ranking is capable of functioning in both online and offline settings. Following Box Re-R-Ranking, target box labeling can occur either through annotation or through self-supervised learning. This means that Box Re-R-Ranking is compatible with both weak and strong unsupervised learning methods. Consequently, Box Re-R-Ranking is capable of facilitating a range of unsupervised learning approaches, extending domain adaptation and weak supervision applications. This suggests a wide range of potential applications for the technique in the future. Analysis of the approach has also resulted in the discovery of two inherent biases within Box Re-R-Ranking. Firstly, Box Re-R-Ranking is sensitive to the presence of boundary false positives, resulting in these positives being incorrectly eliminated. This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions that render the audio unusable. A novel approach is taken by first developing a technique to translate or remake the musical structure in an image format, drawing on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) technology. The resulting musical information is then converted into an audio format via a process called vocoding, which is based on Linear Discriminative Analysis (LDA). This method is distinguished from other correction methods relying on manual adjustment, offering a full automation of the improvement process. When evaluated against standard methods for improving audio quality in a competitive context, it was found that not only does it produce more natural-sounding results but also preserves the audio's original spiritual essence more effectively. An accompanying audio demonstration can be accessed at the provided website. Additionally, a related patent has been filed.

Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants have a greater propensity to identify errors with a late point of release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's field of view and the trajectory of the ball influence the perception of release timing. These findings align with prior research and offer novel insights for the creation of realistic throwing animations. Based on the results of our study, we have developed a set of heuristics for overarm and underarm throwing motions, which can be used by artists to refine their animations and make them more realistic. Our animation guide is tailored towards the needs of professional animators but may also be applicable to real-time applications like virtual reality simulations and game development. Our paper is accompanied by an animation showcase of underarm and overarm throws with varying points of release, which were created in accordance with our heuristics. These animations can serve as reference materials for the creation of realistic throwing motions in the respective domains. Lastly, we propose two algorithms, Baumgarte Integrator and Euler Integrator, for the simulation of ball behaviors that are easily implementable in the existing work of animation researchers and practitioners. These algorithms were in fact used by researchers to generate the ball motions in our study. A thorough examination of the strengths and weaknesses of these algorithms in the context of our study has further highlighted the necessity of accurate virtual physics in the simulation of realistic throwing motions. Ultimately, our research has has helped to clarify that advanced simulation of physical behaviors is essential for the creation of realistic animations, even in cases where the accuracy of simulation is challenging to evaluate. In this work, we combine the capabilities of neural machine translation and parsing by proposing a unified model that can translate and parse sentences simultaneously in a synergistic manner. Based on an abstract syntax tree representation, our model starts from a root node and iteratively selects child nodes to generate sentence translations that are guided by parsing decisions. To facilitate decoding, we introduce a new top-down tree structured translation approach with a reparameterized variational objective to balance accuracy and completeness. Furthermore, we present a novel method to incorporate syntactic sentence structures into translation by preserving the linear ordering of syntactic children. Experimental results on English-Chinese and English-Japanese translation tasks demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, yielding an average improvement in BLEU score of 1.21 and 0.36, respectively, when compared to baseline models. Additionally, our model outperforms lattice-based baselines in sentence-level average precision by a significant margin, serving as a robust parser in a translation setting. Moreover, we provide detailed parsing examples and engage with the community through a dedicated webpage. A new parser based on this work has been successfully applied in a state-of-the-art machine translation system for 20 languages, where it significantly improves the results. The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values, which measure the strength of molecular associations. Although vast databases of binding energies exist, most rely on outdated, average values that no longer reflect current understanding. Furthermore, many recent high-precision bindings energies remain unaccounted for. To address this, we've launched the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform, a comprehensive database containing microstate-specific binding energies derived using quantum chemistry. BeEP includes a database of more than 22,000 unique binding sites involving 20 different molecules such as water and ammonia, providing detailed information that can be used to refine astrochemical simulations. By comparing our results to experimental data and other quantum chemistry studies, we've observed a level of agreement, with the majority of cases converging with experimental data. With a range of statistical mechanics models already implemented, BeEP aims to streamline the incorporation of precise binding energies into astrochemical simulations, promoting reproducibility and increasing our understanding of the complex interactions within interstellar clouds. By facilitating this workflow, we hope to improve interstellar gas chemistry models and gain insight into interstellar cloud dynamics. The platform can be accessed at beep.heig-vd.ch. Our primary strategy involves employing random Clifford circuits of moderate depth to create a measurable connection between the state and its representation of forward circuit effects. This relationship is captured through the calculation of a state's average expectation values after undergoing the forward effects of the circuit. Our protocol ensures that the state's characterisation is both precise and reliable, particularly in scenarios where the state is mixed in nature. We extend this strategy by adapting it to the challenging task of state discrimination where we aim to differentiate between two states. Our methods facilitate significant advancements in state discrimination performance, particularly for schemes initially suggested by Campbell et al. in 2019. Our techniques also provide statistical guarantees for accurate state identification. Our protocols, when applied to the complete set of Pauli matrices, result in optimal results among all possible shallow protocols, regardless of the circuit depth. Our methods primarily utilize classical shadow techniques but adapt them to the complexities of quantum mechanics. Our work contributes to quantum learning, and our findings have the potential to be applied in quantum speedup protocols. Our methods for estimating state expectations, maintaining reliability through shallow protocols, may also be applied in diverse fields of quantum research. Our work offers new perspectives on the application of shadow techniques in quantum learning and may lead to similar innovations in other areas of quantum studies. To address this challenge, we've developed a concept of text transformation variability by suggesting a method to produce a class-dependent set of robust transformations. Our proposed approach involves creating a set of base transformations, determining the sensitivity of each class to these transformations, and applying the sensitivity-driven transformation rule to generate new, class-dependent variations of original texts. This mechanism can enhance the variability of text transformations,-enabling the utilization of advanced neural network variants, such as self-ensemble networks and adversarial ensemble methods. By producing a multitude of texts, each corresponding to a specific class, we can strengthen the confidence of text classification models, increase the difficulty of adversarial attacks, and enhance the overall flexibility of text representation learning. By leveraging text transformations, SIFT-RSC aims to train resilient text representations that are resistant to adversarial perturbations and maintain their effectiveness even when used in classification tasks on unseen classes. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method for developing high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it's discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily relies on several preconditions, making it a somewhat unreliable method for model compression. To improve on this, we explore post-training quantization as a means to compress these models. Ultimately, while distillation was found effective in translating single utterances with limited data, it's at a lower efficiency rate compared to quantization when dealing with entire MT datasets. This presents quantization as a more reliable compression method, especially for large-scale languages. Inspired by its potential, we directly applied quantization to the teacher model, resulting in significant size reductions from a 7.32-fold to 12.65 reduction, yielding minimal performance degradation and ultimately producing a model that is as efficient as a small supervised MT model. This state enables simultaneous translation and generates training data efficient enough to train a small model with a small dataset, effectively closing the resource gap between large supply languages and low-resource languages in the process. This leads to the creation of training data for the Hungarian-Serbian MT task via cross-lingual pretraining, resulting in notable improvements over the previous best results. Finally, the newly developed small model is then used in various post-processing techniques such as reordering to achieve highly improved results, surpassing the previous best results with notable improvements. An analysis of the techniques and techniques and an examination of the techniques and results are presented. This leads to the attainment of state-of-the-art performance, outperforming previous models and settings. The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show that the Lagrangian density of a specific 3-uniform graph is sqrt(3)/3, resulting in an irrational Turan density, which answers an open question posed by Baber and Talbot. Our method involves constructing a family of 3-uniform graphs with an alternating sum of edges converging to sqrt(3)/3. We also show that edges in three of our graphs with an sqrt(3)/3 density have a common property: for large n, the number of these edges in any n-vertex graph is always even. In the process, we correct an error and provide a proof that edges in three of our graphs with an sqrt(3)/3 density have a common property: for large n, the number of these edges in any n-vertex graph is always even. The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training fully convolutional neural network models on subsets of various sizes from a total dataset, each model undergoes a different image enhancement, and its resulting performance is evaluated using the area under the curves on the remaining models. Ultimately, we discovered that using rotate image enhancement results in a notable improvement in validation AUC, and slightly improved AUC at test time compared to using original images. While not leading to a statistically significant enhancement at test time, we also examined combined rotate and resize image enhancement, which shows promising potential for further investigation in future work. When applying the trained models to test data, and employing a confidence-based post-processing step, the results indicate that image enhancement leads to a slightly improved AUC of 0.8612 compared to the original data. Furthermore, we found that using a ensembling of the original and enhanced models leads to a notable improvement in performance, with AUC rising to 0.8661 after validation and 0.8668 after test. Consequently, the main contribution of this research is the confirmation that using image enhancement techniques can lead to a notable improvement in performance, and also potentially lower the required labelled data for training semantic segmentation models in the detection of pneumonia from X-ray images. This paper investigates whether prompts can be used to control the style of image captioning models, particularly in the context of value-oriented objectives such as increasing the fluency and coherence of the captions. We begin by developing a range of prompts that aim to improve the fluency and coherence of the captions, and subsequently, based on our findings, we construct a single prompt that can effectively lower the average length of the captions. This length-reducing prompt is further combined with an autoencoding loss to facilitate the transfer of styles between various image captioning models, and remarkably, the results indicate that the lengths of the captions can be reduced by more than they originally produced, and the quality of the captions is maintained. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems. The definition's value lies in qualitative harm assessment, helpful in system design, evaluation, and addressing social concerns, as well as serving as a foundation for developing safety standards for autonomous systems. The qualitative definition of qualitative harm facilitates more nuanced discussions of qualitative aspects of harm, leading to a better understanding of system behavior and allowing users to tailor explanations and causes of harm to their needs, whereas contrastive causality generally enhances causal explanations in general. The analysis also explores qualifications for qualifying harm, such as negligence and intent, shedding light on their implications for system safety. The analysis demonstrates that intent, in contrast to negligence, is expected to correlate with system utility, while consideration of negligence is expected to minimize contrastive utility, leading to safety improvements. The resulting theory of qualitative harm and its applications can serve as a model for more precise definitions of qualitative concepts in general. The work's limitations are acknowledged, particularly its focus on actual harm caused by preferred actions, leading to potential extensions of the definition to other concepts like inductive risk. The definition of qualitative harm, focused on actual harm and contrastive actions, is expected to be useful in system design, evaluation, and safety standards for autonomous systems, serving as a foundation for discussions of qualitative aspects of harm and causal model applications in autonomous systems. The analysis also extends to qualifications for qualifying harm, specifically intent and negligence, revealing system-level correlations with these concepts, particularly intent being correlated with system utility and negligence leading to minimal contrastive utility. This relationship holds for autonomous systems but not necessarily for human actions, highlighting a beneficial effect of intent in these systems, a property not likely to be adopted in human-interactive policies, which tend to penalize intentional actions. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a balance of change without the dissipation limitation. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain. Consequently, our analysis yields a broad class of equations, encompassing linear and nonlinear versions of the heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, as well as systems with memory retrograde flows, including their linear and nonlinear counterparts. Moreover, we establish that the interior and boundary equations, intertwined by means of the boundary condition, form a well-posed problem in a combined context of space and time with optimal regularity results. This work is a natural extension of prior research, including the standard situation with no memory and the linear situation with nonlinear boundary conditions. To tackle the problem of regularity, we develop a novel approach by proving the continuous dependence of solutions on the initial conditions within the initial value problem setting. Furthermore, our findings lead to the well-posedness of the problem defined by the free boundary value problem consisting of a system of equations, a dynamic boundary condition, and a boundary condition involving memory flows. This problem arises in the context of a variety of physical and biological processes. More specifically, our models can be applied to the description of physical processes characterized by heat transfer absorption on the surfaces of solids with memory, a topic also explored by Miller and Miller (2013). In addition, our work has implications for the study of cell culture processes, as discussed by Wisniewski and Laref (2019). Lastly, our results can be extended to the analysis of systems comprising one or more equations subject to multiple dynamic boundary conditions, thereby covering a wide range of theoretical and application-based models with memory. Consequently, our work contributes to the extension of the traditional heat conduction theory to systems with memory, characterized by fading memory in the interior of the domain and general memory on the boundary with dynamic boundary conditions. Moreover, our approach leads to optimal regularity results, thereby allowing for efficient numerical simulations with these types of processes. The research is a natural extension of prior studies, including the standard situation with no memory and the linear situation with nonlinear boundary conditions.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods frequently struggle to characterize these spikes adequately. This issue highlights the need for an alternative approach combining probabilistic forecasts with peak demand predictions, which can improve overall forecasting performance, particularly during peak hours and at lower network levels, where the incorporation of peak forecasts yields a significant improvement exceeding 10% CRPS. In contrast, the integration of peak forecasts demonstrates minimal utilization in medium-sized networks and those with fewer customers, indicating greater room for improvement in these areas. Consequently, a decision was made to apply peak forecasts universally to all network sizes, aiming to enhance the precision of short-term, high-agency LV network demand forecasts, ultimately contributing to the advancement of distribution system operations analysis. This was achieved by incorporating peak forecasts into the stochastic forecasting model, which has the additional advantage of increasing reliability in the management of daily peak demands throughout the forecasting horizon. Furthermore, the developed fusion model was compared to existing forecasting methods, including a multi-model combination analysis, revealing that the incorporation of peak forecasts leads to the most significant improvements in forecast accuracy among all considered approaches, specifically at the individual customer level where the incorporation of peak forecasts yields an average increase in accuracy of 43.6%. Additionally, a cost-benefit analysis of forecast fusion was conducted, which provides key insights into the optimal balance between the diversity of forecasts being combined and their similarity to the actual behavior. This has the potential to expand the application of forecast fusion techniques not only to demand forecasting but also to other forecasting domains, potentially leading to new areas of investigation. Moreover, the source code of the used R and Python environments, along with the associated dataset, is available for further use and is expected to contribute to the advancement of the field through its replication and continuation. However, certain pathological variations (e.g. vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging limitations (e.g. metallic implants, low resolution, and artifacts) make fully automated localization and identification challenging. Existing methods often rely on complex user input or necessitate extensive user intervention. In this study, a novel, autonomous pipeline for vertebrae localization and identification is presented. It involves three key components: (i) a vertebrae detection module that adapts to changing vertebral shapes; (ii) a spine rectification module which ensures vertebrae are consistently aligned in the coronal plane; and (iii) an anatomically-constrained optimization module, grounded in biomechanical principles, which efficiently and reliably adjusts intervertebral angles while optimizing vertebral body and endplate detection. A comprehensive dataset consisting of normal/spine pathology CT scans is used to validate the pipeline's effectiveness and robustness. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed pipeline surpasses existing competition in both localization and identification accuracy. Moreover, the pipeline is versatile, as its modules can be separately applied and combined with other existing techniques. The study provides essential insights into the pipeline's stability and reliability, particularly in the presence of common pathology and image issues. An expanded version of this research, including related code and pre-trained models for the vertebral column, is made available for reference. Additionally, a user-friendly, interactive module is included to facilitate the visualization and correction of potential errors. A related clinical study, which incorporates the proposed pipeline, is referenced for further analysis. The study's results highlight the significance of accurately localized and identified vertebrae in various spinal disorder diagnosis and surgical planning applications. Ultimately, the pipeline's effectiveness and robustness are demonstrated in the presence of diverse normal/spine pathology and imaging characteristics. The proposed pipeline's current limitations are also explored, including potential errors and inaccuracies resulting from vertebral compression fractures, vertebral fixation, and imaging artifacts. Based on these findings, suggestions for future research are proposed. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated through central pattern generators, whose parameters are fine-tuned to rapidly develop an open-loop controller for efficient walking. Following this, we implement reinforcement learning to enhance the controller's resilience and efficacy by introducing corrective actions in real-time, all based on the existing CPGs. Ultimately, we successfully apply this approach to the elastic quadruped Bert from the SPRING lab, achieving notable increases in power efficiency and step regularity. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random measurements. We also use numerical methods to determine the closest separable states for maximally entangled multipartite X-states. Our results indicate that NISQ devices may leverage the VSV's efficiency to tackle unsolved quantum problems related to entanglement detection and classification. Such applications could significantly enhance the performance of quantum-enhanced machine learning protocols, particularly those employing variational quantum algorithms. Our work also outlines a potential path for scaling the VSV on near-term quantum devices, starting with low-dimensional quantum systems like a two-qubit quantum computer. Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories in a way that's consistent with their underlying physics can be complicated. We utilize the formalism of double field theory to construct actions for gravity that incorporate oscillating and anisotropic behaviors typical of alternative gravity theories. By doing so, we identify the conditions necessary for these actions to meet the requirements of closure and well-definedness. We then investigate the resulting theory's implications on the energy density, coupling of the gravitational field, and properties of the gravitational potential, revealing novel and intriguing features. Our analysis demonstrates that the theory's energetic assumptions are less restrictive than those found in existing literature, while the theory's predictions for the non-Riemannian gravitational potential exhibit novel and intriguing characteristics. A key aspect of our work is the ability to introduce a time-dependent gravitational potential with constraints, opening up the possibility of exploring more general time-dependent modifications of the gravitational field. We conclude by examining the conditions of matter compatibility and investigating the equation of motion for a scalar field within the framework of the developed theory. Our results indicate that the theory's energetic and kinematic characteristics suggest the existence of a non-trivial de Sitter space with significant potential for exploring modified gravity behaviors at the quantum level. We have made our code available for public use. We anticipate that the theory of gravity developed in this work will facilitate a deeper understanding of the behavior of matter under strong non-Riemannian gravitational fields and may be applicable to the modeling of systems with non-relativistic symmetry, explorations of quantum gravity, and condensed matter systems.
